fix(cua-driver): focus the field under a macOS background pixel type_text in Firefox (#8092)

* test(cua-driver): pin when macOS focus holds a background pixel

A focused container whose rect encloses the point counted as the field
there holding focus, so a pixel type_text into a Firefox input skipped the
focus step and typed into the page document (#5384). The decision moves
into focus_holds_pixel with its current rule; the new tests fail on it.

* fix(cua-driver): focus the field under a macOS background pixel type_text in Firefox

The focus step now counts focus as held at the point only when the field
there has it: the focused element is the hit-tested element or inside it,
or is itself a text input, or the hit-tested element reports AXFocused.
Firefox's focused page document no longer stands in for the input, so the
focus click runs and the text reaches the input.

fix(cua-driver): do not retype a macOS web AX write as keys when AXValue lags (#8089)

* test(cua-driver): pin that an accepted macOS web AX write is not retyped as keys

Moves the choice that follows an AX write which did not read back into
after_unlanded_ax_write, unchanged, and adds a test for the behaviour
#5383 needs. It fails here: an unchanged read-back inside an AXWebArea
still falls through to key events.

* fix(cua-driver): do not retype a macOS web AX write as keys when AXValue lags

Firefox accepts an AXSelectedText write and applies it, but its AXValue
read-back still shows the old value right after the write. type_text
took that as a failed write and typed the same text again as key
events, so one call inserted it twice. An accepted write whose
read-back has not moved inside an AXWebArea now returns an unverified
ax result and sends no keys.

Fixes #5383

fix(cua-driver): wait for the menu a macOS menu-button press opens (#8103)

* test(cua-driver): cover a background press on a SwiftUI Menu

The SwiftUI fixture gains a Menu (AXMenuButton). The new E2E cell presses it
in the background and expects its items in the snapshot taken right after
the press, as #6082 reports they are not.

* fix(cua-driver): wait for the menu a macOS menu-button press opens

A background AXPress on an AXMenuButton or AXPopUpButton returns before the
app publishes the menu, so a snapshot taken right after the click has no
items. When no menu is beside the control before the press, poll its
children and siblings for an AXMenu with items for up to 1 s. Once it
appears the click reports effect confirmed; otherwise it says no menu
appeared. post_action_wait:"none" skips the wait.

Fixes #6082

* docs(cua-driver): regenerate the macOS click reference

* fix(cua-driver): bound each AX read of the macOS menu wait by its deadline

An app that stops answering after the press could hold a single read of
the scan for the walker's 2 s messaging timeout. Cap each read at 100 ms
and at what is left of the budget, stop the scan at the deadline, and
never sleep past it.

* fix(cua-driver): start no AX read after the menu wait's deadline

Recheck the budget after capping a node's messaging timeout, and stop
reading once a populated menu is found.

docs(managed-agent): correct identity budgets and record duplicate-key survey in de-hash design (#17960)

* docs(managed-agent): record duplicate business key survey in de-hash design and plan

Correct the workspace_id budget. Receipt-minted workspace ids are 74 characters
(workspace- plus a 64-hex receipt key) and storage ids 72/73, but the binding
limit is the public contract: external registrations and workspace selection
accept ids of up to 128 characters, so both columns need VARCHAR(128) unless the
contract is tightened. Dropping the id prefixes would not help, since they
discriminate receipt-minted ids and record created versus imported storage.
Record why no duplicate-key hash can be removed ahead of the VARCHAR conversion,
that receipt_key and key(tenant) mint public ids and filesystem paths, the
registered-Session restriction carried by the ma_session hash columns, the
missing raw columns on ma_read_lease, and the non-uniform operation_key
derivations. Both languages updated together.

* docs(managed-agent): decide the de-hash survey questions

Record three decisions in the design and plan, both languages:
- receipt_key stays as a minted identifier: it is the identity root of created
  and imported workspaces, and storage roots and workspace defaults resolve
  through it.
- workspace_id and storage_id keep their contracts (128 identifier characters,
  256 printable ASCII) and become VARBINARY(128) / VARBINARY(256), which keeps
  equality byte-exact and costs a quarter of the index width of utf8mb4 VARCHAR.
  This also corrects the storage_id limit to the 256-character contract.
- Tenant-addressed operations (SSH workspace creation, the WorkspaceOperations
  kinds, workspace uploads) keep their uniqueness through a generated
  tenant_operation_id column with a unique key, instead of relying on
  operation_key.

fix(managed-agent): hand the Hosted Harness client over under one lock (#17961)

The lazy client is published by client() and taken by close() under
clientLock, but generation adoption swapped it out under the connector
monitor. The two locks do not exclude each other, so an adoption and a
close could both take the same client and close it twice, and an
adoption did not wait for a renegotiation in progress as the handoff
documentation says it does. Adoption now takes clientLock for the same
check-and-take, and the documentation names the lock it actually uses.

A regression test holds clientLock and asserts that an adoption queues
behind it instead of closing the client underneath it.

feat(channels): bind the email ledger to its registration identity (#17925)

* feat(channels): bind the email ledger to its registration identity

The managed email ledger was keyed only by the configured mailbox, so a
claim staged under one control-plane registration was loaded and replayed
when the same mailbox restarted against another registration. Key the
ledger file by sha256(destinationKey) beneath the unchanged shared Legacy
mailbox lock: one owner per mailbox is preserved while pending claims are
isolated per registration.

Mirror the WeCom / DingTalk / GitHub shape: split load() into read / parse
/ validate arms that name the file and keep the cause, and report then
archive (never adopt) the stranded pre-upgrade managed-state.json once the
start succeeds. A fresh ledger starts at the current mailbox tip, so the
stranded claims' older UIDs are never re-fetched; the notice names inbound
and outbound loss separately and flags an unreadable legacy as unknown
rather than a quiescent empty ledger.

* fix(channels): close email keying review gaps (R1-1..R1-8)

Address the first review round on the email registration-identity keying:

- Name the skipped offline window even for a quiescent cursor-bearing
  legacy: strandedLegacyLedger returns the legacy lastUid, and the notice
  adds an independent clause (gated on a fresh window) so mail received
  after the legacy cursor while stopped is not reported as loss-free.
- Seed only the monotonic generation from a readable legacy so a mailbox
  that already re-keyed registers its prior generation instead of being
  refused channel_generation_stale on every start; guard it to a safe
  integer so a corrupt value cannot brick the fresh ledger. No
  pending/cursor adoption.
- Gate the inbound "does not re-fetch" clause on a fresh window so a
  roll-forward after a rollback is not told a loss that does not happen.
- Count only unknown-status outbound segments (filter accepted/rejected
  receipts), mirroring the GitHub store, and align the notice wording.
- Update the shared destinationKey doc comment to list email among the
  binders; record the post-upgrade identity-change gap (item 1 of #17769)
  and the new diagnostics in both design docs.
- Pin the mid-connect ownership re-check and the deferred archive with
  witnesses (lock lost during connect; failed first start leaves the
  legacy unarchived), killing the two mutations the review found surviving.

* fix(channels): carry the email generation high-water across registrations

Close the second review round on the email registration-identity keying:

- The generation seed was one-shot and legacy-only, but the control plane
  fences account_generation on a (tenant_id, channel_id) row shared by every
  registration identity of the mailbox, and the first successful start
  archives the literal legacy. A second registration then registered
  generation 1 and was refused channel_generation_stale on every start. Seed
  the monotonic counter from the highest safe-integer generation durable
  anywhere in the mailbox directory (live legacy, sibling keyed ledgers, and
  .stranded-* archives), idempotent and skipped while pending claims are
  staged so their dedupe key is never changed. Still no pending/cursor
  adoption.
- Derive the fresh-window reporting gate from the cursors rather than
  load-ness, so the retry after a first start that failed once openMailbox
  pinned a fresh ledger to the tip still repeats the inbound and
  offline-window loss clauses, while a roll-forward whose keyed cursor still
  re-fetches the legacy window is not told a loss that does not happen.
- Flag a parseable non-ledger as unreadable (unknown counts), never a
  loss-free 0/0 all-clear, mirroring the GitHub store.
- Pin both halves of the archive-rename-failure path (store returns undefined
  and keeps the legacy; adapter logs and re-reports it next start).
- Add the house inline update notes to the GitHub and DingTalk design docs
  (both languages) so the keying lineage no longer calls email the remaining
  follow-up, and sync the email design docs to the directory-scoped seed and
  cursor-based gate.

* fix(channels): heal the email generation to the row high-water before registering

Root-cause the third review round's generation cluster instead of patching
instances: the healing was fragmented across openMailbox's epoch branch and a
late connect() seed, so a ledger that missed several epoch changes registered a
+1 still below the shared (tenant_id, channel_id) row and was refused before the
seed ran, and a lagging ledger with staged claims wedged on every start.

- Clamp both the fresh and the epoch generation to the durable high-water in
  openMailbox, before that branch registers; connect() then heals a loaded
  ledger whose epoch matches but whose generation still lags. A staged claim
  below the high-water is already dead (its generation can never be registered),
  so healing drops it visibly — never re-offering it at a raised generation,
  which would change its dedupe key — giving the lagging ledger an exit.
- Drop the redundant inline legacy term; highestSiblingGeneration() is the
  single source, and it now returns the unreadable sources it skipped so the
  adapter logs them rather than dropping them silently.
- Split the loss-clause gates: the pending clause keeps >= (claims sit at/below
  the cursor), the offline-window clause uses strict > (the window begins at
  cursor + 1, so at equality the next poll admits the mail — no false alarm).
- Carry a restore instruction in the unreadable-legacy notice (the generation it
  held is the only local copy), and document the reverse-direction rollback cost
  (the archive removes the only generation carrier) in both design docs.
- Strengthen the witnesses: a real message so the cross-tenant replay is pinned
  at the wire, the load cause assertion, the keyed-sibling-dominated carry, and
  new cases for the epoch clamp, the visible heal, the equality gate, and the
  restore instruction.

* fix(channels): converge email keying review — independent fixes, defer cross-row heal

Round 4 flagged the generation-heal cluster as diverging (R1-8 -> R3-1/R3-2 ->
R4-1). Per the maintainer's convergence decision, land the core identity keying
with the independent review fixes and defer the cross-row generation carry to
#17769 (item 10), which needs a row-scoped channel-base contract key.

- Emit the stranding notice after openMailbox pins the cursor, so the
  offline-window clause consults the actual window: a quiescent upgrade whose
  tip equals the legacy cursor skipped nothing and reports no loss (the pending
  clause keeps >=, the offline clause is strict >). Fixes the common-case false
  alarm and the design-paragraph drift.
- Keep an unreadable legacy in place instead of archiving it, so the repair
  instruction stays valid and the corrupt file does not become a permanent
  unreadable generation source.
- openMailbox() now logs the unreadable generation sources it skips (the
  tick()/poll() reopen paths), once per start; the connect heal reads only the
  number so it does not re-log.
- Drop the dead generation field from strandedLegacyLedger (the seed comes from
  highestSiblingGeneration); correct the JSDoc and design docs.
- Make the .stranded-* archive arm decisive in the carry witnesses (store and
  adapter), and add witnesses for the lossless upgrade, the kept unreadable
  legacy, and the runtime-reopen diagnostic.

R4-1 (directory-scoped carry vs the (tenant_id, channel_id) fence row) is
recorded in the design Scope boundaries and #17769 item 10 as a cross-cutting
follow-up; the maintainer accepts the residual risk for the multi-row directory
edge configuration. The core cross-ownership pending isolation is unaffected.

* fix(channels): accurate stranding notice wording for loaded ledgers

Round 5 wording fixes (the only Critical, R4-1, is the carried deferred item
the maintainer already accepted into #17769):

- The stranding notice no longer describes a loaded ledger as fresh: the
  inbound clause names that ledger's own pinned cursor on a loaded start, and
  the offline-window clause is bounded by the pinned cursor ("mail between the
  legacy cursor and the pinned cursor"), so mail above the pinned cursor that
  the next poll admits is not reported as lost. The fresh-upgrade wording is
  unchanged. The retry witness now appends mail after the failed start and
  asserts the notice neither calls the ledger fresh nor names the new UID as
  lost, and that the next poll admits it.
- Correct the readable-only archive rationale: keeping an unreadable legacy in
  place preserves the repair instruction it printed; the earlier claim that
  archiving avoids a "permanent unreadable generation source" was false (the
  carry scans the bare legacy name too), so it is removed from the comment and
  both design docs.

fix(managed-agent): load transport wakes through the passive verb (#17955)

The transport's wake load took the active verb, whose takeover load and
new-work attachment can drive a crashed Session's Runtime recovery and its
foreground Turn. The control-plane wake design requires every wake load to be
passive, as the backstop scan already is, so the transport now loads through
the passive verb. A passive load always round-trips and is answered from a
resident Session, so the stale-reference eviction and the already-attached
outcome the active verb needed have no counterpart here.

feat(web-shell): bind the daemon chat controller to the session provider (#17895)

* feat(web-shell): bind the daemon chat controller to the session provider

Slice 2d: useDaemonChatController constructs createDaemonChatController once per session from live DaemonSessionProvider state, wiring intent transports to the session actions and bridging prompt settlement from the terminal-event subscription. Approval currency and decision settlement are derived from the pending-permission set via the pure, unit-tested derivePermissionSignals (answered requests emit an applied decision and stay live; unanswered departures are superseded). Storage key reuses getComposerDraftStorageKey; capabilities derive from the feature tags. pendingQuestions/statusFacts/settledPhase and the optional sub-controllers are bound conservatively pending the ChatSurface switch. Renders nothing on its own; 6 new helper tests, 95 daemon-chat tests green.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* fix(web-shell): vote the question submit option instead of cancelling

fix(cli): attribute daemon log lines and bind late channel restores to the boot conflict decline (#17904)

* fix(cli): attribute daemon log lines with pid and port

Daemons that share one log sink were unattributable line by line: the
stderr tee carried no process identity at all, and the file log carried
pid but no port, so counter-based diagnosis across sibling daemons
required guessing which process wrote which line (#17479 B.3).

Tee lines now carry pid= and, once listening, port=; file lines gain
port= after the existing runId=/pid=. The port is late-bound through
DaemonLogger.setPort(actualPort) in onListening, so ephemeral port 0
and EADDRINUSE fallback both report the real listening port; pre-listen
records carry pid only. Caller ctx.pid (worker pid) stays rendered in
the tee alongside the daemon identity.

* fix(cli): bind late channel restores to the boot conflict decline

A daemon whose settings-derived channel selection was downgraded at boot
because another instance held the channel-service lease re-admitted those
channels as soon as a non-primary workspace registered after boot and the
holder's pidfile record disappeared (holder exit, stale sweep): the runtime
lease re-check only sees the pidfile's current state, so nothing remembered
the boot decline. The duplicate then ran side-effecting channel workers
behind the operator's back (#17479 B.2).

The registration hook now skips the late restore while the decline stands,
before consuming the workspace's once-per-run restore mark and alongside
the operator-stop sibling, so a refused workspace gets its restore back
when an explicit selection commit clears the gate and it registers again.
addChannelsToSelection keeps a defense-in-depth refusal for any other
caller. Only a successful explicit commit clears the gate; a failed one
leaves it set. The boot downgrade itself stays non-fatal best-effort:
settings-derived channels must not block daemon startup.

* fix(cli): reserve daemon log identity keys and restate the channel decline reason

Address review R1-1/R1-2 on the log-attribution and channel-gate fix.

The tee rendered caller context unfiltered, so a worker pid passed as ctx.pid
produced a second, conflicting pid= key (a last-key-wins pipeline attributed
the daemon's line to the worker), and the bare diagnostics that bypass the tee
(write/rotation/retention warnings, queue overflow) carried no identity at all.
Both renderers now strip the reserved identity keys (runId/pid/port) from caller
context, the worker pid travels as childPid, and a shared identity holder feeds
the late-bound port to every stderr line including the bare diagnostics. The
file renderer's strip and the desktop smoke parser's first-pid= read are unchanged.

The refused late restore now restates the boot decline reason (the conflicting
holder, sanitized) in the skip line and the defense-in-depth refusal, so it stays
diagnosable after the boot warn rotates out on a long-running daemon. It records
no channelRestoreFailures entry, keeping parity with the operator-stop sibling.

* fix(cli): exclude the transient channel startup race from the boot decline gate

The boot conflict gate latched on channelServiceStartingConflictError too —
the transient exclusive-create race where no holder record was ever read —
so a daemon that hit the race refused automatic restores for the rest of the
run even though no instance held the lease, and the boot message's "retry
after the current startup finishes" invited a retry the gate then refused.
Mark that error `starting` and set the gate only on a real holder conflict;
the runtime lease re-check handles the transient race instead. A real holder
record (including one this machine cannot verify) still latches the gate.

Also make the gate suite portable and load-tolerant: match the rendered
workspaceCwd form (renderCtx quotes values containing whitespace, so a TMPDIR
with a space broke five cases), and give the file an explicit 60s testTimeout
(the first case pays the cold module load and sat 2.5s under the default 15s).
Adds a transient-race case proving the gate does not latch and the restore
fires once the race clears.

* docs(users): scope the channel decline recovery and per-record log attribution

Scope the boot-decline recovery instruction to automatic restores: a successful
qwen channel set re-enables automatic restores on later registrations and a
restart re-evaluates the lease, while starting a single channel independently
runs that worker without re-enabling automatic restores. Note the transient
"already starting" race is not latched. Describe log attribution per record
header (an error's stack frames follow as continuation lines under the pid/port
header), not per physical line.

* fix(cli): latch the boot channel gate on a live holder found in the reservation retry

The F2 narrowing marked every exclusive-create EEXIST retry as the transient
"already starting" race, but a competing process can acquire the lease after the
last pre-reservation read: writeInfoExclusive then sees a live holder under the
lock and rethrows EEXIST, and the retry handler threw starting:true, so the boot
gate skipped a real holder. Once that holder released, a registering workspace
auto-started a worker — the reported lease race, reproduced with the production
pidfile. Carry the holder identity out of the locked check (channelServiceHolder
on the EEXIST) and recover it in the retry handler (re-read as fallback); only an
unidentifiable owner is the transient race. Adds a live-holder regression case
beside the transient one.

Also address review R2-1/R2-2/R2-5: unsplice the two helper doc comments; rename
the worker pid to childPid in the paired "channel worker exited" message (it kept
a second daemon-meaning pid= key) and pin both ready and exit records with a
serve-level multi-workspace test; reuse renderIdentityPrefix for the tee identity
instead of a third inline copy. Clarify the defence-in-depth comment as an
intentional, currently-redundant backstop (R2-3, kept per maintainer F3 stance).

* docs: list the boot-decline exclusion in the sibling late-restore contracts

The channels overview, the developer adapter guide, and the protocol spec's
"That restore:" list still closed their exclusions after the --channel and
DELETE /workspace/channel cases. Add the boot lease-conflict decline (latched
until an explicit commit or restart; the transient starting race is not latched)
so an operator whose flagless daemon declined its boot restore reads the same
contract everywhere (review R2-4).

docs(managed-agent): design Runtime-owned background observation (Phase 3b) (#17912)

* docs(managed-agent): design Runtime-owned background observation (Phase 3b)

Add the separate 3b design the Phase 3 control-plane wake design calls
for. The background capture's running digest lives in Harness memory
and resource publication needs the live writer, so the parent's plan to
re-open the direct publisher on wake cannot work. The design moves the
background capture and the Monitor policy into the worker, which owns
the process for the stream's whole life.

The worker turns everything that must become durable into numbered
delivery entries. A resident Harness applies them through its writer,
and the Broker pulls them over the existing lease-fenced transport into
a staging ledger while the Session is suspended. Staged observations and
exits wake the Session, and a staged exit settles its execution row
without a load. A load re-attaches first and then drains staging up to
the point the worker reports. The seal stamp also certifies background
holds, so the recovery view and cleanup retry can tell them from owed
work. Suspension releases probe only and keep the mount, and parked-MCP
reclamation refuses before it disconnects.

The design withdraws the parent's durable staging authorization and
three-party handoff, answers its open questions 4-10, and links from
the parent in both languages.

* docs(managed-agent): revise Phase 3b observation design after review

Settling only the execution row could not release the Runtime Session or
pass the durable retention guards, so an exit now wakes a drain-only load
that commits the journal settle with no model turn. Delivery entries carry
their own resource closure so a stage ref is never deleted before the
journal commit that replaces it, and the drain walks the manifest's page
closure server-side. The staging and seal hint writes are fenced against
each other, closing the detach-to-seal window without pinning consumed
wakes. One puller claims a binding and the routes adopt from durable
records so suspension survives Broker restarts and replicas. A reserved
terminal slot lets a forced stop produce its exit proof under backpressure;
the capability check moves to admission; the detach carries the final
acknowledgement; deleting a Session cleans up its staging.

Re-pin the baseline to a commit that includes the 3a implementation and
refresh the drifted anchors; adopt the review nits on page capacity, the
slice mapping, and the parent section title.

feat(acp): end a tool-calling turn when queued input is sent now (#17825)

* feat(acp): end a tool-calling turn when queued input is sent now

Send now used to do nothing once the model's response had started a tool
call: the queued message waited for the arguments to finish streaming and
for the tool batch to run. It now ends the current turn instead, and the
daemon promotes the queued messages to the next prompt at once.

The turn ends as cancelled, but unlike a user cancel it leaves cron,
background notifications and an active Goal running; an interrupted Goal
turn is handed off rather than paused. A drain already in flight still
brings the messages into the same turn. A tool cut off this way tells the
model a user message follows instead of telling it not to retry.

* fix(acp): keep send-now interrupts from stranding queued input

The daemon now holds a send-now request while a drain that took messages
is still resolving attachments, so the child never reads the request as
proof that the host still holds input the drain did not take. An
interrupted turn takes nothing more from the host at its tool boundary,
and a turn does not end while input a timed-out drain handed over late
waits for the tool boundary.

Completed tools and tools that throw when interrupted also tell the model
a user message follows, on both loops.

* fix(acp): scope send-now interrupts to the tool batch and its turn

A send-now request only ends a turn while its tool batch is running; once
the batch settles, the request waits for the tool-boundary drain or the
next response, so a turn that is already finishing is never cancelled.
The daemon drops a held request when its turn ends and cancels approval
requests still pending under a prompt as it settles, which a turn ended
from inside the child would otherwise leave open.

Interrupted tools on the legacy loop now get the same model-facing notice
as on the shared loop, without the internal abort token.

feat(managed-agent): stamp clean suspensions for wake dispatch (#17908)

* feat(managed-agent): stamp clean suspensions for wake dispatch

Implement slice (1) of the seal-time wake stamp addendum. When the
control plane enables wake dispatch, an idle Hosted Session whose only
pending inputs are deferred, unattempted wake inputs suspends instead
of staying resident. Its seal records what the wake pump would pick
from the committed prefix, and the Store writes that stamp on the
journal head with the revision it certifies.

The wake backstop becomes the due-time dispatcher: a stamped head
leaves the scan until its earliest input is due and is then loaded
without replaying its journal. Every writer acquisition clears the
stamp and caps a stamped future due time at the claim delay, so
crashes and refused loads keep the existing proof path. The recovery
view reports a stamped clean suspension ready right after its seal,
and the transport drops a delayed wake notice for a stamped head with
nothing due.

The capability is off by default and rides the writer grant. The
addendum records the two post-merge review items from #17869 and the
implementation decisions in both languages.

fix(managed-agent-server): keep journal blob reclamation moving past sealed heads (#17907)

The eviction recheck required the session head to be ACTIVE, and its
failure path returned without state change or cursor. SEALED is the
normal resting state between writer leases, so with the default 72h
grace almost every pack reaching the cutoff belongs to a sealed head;
once 32 such packs fill the global oldest-first LIMIT 32 window, every
30s sweep re-selects the same rows and SQL blob reclamation stalls
fleet-wide. Drop the state conjunct: the packed-through-revision
comparison already proves coverage for any head state, and pack-aware
readers resolve evicted bytes for sealed and waking heads alike.

Add a regression test reproducing the stall (32 sealed-head packs aged
ahead of one active pack): red on the unfixed code (every pass returns
0), green with the fix (32 evicted, then the active pack behind the
window, then an empty pass; bytes resolvable for sealed and active
sessions).

Also lower the three class-size ratchet ceilings to the post-#17856
extraction sizes (760/831/796) and correct the AutomationLedgerRows
javadoc, which described the write-side fence proof as read-only.

fix(core): bound JSONL tail diagnostic recovery and cache churn (#17901)

Resolve items 1-3 of #17852, the follow-up tracker for #17771. Item 4
(native Windows and current-head macOS validation) stays open: no such
host was used, and the earlier macOS evidence predates the writer-handle
lifecycle, so it is not reused as certification.

Both behavioral gaps were reproduced against unmodified main before any
code was written. A long churn of distinct uninspectable paths re-warned
on every pass because eviction discarded the very state that suppresses
duplicates: 140 paths over 280 appends produced 280 warnings. And a
repaired debug sink stayed silent forever once a key's three-attempt
delivery budget was spent, even after a marker write proved the sink
healthy again.

The spent budget now admits exactly one probe per 60s cooldown window,
matching the existing token-usage write-failure cooldown magnitude, and
the attempt counter is never reset so a permanently broken sink cannot
become a retry loop. Eviction reclaims only slots whose delivery already
failed; a delivered or in-flight suppression owns its slot, which makes
the bound independent of delivery timing. Protecting only delivered
suppressions was measured to be insufficient: a synchronous burst still
produced 129 warnings for 129 paths.

A fatal tail-inspection error now names its file, including the ENOENT
recovery branch whose own descriptor stat runs inside the catch and
would otherwise escape unannotated. The error is annotated in place so
callers that match on its identity and code keep working, and the
original message stays a verbatim prefix.

Adds witnesses for the explicit writer sync/close lifecycle, the FIFO
writer-handle target, a replaced in-flight delivery, and a failed debug
append combined with a throwing delivery observer. Every guard has an
executed mutation that reddens a named case. One mutation deliberately
survives and is documented: deleting the stale-completion guard line
alone changes nothing observable because the callback closes over its
own entry, so the witness pins the isolation property and a variant that
writes to the current map entry reddens it instead.

Focused suites 150 -> 171 passing; root build, typecheck and bundle exit
0; Prettier and ESLint clean. The case encoding the old evicted-path
re-warn expectation is replaced with exact counts under the new policy,
not weakened, and a separate case keeps failed-slot eviction observable.

in the packaged arm. Count the ingredients instead — the block allow literal

the decision variable exactly three times. Three mutation witnesses redden
(the reported post-gate sibling, a usage-line ?? fallback, and a sibling
that re-derives the allow through the helper), each restored byte-equal.

Refresh the stale suite counts in both design docs and record the verify
report's disposition.

* test(managed-agent): pin the loop guards by structure and derivation, not spelling

Round 3 found three instances of one root cause: a pin asserting source
spelling instead of the mechanism it claims to guard.

The classifier ingredient counts could not see a post-gate sibling that
re-derives the allow through the helper under a second binding, and they
reddened on prose naming the binding. Replace them with an AST inventory of
the helper bindings, the !== undefined gates, every respond_in_schema answer
site (any call id) and the tool-name literals, executed against a hostile fake
so the scanner cannot be vacuous.

The Nd caveat's bound and example gaps were hand-written prose, which is how
N <= 31 survived two rounds. Derive them from parseCron instead.

The Java pin stopped at the sidecar supply map; forProfile's routing chain
decides reachability and was unbound. Pin the routing targets too.

Witnessed: the reported sibling, a different-call-id sibling and a hand-built
tool call each redden; a comment naming the binding stays green; N <= 45 plus
regeneration reddens the derived bound; deleting the SHELL_V3 branch reddens
routing while the supply-key assertion passes. All restored byte-equal.

* test(managed-agent): pin the allow construction site and derive the caveat from the Managed compiler

Round 4 found three holes, two of them opened by round 3's own replacement.

Dropping the ingredient counts removed the only assertion about where the
block allow is built, and the AST inventory inspected neither object literals
nor reassignments, so a let decision reassigned to an inline allow after the
gate stayed green. The scanner now collects every { shouldBlock: false }
construction site with its enclosing function (exactly one, inside the helper)
and every reassignment of the decision or its input under any assignment
operator, so ??= and ||= are covered too.

The declarations inventory recorded only the argument token, so a fabricated
blockProperties initializer passed while making every side query look like the
block schema. Record each initializer text and require the schema-tool lookup.

The caveat derived its bound from utils/cronParser, which serves the local CLI
scheduler; Managed bodies are fired by Java CronSlots, whose TypeScript twin is
compileCron. Derive from compileCron so a Managed slot-semantics change cannot
leave the caveat teaching a bound the Managed scheduler no longer honours.

Witnessed: the reported let+reassignment, a ??= rewrite, a fabricated schema,
and lowering the Managed day-of-month bound each redden; the round-3 sibling
still reddens (continuity); a comment naming the binding stays green. All
restored byte-equal. Test and documentation only.

The second verification round measured four survivors of the wiring scanner
and the sixth review round recorded eleven deferred items. Ten of the eleven
and all four survivors are closed; the CronSlots fixture binding goes to
#17673 because it is a cross-language contract change.

The scanner now records in-place writes to the decision input (member writes,
delete, Object.assign/defineProperty), accepts template-literal tool names,
inventories every helper call with its argument, and records computed tool
names. Tool-name sites carry their fake-model callback and the assertions are
scoped to the loop callbacks, so a legitimate non-loop respond_in_schema arm
no longer reddens a loop pin.

The caveat asserts each worked example as one composed clause, so the two
month-boundary gaps cannot be swapped, and requires parseCron and compileCron
to agree on every step. The Java pin parses forProfile into a profile-to-key
mapping and strips comments before scraping. Each profile shell's own Parsing
rule inventory is pinned, including the managed-only rules.

Correct the record: no runtime code changes, but the bundled SKILL.md ships
with the build and is read at runtime, so model-facing content does change;
fix #1 now describes mintedScheduleId rather than the pre-round-2 inline pin.

Witnessed: member write, Object.assign, template sibling, gap swap, routing
key swap, shell rule deletion and parser divergence each redden; a Java
comment spelling an assignment stays green; all earlier shapes still redden.
Every restore byte-equal. Core 33/33, scripts meta 183/183.

* test(managed-agent): witness the delete and computed-tool-name inventories

Post-publication audit found two inventories with no positive control: the
write inventory's delete branch and the computed-tool-name inventory. Both
could have been dead code while the suite stayed green.

The executed hostile control now carries a delete of the input's member and a
fakeToolCall whose tool name is computed, and asserts both are recorded. A
computed tool name injected into the real fire callback reddens the loop pin's
"no computed names" assertion, so that inventory is live too.

* docs(managed-agent): scope the witness claims to what each control actually carries

Audit found the record claiming the executed scanner control carries every
witnessed shape, while the gap swap, routing-key swap, shell-rule deletion and
parser divergence are core-side mutations of the real sources. Say which
control carries which, and record the gate-widening witness so every scanner
inventory is named as witnessed.

* test(managed-agent): close the third verification round's write and tool-call siblings

The third independent round re-measured the four earlier survivors as closed
and found three more of the same family; a fourth was measured locally. All
four are fixed here rather than deferred.

The call-writer branch keys on a name set now — Object.assign, defineProperty
and defineProperties, Reflect.set and defineProperty — so Reflect.set and
Object.defineProperties on the decision input are recorded. The tracked
binding set grows as aliases are declared, so a write through an alias of the
decision or its input is recorded at any chain length. Every element of a
toolCalls array that is not a fakeToolCall call is recorded with its callback,
so a hand-built tool call with a computed name is no longer invisible.

Each shape is in the executed hostile control and was injected into the real
fire callback: all four redden, all thirteen earlier shapes still redden, and
a comment naming the bindings stays green. Every restore byte-equal.

The record also states why this family recurs — a spelling-level guard over an
inline decision has an unbounded evasion surface — and that the seam refactor
which ends it is tracked in #17673, without claiming the packaged arm was
measured failing under each sibling.

* test(managed-agent): key the writer lookup by Map so prototype keys cannot crash it

Audit of the writer name set found it was an ordinary object literal, so a
receiver named constructor or toString resolved to a prototype function and
the optional call on .has threw a TypeError instead of skipping the node.
Use a Map, and carry a receiver of that shape in the executed hostile control.

Round 8's six deferred items are all corrections to what this PR ships, so all
six land here.

Scoping confined four of ten inventories to the loop callbacks; definitions,
declarations, gates, helperCalls and reassignments were file-wide, so an
unrelated fake callback reusing the helper or the binding names reddened a loop
pin. Every inventory now carries its callback and is scoped. allowSites stays
file-wide by design and is commented as such: the one legitimate construction
site is inside the helper, outside every callback.

so a two-argument computed-name sibling was invisible. That branch now runs at
any arity; the answer inventory still needs three arguments to read the call id.

win, while forProfile is an if/else-if chain resolving the first match. It now
resolves first-match into a Map and derives the reachable keys from it.

claimed PR-body correction had not reached the "Why it's needed" section; and
the record had no Round-7 section. All three fixed in both languages, and the
self-labelled Round-8 section renamed to the third verification round so the
numbering matches the review rounds.

already-matched profile stays green while a key swap still reddens; the control's

derives the allow through the helper and returns a whole response under a
foreign call id leaves no toolCalls array in the callback, so every loop-scoped

assertions now require every helper call to take the looked-up properties and
every blockProperties initializer to be that lookup. Sets rather than counts,

control carries the hoisted shape; the real-runner witness reddens the set
assertion (1 failed / 87 passed) and a byte-equal restore returns 88/88.

and is measured to survive, so it stays with the executed-seam residual in
#17673 rather than drawing another inventory.

reds by measurement: two Java ratchets from #17703 (#16346) and the
web-templates export byte budget (#17741), the latter on the required-check
chain. The Java consumer the review could not run is now run:

The comment-blind routing witness proved nothing: a bare assignment comment
has no profile condition, so the branch regex never matches it whether or not
comments are stripped. Both variants are replaced by comments spelling a whole
branch, which win first-match if scraped, so removing either stripping step

The allow-list guard threw "teaches a non-expanding sentinel" for any token
outside the list. For an unknown sentinel the guard has established membership
only: a newly added token may well expand somewhere, so the message asserted a

Judge, loop, browser, llm and ultrafast suites: 305 passed. pyright: 0 errors. Every PR was green on its own head. BU Bench v2.1, 200 tasks, judge on, the first 4 PRs vs 1.0.6: score 78.3 vs 76.3 (a tie), model cost $0.164 vs $0.199 per task. **Risk:** a pre-release; `pip install browser-use` stays on 1.0.7. Gateway calls ask for 16384 output tokens, not 32768

The Browser Use gateway holds credit for a call's worst case (whole input plus
max_output_tokens) before running it, so the 32768 cap made a small balance
refuse calls it could pay for. Agent turns stay far below 16k; a turn that
reaches the cap is a 'length' finish the loop already recovers from. Direct
OpenAI and every other provider keep their settings.

commits.message:
Add standalone Redis phone pager (#25857)

## What changed and why

SCA-2116 adds a request-based pager for the Redis pilot. The relay
admits a signed Grafana event for one rule and target, chooses the Bark
recipient server-side, and uses an operations-only Firestore database
for delivery attempts and duplicate suppression. Provider acceptance and
handset acknowledgement are recorded separately. The pager image
registration is build-only.

- **Serving-network probe.** The Helm source defines one candidate
Deployment, `omi-redis-serving-probe`, and its Prometheus scrape binding
in `prod-omi-gke / prod-omi-backend`. It uses the serving Redis RESP
transport and a workload-scoped PING-only identity. It attempts
authenticated PING every 30 seconds with a two-second overall deadline,
exports an explicit 1/0 result and a last-attempt timestamp, and
declares the selector `job="omi-redis-serving-probe",
target="prod-serving-redis"`.
- **Single Grafana rule.** Both split and combined monitoring sources
scope the paging change to `omi-redis-cache-conn-page` with
`paging_target=prod-serving-redis` and the dedicated timestamped-HMAC
receiver `Omi - Redis phone wake`. The query uses the probe selector and
retains the last state when telemetry is missing. The provisioner and

## Summary

SCA-3176 adds durable idempotency to the Python LLM gateway. This
gateway-only PR replaces the combined draft #25815. The Go adapter and
its review fixes belong in #25803.

- Keyed non-streaming calls claim the authenticated operation
transactionally before a single provider dispatch. Matching requests
replay the committed response. Lookup never dispatches, and unkeyed
calls retain their existing behavior.
- Firestore retains claims for 30 days from first claim and encrypted
results for 24 hours from settlement, capped by claim expiry. Replays do
not extend retention. A stale worker cannot settle an operation after
the claim has expired or been replaced.
- `LLM_GATEWAY_IDEMPOTENCY_ENABLED` defaults on. Setting it to `off`
refuses keyed submissions and lookups before provider dispatch. Claim,
settlement and lookup transactions read the account deletion marker.

## Queue horizon and rollout

The default Go queue allows five work attempts, twenty reconciliation
retries, one automatic work-budget requeue after 45 minutes, a 60-second
lease and backoff capped at 30 seconds. Counting two full cycles,
including a spare reconciliation slot per cycle, gives at most 123
minutes of nominal lease and scheduled-backoff time under those
defaults. The calculation excludes time spent without a ready worker,
larger caller delays, BYOK gates and operator redrive. The default BYOK
abandonment interval is 14 days.

The queue's count budgets do not impose an absolute job age. Before
keyed Go traffic is enabled, the paid path must enforce a 29-day cutoff
from durable job creation for every same-key submission, including
takeover and manual redrive. The 30-day claim TTL then covers the entire
allowed replay horizon, including a one-day margin. After Firestore
deletes a claim, the gateway has no record of its prior key.

The release owner must activate `expires_at` TTL on both Firestore
collection groups before rollout. The production readback is zero excess
provider dispatches per 1,000 keyed POSTs with replay traffic and
complete accounting coverage.

## Production readback query

Measure excess provider attempts per 1,000 keyed POSTs over a settled
window
that contains replay traffic. The first production readback uses only
`prod`. The dev and prod charts set
`LLM_GATEWAY_IDEMPOTENCY_ENVIRONMENT`
explicitly. It stamps new claims, keyed ledger rows and the keyed POST
counter.
Use
`sum(increase(llm_gateway_keyed_posts_total{environment="prod"}[<window>]))`
as the denominator, evaluated at the window end. Collect the read-only
inputs
before claim TTL or account erasure can remove cohort records.

- `claims` projects the customer Firestore claim document ID as `scope`,
plus
`state`, `started_at` and `environment`. Extract the chosen environment
and
  `window_start <= started_at < window_end` from the
`llm_gateway_idempotency_claims` collection group. If the range index is
unavailable, scan those projected fields during the bounded rollout and
  apply the same filters in the extract.
- `attempts` projects `idempotency_scope AS scope`, `attempt_id`,
`occurred_at` as a timestamp, and `idempotency_environment AS
environment`
from the participating replicas' `llm_gateway_attempts` ledgers. Extract
rows in the chosen environment for each cohort scope, including late
rows
after window end, and all scoped ledger rows occurring within the
window.
  Keep `user_uid` for the next lookup only.
- `claim_lookup` contains point reads in customer Firestore for every
  in-window ledger scope absent from the claim cohort. Read
  `users/{user_uid}/llm_gateway_idempotency_claims/{scope}` and project
  `scope`, `started_at` and `environment` for found documents. Only a
  matching-environment claim confirmed outside the window excludes a
  ledger-only scope. Missing claims, mismatched stamps, and found claims
that should have been in the extract leave coverage unknown. Treat
lookup
  errors as an incomplete measurement.

Run the query with `@environment = 'prod'`, `@window_start` and
`@window_end` matching the scrape window, and `@keyed_posts` set to the
environment-filtered denominator. A committed pre-dispatch rejection
with
no ledger row is conservatively unknown as well.

```sql
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT scope, state
  FROM claims
  WHERE environment = @environment
    AND started_at >= @window_start AND started_at < @window_end
), by_scope AS (
  SELECT scope, COUNT(DISTINCT attempt_id) AS attempts,
         MAX(CASE WHEN occurred_at >= @window_start AND occurred_at < @window_end
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS in_window
  FROM attempts
  WHERE environment = @environment
  GROUP BY scope
), scoped AS (
  SELECT c.scope, c.state, COALESCE(a.attempts, 0) AS attempts, 1 AS has_claim
  FROM cohort AS c LEFT JOIN by_scope AS a ON c.scope = a.scope
  UNION ALL
  SELECT a.scope, NULL AS state, a.attempts, 0 AS has_claim
  FROM by_scope AS a
  WHERE a.in_window = 1
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM cohort AS c WHERE c.scope = a.scope)
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM claim_lookup AS l
      WHERE l.scope = a.scope AND l.environment = @environment
        AND (l.started_at < @window_start OR l.started_at >= @window_end)
    )
), coverage AS (
  SELECT
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN attempts > 1 THEN attempts - 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) AS observed_excess,
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'committed' AND attempts > 0 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END), 0)
      AS unknown_scopes,
    COALESCE(SUM(has_claim), 0) AS claims
  FROM scoped
)
SELECT observed_excess, unknown_scopes, claims,
       CASE WHEN unknown_scopes = 0 AND claims > 0
            THEN 1000.0 * observed_excess / NULLIF(@keyed_posts, 0)
       END AS excess_per_1000_keyed_posts
FROM coverage;
```

Require complete claim and ledger extracts. Independently compare the
keyed
provider-attempt and accounting-delivery counter deltas from the same
environment's scrape targets. A known extract or counter gap makes
coverage
unknown. Accept the zero target only with a nonempty cohort, replay
traffic,
and complete coverage. A claim removed by TTL or erasure makes the
affected
window incomplete. Track replay, conflict, pending, indeterminate,
saturation and storage errors in
`llm_gateway_idempotency_outcomes_total`.

different environment. The Firestore emulator proof uses the same
`based-hardware` customer project, caller, user, tenant, and key for dev
and prod. It proves each environment dispatches once and can recover
only its own response. It also exercises mismatched claim and result
records.

Support operator CLI with audited holds, retention, DSAR export; held deletes keep data (#25883)

## Summary

Adds `omi-support-ops` (`backend/scripts/support/ops.py`), the single
audited path for support work on customer data, and makes conversation
deletes on held accounts keep the data. Tracking: SCA-3339 (design,
DESIGN update and measurements are on the issue).

- **Audit trail.** Every command, read or write, first writes
`support_actions/{id}`: ticket, requesting human, agent name, the ADC
principal it ran under, reason and outcome. No customer content is
stored. If that write fails, the command does not run. Writes are dry
runs unless `--apply`.
- **`hold place | release | status | list`.** Legal holds now record
ticket, reason, placed_by, review_by (default 180 days, max 730) and an
append-only `legal_holds/{uid}/events` history, written in the same
transaction as the hold. Placement and release re-check the deletion
fence. `legal_hold.v1` documents without the new fields still validate.
`list` flags overdue reviews and holds with no audit fields.
- **`retention check`.** Read-only report for chosen conversations:
Firestore records, audio objects (live, noncurrent, soft-deleted), hold
and gate state, and Firestore backup coverage.
- **`dsar export`.** Reuses `iter_user_data_export` (the in-app "Export
All Data") plus retained audio (chunks, playback MP3s and
per-conversation WAV recordings). Builds a zip with a SHA-256 manifest
in `gs://based-hardware-privacy-exports/<ticket>/` (generation-0
precondition) and returns a V4 URL valid for at most 7 days, signed
through IAM signBlob with no key file. Requires an approval reference.
- **`account summary`.** Read-only.
- **Held-account deletes (P7 Decision 4: a hold blocks physical
disposal, never product access).** Before this change, the default
`cascade=false` delete never consulted the hold and physically erased
the record, audio and frames, while a held cascade delete answered 409.
Now both return 204 with `X-Omi-Delete-Outcome: held_deferred`: the
conversation is hidden and tombstoned for the user and physically
retained. A cascade delete keeps its erasure obligation; the existing
runner finishes it `held`, rechecks hourly and erases after release. A
non-cascade delete arms no obligation, because the runner only cascades
and would delete more than the user asked for. `hold release` reports
these for follow-up. The hold lives on the data-plane client, so it
cannot join the tombstone transaction: a held non-cascade accept
re-reads the hold after commit and, if it was released in between, falls
through to the normal delete, so release's follow-up scan never misses
it. A held retry marks an existing tombstone and never un-arms erasure.

Ships on by default behind the kill switch
`LEGAL_HOLD_DEFER_SINGLE_DELETE`, registered as `ops_kill` in
`config/feature-flags.yaml`. Setting it to `false/off/0/no` restores the
previous behavior. Only two accounts are held today, so the user-visible
change is confined to them. The release classifier treats this flag as
high-risk; David signed off on 2026-11-20 (SCA-3339, anx
`card:omi-daily-support-triage`).

Measured cost (ro-prod, last 2 days, sampled logs, so lower bounds): 865
`DELETE /v1/conversations/*` request entries, 360 `cascade=True` and 7
`cascade=False` delete log lines. The change adds one direct
`legal_holds/{uid}` read per delete.

READBACK after serving: `hold list` shows both existing holds (with
ticket and actor after backfill), plus a log count of
`event=conversation_delete outcome=held_deferred`, expected to be 0
unless a held user deletes.

## Known gaps (follow-ups on SCA-3339)

- A non-cascade erasure obligation kind, so release erases held
non-cascade deletes automatically. It touches batch-custody code.
- A hold does not stop GCS lifecycle expiry (`playback/` at 30 days,
`merged/` at 3 days); `hold place` should also set object holds on
retained audio.
- `retention check` reads the legacy private-cloud-sync and recordings
buckets only, not the regional audio buckets.
- DSAR export does not yet read the regional playback bucket, the
derived-audio bucket or `raw-live/` packs; the zip's README says so.
- The held-delete behavior covers the app route `DELETE
/v1/conversations/{id}` only. The developer API conversation delete
(`routers/developer.py`) has never checked holds and still does not.
- A non-cascade delete does not take the per-account gate, so a hold
placed in the same instant as the delete does not stop it (pre-existing;
this change narrows it).
- DSAR export zips stay in `gs://based-hardware-privacy-exports` after
the signed URL expires; the bucket needs a lifecycle rule. Conversations
a held user deleted are absent from `export.json` (the README says so).

feat(conversations-v3): per-owner live re-derive for fragmented live windows (#25817)

## What

`backend/scripts/conversations_v3_backfill.py run --mode rederive-live`
replans one owner's finished live v3 windows in one `[since, until)`
window from their source recordings with the current planner (#25764
manual cuts and exclusive claims, #25786 stretch cohesion), and commits
the result. Until now the repair tool could only re-derive legacy donors
(`derive`) and rows a backfill had made (`rederive`). Finished live
windows are kept as they are by `planner.preserve_finished_windows`, so
the fragments built before those fixes (a lunch tail of ~18 tiny visible
`manual_end` cards, ~66 hidden `below_word_minimum` topic pieces on
11-19) stay fragmented.

It runs as an ordinary backfill run: same ledger, start marker, queue,
`backfill-builder` lease, outline and notes path, `status`, `resume` and
`undo`. `CONVERSATIONS_V3_BACKFILL=off` still stops all of it.

## DESIGN:

**Reads and writes per owner-day.** Sized against one real owner-day
(2026-11-19 UTC, ro-prod metadata-only `runQuery`, counts only): 503
documents started that day (203 sources, 244 v3 rows: 86 visible and 158
hidden; 56 deleted or merged).
- Dry-run: one metadata read of the window (503 reads), then per
partition (≤192 documents planned, ≤256 loaded) the started_at range
read plus by-id reads of sources and rows named by claims outside the
range, plus one lease read. About 1,000 reads. No writes, no model
calls.
- Run: the same loader reads (~550). Each commit batch's transaction
reads its sources and the rows it writes or retires, plus a tombstone
per written row (~400–700). It writes:
  - the rebuilt and created rows;
  - a 5-field retire patch per absorbed row;
  - a claims-only update per affected source;
  - one prior document per changed, created or retired row;
  - about 10 ledger updates per partition.

For the sized day that is at most ~700 writes, and fewer when windows
are unchanged, because an unchanged window gets no write.
- Priors: each partition reads its own copies by id twice, before its
commit and when it settles (at most 256 each). `resume` and `undo` list
the run's copies once (pages of 200). So prior reads grow linearly with
the run, not with partitions times copies.
- Undo: lists priors (pages of 200), reads each row, its tombstone and
its sources once per group, and writes each restored row and source
once.

**LLM cost.** One outline call per stretch in the partition (cache hits
are free), then notes only for windows that changed. Unchanged windows
keep their row and their notes. The dry-run prices this at the gateway
Luna card, the same as the backfill estimate: outline per stretch, plus
notes, agentic notes or tasks-only by word count for every window after.
By that card an owner-day plans at well under $1 (a planning estimate;
gateway usage has the actual spend). The coordinator reads the exact
number from the dry-run before running.

**Custody.**
- *Adoption.* A rebuilt window keeps the id of the earliest row it
absorbs (`service._match`). A rebuilt window whose speech, bounds,
claims and Home decision equal the stored row is not written, so its
notes do not re-run.
- *Retire.* Every other absorbed row becomes a sync bridge to its
survivor: `deleted`, `discarded`, a cleared `summary_due_at`,
`sync_merged_into`, `v3_claims_transferred_to`, a bumped
`sync_content_revision` and `v3_derived=false`. That is the patch a sync
merge gives its absorbed rows, so deleting a bridge later releases none
of the survivor's claims. The survivor lists its bridges in
`sync_merged_from`, so deleting it purges them, as with a sync merge.
That list lands in the final commit batch together with the retirements,
so it never names a row that is still live. Nothing is hard-deleted,
subcollections stay, and reads by id follow the bridge. Dropping
`v3_derived` keeps every v3 planner read (claims closure, time queries,
adoption) from treating it as a user deletion. Its claims leave the
sources in the same commit that writes the survivor, so no claim is
orphaned and claims stay deduplicated. Audio pieces come from the
planner's exclusive claims, so no audio is duplicated.
- *No derived effects.* Rebuilt rows are stamped `backfilled` and
`v3_rederive_live_run`. Their notes take no memories, tasks, webhooks,
notifications or created fanout, and they use the backfill's own notes
marker.
- *Never touched.* These are offered to the planner as published
finished rows, so their lines, claims and audio stay theirs. They are
never written, and the ledger counts each one:
  - open windows, and every source an open window holds;
  - rows overlapping `since` or `until`;
- deleted rows, because until their claims are released those claims
still fence their speech;
- rows with app results: the owner can edit those with no marker, and a
replan never regenerates them;
- rows whose summary the owner rewrote. The summary endpoint deletes the
generated sections, so a card with notes, an overview and no sections
counts as edited, which is the rule refinement already applies;
- edited rows (user title, overview or corrections, transcript
corrections, speaker assignments, star, folder, photos, kept-by-user,
absorbed by a merge);
- locked, shared, private, discarded, deleted, unreadable,
legacy-backfilled, notes-pending and transcribing rows;
- rows on sources that are pending, unsealed, transcribing, failed,
purge-pending, private, deleted or legacy donors;
- rows on a source whose stored document plus a few more claims would
pass the 1 MB document limit (`sources_blocked_size_limit`, the SCA-2791
shape). The dry-run reports this per partition before any write.
- *No audio purge.* The commit for a live re-derive writes only `claims`
on its sources, so it never arms or cancels an audio purge.
- *Speech coverage.* The pass blocks (`rederive_live_coverage`) and
writes nothing if any segment an eligible row held would not be in a
rebuilt or protected row.
- *Fail-closed blocks.* `rederive_live_open` covers speech within five
minutes of now, and is checked before any paid call.
`rederive_live_boundary` covers a window that would cross `since` or
`until`. `rederive_live_outline_failed` means a repair never commits
fallback failed tiles. `document_too_large` means a source's claims
would grow past the limit or a prior is too large to record, and is
checked before any write.
- *Partial failure.* Priors are written before the first commit batch,
and the run's own rows are recognised on a resume. So a commit that
fails after some batches can be resumed to finish, or undone exactly.
Retirement happens only in the final batch, so nothing is hidden before
its survivor exists.
- *Undo.* Before each commit, the run writes every changed, created or
retired row's stored document and its claims with their list positions
to
`conversations_v3_backfill_runs/{run_id}/conversations_v3_rederive_priors`.
That collection sits under the owner, so account deletion purges it, and
it has a budget in `.github/firestore-collection-budgets.json`.
- No copy outlives what it copies. Priors are never written for a
conversation already deleted, or once account deletion began. Deleting a
conversation a run stamped empties its priors and its bridges' priors to
a `purged` stub, in every live run of the owner, before anything else.
Every copy belongs to a row a run stamped after the copy was made,
because a commit that fails for any reason drops the copies of rows it
did not write, and a resume records them again. Each partition's attempt
first drops the run's copies of the rows it loads that no run stamped
since, and `resume` and `undo` do so for every copy of the run, which
covers a process that stopped between recording a copy and stamping its
row. Undo never restores such a row, so these copies would only ever be
retained content. So the stamp-gated deletion path always reaches a
copy. After a protection migration has written its rows and photos, it
empties the copies of every stamped row it reached that were stored at
another level. It records those rows on every attempt, so a retry after
a failed purge purges again. The commit also checks the tombstones of
the rows it retires, so a row the owner deletes before its retirement
fails the commit. A run with a stub refuses undo as a whole rather than
restoring around it. Rows no run touched pay nothing. A finished undo
deletes the run's priors.
  - Undo takes both builder leases and waits for in-flight notes.
- It restores each group of rows that share a source in one transaction:
documents back exactly and each source's claim list back in its original
order. A row the run created is hidden in that transaction, then erased
with the conversation deletion helper, so its child collections go too.
- It refuses after the owner deleted a rebuilt row
(`owner_deleted_rebuilt_row`), or while a newer live run restamped one
(`undo_newer_run_first`). It also refuses after the owner changed a row
the run wrote, created or retired (`owner_edited_rebuilt_row`). Once a
partition settles its notes, the run records a digest of each row's
owner surface: title, overview, edit fields, star, folder, photos,
visibility, lock, deletion and merge. Undo compares against that digest.
Before the digest exists, it checks the edit fields, visibility, lock
and any merge against the stored prior. A row the owner changed before
its partition settled gets a baseline that never matches. A retired row
must still be the run's bridge to its survivor. It checks every prior
before restoring any group, and each group's transaction checks again.
- An interrupted undo is rerun as is. Rows it already restored, and
created rows it already hid (`v3_rederive_live_undone`), are finished,
not refused. That holds when they carry an earlier run's stamp, too.
- Restored rows pass through the recurring-voice fence the commit uses,
so a voice link the owner revoked is never written back.
- Undo refuses when a source named by the run is gone
(`undo_source_missing`). It checks every source of every group before
restoring the first group.
- A copy is never recorded at a protection level its row has left:
`save_priors` reads each row's level in its transaction.
- A resumed attempt keeps the first copy of a row, so claim positions
are the ones from before the run.
- Undo refuses once account deletion began (`account_deletion`). Before
restoring anything, it refuses a group of rows sharing sources that is
too large for one transaction (`undo_group_too_large`: more than the
write cap or 8 MB).
- The test compares every conversation document before the run with
after undo, byte for byte. In production, the Firestore commit hook also
stamps `home_source_version` and `home_content_invalidated` on every
conversation write. So a restore is exact apart from those two fields,
and the rerun check ignores them.

**Production number that proves it.** After deploy, the coordinator runs
the dry-run on the named owner's 11-19 and then the run. The readback is
the run ledger's `windows_after`, `visible_after`, `rows_retired` and
`outline_calls`, taken against the dry-run's before counts. For the
lunch tail and the 08:16–12:56Z stretch, the target is visible finished
v3 windows shorter than 30 s per active source-hour going from the
2.538/h lunch baseline to near 0, with 0 same-file duplicate pairs.

## Not in scope / known limits

- 34 of the sized day's sources are stuck `in_progress` for hours. They
count as unsealed, so rows on them stay protected and the dry-run
reports them as `sources_blocked_unsealed`.
- A late live speech append to a rebuilt row after the run is replaced
by the restored document on undo. The runbook states this.
- Before a partition settles, the run's own notes
(`process_conversation`) may discard a rebuilt card or add app results
to it. So an owner discard or app run on that card during the notes
drain cannot be told apart from the run's output, and undo before settle
can restore over it. After settle, the baseline digest covers both. The
runbook says to undo only settled runs.
- Dry-run "after" counts outline each stretch as one chapter, so
`windows_after` is the fewest windows the run can produce and
`rows_retired_est` (eligible rows minus the windows that adopt one) the
most it is expected to retire. The run ledger has the exact counts.
- A partition whose final commit would exceed the transaction write cap
(sources + retired rows + row + lease over 450) blocks as
`backfill_partition_budget` before any write.

## Verification

Unit tests at the code layer only. Nothing ran against the emulator or
production.
- New `tests/unit/test_conversations_v3_live_rederive.py` has 58 tests,
plus two deletion wiring tests in
`test_merge_conversations_canonical_delete.py`. They run the real
loader, planner, commit transaction and undo transaction on the strict
in-memory Firestore:
  - the fragmented lunch folds into one card that keeps the earliest id;
  - hidden topic pieces of one stretch become one visible card;
  - a second pass over its own result writes nothing;
  - open windows and rows past `until` stay byte-identical;
  - edited and locked rows are skipped and keep their speech;
  - unsettled speech refuses before a paid call;
  - lost speech blocks the pass;
- undo restores every row and claim exactly, and a rerun of undo is
idempotent;
- undo refuses after an owner deletion, an owner edit (title, star,
photos) of a rebuilt or created row, a summary edit or merge after
baselines, a merge before baselines, or a newer run;
- an over-cap partition, a window crossing `until`, an oversized prior
and claims growth past the document limit each block before any write;
- a source already near the document limit is reported by the dry-run
and left alone;
- a commit that fails after its first batch leaves the absorbed rows
untouched, resumes to the full result, and undoes byte for byte;
- an undo interrupted before erasing a created row finishes on rerun,
and an undo of a later run over an earlier run's rows can be rerun, then
the earlier run undone;
- an owner star before the partition settles is never taken as the
baseline;
- priors are never written once account deletion began, or for a
conversation the owner deleted, and deleting a rebuilt conversation
purges its priors and its bridges' priors;
- undo refuses once account deletion began, and refuses a group too
large for one transaction before restoring any;
- the survivor lists its bridges in `sync_merged_from`, and the dry-run

- a deleted row whose claims are not yet released still fences its

- a card whose summary the owner rewrote is left alone, and undo refuses

- deleting a retired bridge releases none of the survivor's claims, and

- a resumed attempt keeps the first copy of a row; a failed commit keeps

- a row deleted before its retirement fails the commit, and a card with

  - a failed commit empties the copies of rows changed meanwhile;
  - undo applies the recurring-voice fence;
- the run ledger counts unclaimed speech, and in a partial commit the

- a deleted or re-protected conversation keeps no undo copy and undo

and a restored row is recognised despite the commit hook's stamps;

- Main was merged in again (#25829 settle-on-landing stretches; the live

SCA-2865: record an empty first-summary merge instead of failing the request (#25890)

Multica: SCA-2865.

## What

`merge_result` raised `SummaryOutputUnavailable` for every open
first-summary obligation whose structured output was empty. Only the
enrichment consumer catches it and records a bounded empty-output
strike; request paths (from-segments, finalize) and direct sync persists
let it escape, aborting the completed write and surfacing as a 500 on
`POST /v1/dev/user/conversations/from-segments`.

The fence now raises only where a caller can act on it:

- **A consumer owns the write** (`PROCESS_CONTEXT`): raise, so the
consumer records the bounded strike before releasing the lease.
- **A finalization job owns the row** (`finalization_job_id` set, no
verified batch-projection handoff): raise, so the job stays retryable.
The repair pass refuses this shape as `generation_owned`, so committing
would let the finalizer complete its job and leave the armed debt with
no repair owner.
- **No consumer and no retryable job** (from-segments, direct sync
persist): commit the empty attempt with `summary_due_at` still armed.
The repair pass re-wakes the row and the consumer's three-strike budget
bounds the retries.

The consumer also acks an empty reprocess output on an already-enriched
row instead of retrying it forever.

An empty structured is still never a delivered summary. Prompt content,
model routing, metering and the from-segments identity/retry contract
are unchanged.

## Account deletion barrier

SCA-3174. The Python Cloud Tasks executor preserves the current grace,
legal-hold and billing behavior. It arms the Go erase only after the
grace deadline and successful billing cancellation. This preserves the
existing restore paths. A current, durable queue erase receipt gates the
first data-wipe step. An already armed generation remains gated on
retry.

Workerd accepts erase requests on a separate private TLS listener. The
Python client requires TLS 1.2 or later. It verifies the Google ID-token
audience and allowed service-account subject, reads the matching armed
marker, and uses Lane B's committed queue-only operation. The marker
project and database are explicitly bound to the Python executor’s
authoritative data plane, including named databases. A lost
acknowledgement is safe to repeat. Python's opt-in recovery uses the
same routine over a separate, restricted connection. Both paths retain
the Firestore fence. The protected Firestore running transition verifies
the current generation and invalidates prior grants. An unarmed flag-off
task uses the original running-marker update and the 30-minute lease.
The existing lookup and claim reads keep already armed retries
protected. Grants expire 25 seconds after the claim check starts.
Recovery closes a stalled connection and checks the deadline again
before issuing COMMIT. Unknown remote outcomes keep the legal-hold
barrier held until a committed receipt is verified. The queue routine
and the separately approval-gated role grant are in Lane B
[#25825](https://github.com/BasedHardware/omi/pull/25825). The narrow
marker reader landed in Lane B
[#25827](https://github.com/BasedHardware/omi/pull/25827) at
`a6b59aa905` and is present on this branch. The opt-in listener requires
the queue routine and marker reader to start.

The environment-level deployment boolean `go_queue_erase_required`
renders one value across the Cloud Run backend runtimes and the shared
GKE backend ConfigMap. Admission, restore, grace reconciliation and the
Cloud Tasks executor consume the rendered `GO_QUEUE_ERASE_REQUIRED`
value locally. Missing and false preserve the legacy path without any
settings I/O. In the first live Go family's release, configure and
verify the barrier, readback, and paging, then turn the barrier on
before admitting tenant traffic. Turn it off only with all live Go
tenant traffic disabled and the tenant backlog and armed deletions
handled. No role or grant has been applied. Recovery stays off until
David approves role creation, the environment has the approved
execute-only login, and operators verify and pin the intended workerd
queue identity. Postgres compares that pin with the physical writer,
database and schema's queue objects before invoking the erase in the
same statement. A mismatch fails closed without a receipt. Firestore
records the verified fingerprint with each Postgres recovery receipt.
Worker or database failure leaves the wipe pending, with retry and
escalation. The repository runbook records the enablement and rollback
sequence.

Before live Go tenant traffic, verify every serving deletion revision
and pod has the same rendered value and drain any in-flight deletion
that observed the previous value. With the shared flag enabled,
credential deletion runs only after the executor obtains a committed
erase receipt.

The readback is the share of armed deletion generations in the matured
trailing seven-day cohort with a durable receipt within 15 minutes and

synthetic verification result. Production observation and paging

fix(batch): classify every failure on a stopped allowance migration page (SCA-2195) (#25874)

## What

The allowance parking migration CLI
(`backend/scripts/batch_pipeline_allowance_migration.py`, SCA-2195)
reports every failure as `{"errors": 1}`. The 2026-11-17 production run
stopped that way after 2,029 pages, with 202,834 rows parked and 64
fenced. Nobody could classify the stop, so the replay has stayed on hold
since.

The stop line now names only classes, never a message, which can name
documents:

```json
{"errors": 2, "error_type": "...FirestoreContentionExhausted", "cause_types": ["...RetryError", "...Aborted"], "sibling_types": ["...DeadlineExceeded"], "retryable": true}
```

- **`retryable`** is true only when every failure on the page qualifies,
through its whole explicit cause chain. A failure qualifies if it is:
- a transient RPC class: Aborted, DeadlineExceeded, InternalServerError,
ResourceExhausted or ServiceUnavailable;
- an expired transaction, using the existing
`firestore_transaction_retry` check, now exposed as public
`is_expired_transaction` and applied to each link by its own class;
  - `FirestoreContentionExhausted`;
- the new `MigrationOwnerChanged`, raised when a stale owner hint is
found before that row is parked.

A fatal RPC status anywhere in a chain, such as PermissionDenied or
NotFound, blocks retry even when an outer link or its own cause is
transient. A non-exception `RetryError.cause` ends the walk instead of
crashing the handler.
- **Explicit causes only.** The walk is depth-first over every explicit
cause link: `__cause__`, and for `google.api_core.RetryError` also
`.cause`, where the SDK keeps its last error. A RetryError carrying both
is checked on both, so a fatal status on either link blocks retry.
Implicit `__context__` is never followed, so an incidental transient
error can't turn a fatal stop retryable.
- **Concurrent pages.** Only the first owner group's error propagated
before. The others are now attached as `migration_sibling_errors` after
the drain, which already existed, so one transient error can no longer
hide a non-retryable sibling.
- **Stop line output.** It is printed with `flush=True` by a tested
`run()` handler.

The failed page is never checkpointed, and state-CAS makes re-parking a
no-op, so a `retryable: true` stop is safe to relaunch from the retained
checkpoint. The runbook says so, and the SCA-2198 recovery disposition
uses it.

Unchanged: paging, fences, privacy checks, rates, concurrency,
checkpointing, and which rows are parked. The owner-change stop keeps
the same message and still fails the page; only its class is new.

Failure-Class: none

## Verification

`pytest tests/unit/test_batch_allowance_migration_cli.py
tests/unit/test_batch_allowance_migration.py
tests/unit/test_firestore_transaction_retry_deadline.py` passes. The new
tests cover:
- every retryable class;
- PermissionDenied and ValueError as non-retryable;
- the chain FirestoreContentionExhausted → RetryError → Aborted;
- an expired transaction;
- implicit context, suppressed or not, being ignored;
- a fatal RPC status anywhere in a mixed chain blocking retry, including
one raised from a transient cause;
- a non-exception RetryError cause still yielding a stop line;
- a real two-owner concurrent page carrying its sibling errors through
to `error_report`;
- a RetryError whose explicit and SDK causes differ (Aborted and
