Frozen prefix skip: looped stacks, bypassed stacks, outer fullgraph compile, Qwen3-VL in-place writes (#18632)

Follow-up fixes for #18442, found while re-checking the PRs merged on
2026-11-19. One commit per fix; every fix has a test that fails on main
and passes here.

| Fix | Follows up | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Frozen-prefix skip: looped / recurrent-depth stacks | #18442 | P1 |
| Frozen-prefix skip: no per-forward plan walk when nothing can be
skipped | #18442 | P2 |
| Frozen-prefix skip: a planned stack the forward bypasses | #18442 | P1
|
| Frozen-prefix skip: stand down under an outer torch.compile | #18442 |
P1 |
| Frozen-prefix skip: nested inputs that require grad | #18442 | P2 |
| Frozen-prefix skip: in-place writes into the skipped hidden states
(Qwen3-VL DeepStack) | #18442 | P1 |

## Tests (this branch vs main `54af93780b`, CPU)

- New and changed tests: main 13 failed / 11 passed, this branch 24
passed. Each test loads the code of its own tree.
- Neighbouring suites on this branch: frozen-prefix suites: 34 passed.
- `prepush_gate.py` passes.

## Frozen-prefix skip: looped / recurrent-depth stacks (follows up
#18442)

#### What broke

The frozen-prefix skip from #18442 assumes each decoder layer runs once
per forward. Recurrent-depth models run the whole stack several times:
Ouro (`ByteDance/Ouro-1.4B`, remote code, `modeling_ouro.py` line 592)
loops `self.layers` `total_ut_steps` times (4 by default), and its
`OuroDecoderLayer` is a `GradientCheckpointingLayer`, so the skip
engages.

With adapters only on the upper layers (`finetune_last_n_layers`,
`layers_to_transform`) and gradient checkpointing, the skip detached the
frozen prefix's inputs and cut layer k-1's output on every pass. From
the second pass on, the prefix is fed by the trainable upper layers of
the previous pass, so their gradient was dropped. The loss is unchanged,
only the gradients are wrong, so nothing warns.

Repro (CPU, tiny Llama with the stack run twice per forward, LoRA on
layers 2 and 3, reentrant checkpointing, `enable_input_require_grads`),
skip on vs off:

| Arm | Loss | Worst LoRA grad relative error |
|---|---|---|
| main | 4.886710 vs 4.886710 | 1.07 |
| this branch | 4.886710 vs 4.886710 | 0 |

#### Fix

`unsloth/models/_frozen_prefix.py`: the cut now fires once per forward.
As soon as layer k-1's output has been replaced by the leaf, the prefix
hooks are removed and the prefix layers get their checkpointing flags
back. Later passes through the prefix run exactly as without the skip.
The first pass still runs the frozen prefix once without a graph, so the
speedup for normal (single-pass) models is unchanged. The end-of-forward
restore is idempotent.

#### Tests

New `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip_looped.py`: 1, 2 and 3 passes over
the stack; the skip must engage, the loss must be bitwise equal and
every LoRA gradient must match the skip-off reference, and the layers
must be left with their flags and no hooks. The test loads
`_frozen_prefix.py` from its own tree and asserts it.

| Arm | transformers 4.57.6 | transformers 5.22.1 |
|---|---|---|
| main | 2 failed (2 and 3 passes), 2 passed | 2 failed, 2 passed |
| this branch | all passed | all passed |

The existing `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip.py` passes on both arms.

#### Not covered

No GPU run and no real Ouro weights. The change only affects what
happens after the cut, which single-pass models never reach.

## Frozen-prefix skip: no per-forward plan walk when nothing can be
skipped (follows up #18442)

#### What changed

The frozen-prefix skip (#18442) plans before every training forward with
gradient checkpointing on. The plan first builds the set of every
trainable parameter in the model, then walks each decoder layer. In the
common case, adapters on every layer, the first layer of each stack is
trainable, so no frozen prefix can exist and the answer is always "no
skip". The full walk still ran on every forward.

Host time of the plan on CPU (Xeon Platinum 8559C), PEFT LoRA r=4 on all
seven projections, 36 layers, 831 parameters, mean of 50 calls:

| Arm | Plan per forward |
|---|---|
| main | 6.4 ms (of which `model.parameters()` on the PEFT tree: 4.1 ms)
|
| this branch | 0.01 ms |

This runs before the first kernel of the forward, so it is not hidden
when the GPU is idle at the start of a step (after a host sync).

#### Fix

`unsloth/models/_frozen_prefix.py`, `_plan`: each stack is settled from
its first trainable layer before anything else. A stack that trains
layer 0 (adapters everywhere), or nothing at all (a frozen vision
tower), takes a short scan and is skipped. The set of every trainable
parameter in the model is only built once a stack with k >= 1 is found.
The plan is the same in every case: the old loop also skipped such
stacks and only used the model-wide set to validate a k >= 1 stack.

#### Tests

New `tests/test_frozen_prefix_plan_fast_path.py`: with every layer
trained, the plan returns no cut without calling `model.parameters()`.
The same holds for a tiny Qwen2-VL with adapters on every text layer and
a frozen vision tower. With adapters only on the upper layers it still
returns the same cut (layer 2). A trainable norm outside the stack still
turns the skip off. The test loads `_frozen_prefix.py` from its own tree
and asserts it.

| Arm | Result |
|---|---|
| main | 2 failed (the full walk ran, LLM and VLM), 3 passed |
| this branch | 5 passed (transformers 4.57.6 and 5.22.1) |

The existing `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip.py` passes on both arms.

#### Not covered

No GPU step-time A/B. The saving is host time per forward; whether it
shows in wall time depends on whether the GPU is idle when the forward
starts.

## Frozen-prefix skip: a planned stack the forward bypasses (follows up
#18442)

#### What broke

The frozen-prefix skip (#18442) picks the first stack whose trainable
parameters start at layer k >= 1. The model's forward does not always
run that stack. Take a VLM where only the top vision block and an untied
`lm_head` are trained. The plan picks the vision tower, but a text-only
batch never enters it. The cut on layer k-1 then never fired, and the
end-of-forward check treated that as a failed cut. It raised
`RuntimeError: Unsloth: the frozen-prefix skip could not mark the first
trainable layer's input` and disabled the skip, although the forward had
skipped nothing.

Repro (CPU, tiny random `Qwen2VLForConditionalGeneration`, reentrant
checkpointing, text-only batch):

| Arm | Result |
|---|---|
| skip off | trains, `lm_head` grad norm 3.21 |
| main, skip on | `RuntimeError` after the forward |
| this branch, skip on | trains, loss and `lm_head` grad bitwise equal
to skip off |

Reproduced on transformers 4.57.6 and 5.22.1.

#### Fix

`unsloth/models/_frozen_prefix.py`: the cut hook records that layer k-1
ran. The end-of-forward check raises only when that layer ran without
being cut. When the stack was bypassed, the forward is treated as not
engaged: no error, no count, and flags and hooks are restored as before.

Stacked on the looped-stack fix (one cut per forward), which rewrote the
same hook.

#### Tests

New `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip_bypassed_stack.py`. It asserts the
plan really picks the vision tower. Two text-only steps must then match
the skip-off loss and `lm_head` gradient bitwise, the engagement
counters must stay unchanged, and the vision blocks must keep their
flags and carry no hooks. The test loads `_frozen_prefix.py` from its
own tree and asserts it.

| Arm | transformers 4.57.6 | transformers 5.22.1 |
|---|---|---|
| main | 1 failed, 1 passed | 1 failed, 1 passed |
| this branch | 2 passed | 2 passed |

All frozen-prefix tests pass on this branch (16 passed).

## Frozen-prefix skip: stand down under an outer torch.compile (follows
up #18442)

#### What broke

The frozen-prefix skip (#18442) registers and removes module hooks on
every training forward. When the caller compiles a training step around
the model with `torch.compile(..., fullgraph=True)`, Dynamo traces those
hooks and cannot trace the hook registration. It fails with
`Unsupported: setattr() on unsupported type` at
`register_forward_pre_hook` inside the outer pre-hook. This happens on a
cold call and also after an eager warmup. Without the skip installed,
the same compiled step trains.

Repro (CPU, two-layer checkpointed `GradientCheckpointingLayer` stack,
bottom layer frozen, `backend="eager"` so only Dynamo is involved,
`fullgraph=True, dynamic=True`):

| Arm | Cold | After eager warmup |
|---|---|---|
| skip not installed | trains | trains |
| main, skip installed | `Unsupported` | `Unsupported` |
| this branch, skip installed | trains, grad bitwise equal | trains,
grad bitwise equal |

#### Fix

`unsloth/models/_frozen_prefix.py`: both model hooks return immediately
while `torch.compiler.is_compiling()`, so the forward runs as without
the skip. Eager forwards still engage it.

#### Tests

New `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip_outer_compile.py`: an eager control
that engages the skip. A fullgraph compiled forward and backward, cold
and warm, must match the uninstalled compiled run bitwise and leave no
hooks or changed flags. The test loads `_frozen_prefix.py` from its own
tree and asserts it.

| Arm | Result |
|---|---|
| main | 2 failed (cold, warm), 2 passed |
| this branch | 4 passed (torch 2.14.1 with transformers 4.57.6 and
5.22.1, torch 2.10.0) |

The existing `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip.py` passes on both arms.

## Frozen-prefix skip: nested inputs that require grad (follows up
#18442)

#### What broke

The frozen-prefix skip (#18442) stands aside when the caller wants a
gradient at an input, but it only looked at top-level arguments.
transformers also accepts `attention_mask` as a `{layer type: mask}`
mapping. A float mask requiring grad inside that mapping was missed. The
skip then detached it on the frozen layers below the cut, and its
gradient changed. Loss and LoRA gradients stay bitwise equal, so nothing
else shows it.

Repro (CPU, tiny Qwen3, LoRA on layer 2, non-reentrant checkpointing,
`attention_mask={"full_attention": bias}` with
`bias.requires_grad=True`): relative L2 error of `bias.grad`, skip on vs
off:

| Arm | Mask gradient error |
|---|---|
| main | 1.087850 |
| this branch | 0 (the skip stands aside) |

#### Fix

`unsloth/models/_frozen_prefix.py`: the input check walks nested inputs
(`torch.utils._pytree.tree_leaves` over args and kwargs) instead of the
top level only. A mapping without grad still engages the skip.

Stacked on the outer-compile fix, which edits the lines just above.

#### Tests

New `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip_nested_inputs.py`: a mask mapping
without grad still engages the skip. A mask mapping requiring grad must
make the skip stand aside, with loss, mask gradient and LoRA gradients
bitwise equal to skip off. The test loads `_frozen_prefix.py` from its
own tree and asserts it.

| Arm | transformers 4.57.6 | transformers 5.22.1 |
|---|---|---|
| main | 1 failed, 2 passed | 1 failed, 2 passed |
| this branch | 3 passed | 3 passed |

## Frozen-prefix skip: in-place writes into the skipped hidden states
(Qwen3-VL DeepStack) (follows up #18442)

#### What broke

The frozen-prefix skip (#18442) replaced layer k-1's output with
`hidden.detach().requires_grad_(True)`, a leaf that requires grad.
Reentrant checkpointing needs layer k's input to require grad, but
models that write into the hidden states between layers then fail.
Qwen3-VL's DeepStack on transformers 4.57 adds visual features in place
after the first decoder layers (`hidden_states[visual_pos_masks, :] =
local_this`). With the first trainable text layer at index 3 or below,
an image batch raised:

```
RuntimeError: a leaf Variable that requires grad is being used in an in-place operation.
```

This happened with both reentrant and non-reentrant checkpointing.
transformers 5.22 clones before the write, so the crash is specific to
4.57, but any model that writes in place between layers hits it.

Repro (CPU, tiny random `Qwen3VLForConditionalGeneration`, transformers
4.57.6, text layers 2 and 3 trainable, image batch):

| Arm | `use_reentrant=False` | `use_reentrant=True` |
|---|---|---|
| skip off | loss 5.5245 | loss 5.5245 |
| main, skip on | `RuntimeError` | `RuntimeError` |
| this branch, skip on | loss 5.5245, grads bitwise equal | loss 5.5245,
grads bitwise equal |

#### Fix

`unsloth/models/_frozen_prefix.py`, `_leaf`: the cut subtracts, in
place, a zero-dimensional zero that requires grad. The result requires
grad but is not a leaf, so later in-place writes are allowed.
Subtracting +0.0 is exact for every value, including -0.0, NaN and inf,
so the values are unchanged bit for bit. No full-size tensor is
allocated, and no full-size `.grad` is left on a leaf after backward. If
the output cannot be written in place, for example because it has
overlapping memory, the cut falls back to a copy.

Stacked on the looped-stack and bypassed-stack fixes, which also edit
the cut hook.

#### Tests

New `tests/test_frozen_prefix_skip_inplace_between_layers.py`:
- the cut is exact for -0.0, 0.0, NaN and inf, requires grad, and is not
a leaf;
- a toy stack that writes in place between layers, with reentrant and
non-reentrant checkpointing;
- the tiny Qwen3-VL image batch above.

Each case must engage the skip and match skip off bitwise. The test
loads `_frozen_prefix.py` from its own tree and asserts it.

| Arm | transformers 4.57.6 | transformers 5.22.1 |
|---|---|---|
| main | 5 failed, 1 passed | 3 failed (Qwen3-VL already clones there),
3 passed |
| this branch | 6 passed | 6 passed |

All frozen-prefix tests pass on this branch.

## Not proven here

Recompile count and step time under the default block compile on GPU,
and a run with real Qwen3-VL weights.

Studio: list each GGUF repo from the Hub once per 2 minutes, and wait out a 429 (#18644)

**Problem:** Users without an HF token keep hitting the Hub's anonymous
API rate limit (500 requests per 5 minutes per IP). Measured on a fresh
Studio, opening the chat model picker sends 6 GGUF variant lookups, and
the backend turns each into a full `model_info(files_metadata=True)`
call. The browser keeps that answer for 30 seconds and the backend not
at all, so every reopen repeats all of them. A 429 is also retried on
the very next open, since nothing remembers it.

**Fix:** `list_gguf_variants` keeps the Hub listing for 2 minutes per
repo, credential and `HF_ENDPOINT`. A 429 is remembered until its
`Retry-After` passes (60 s if absent, capped at 10 minutes), and in that
window the existing local cache fallback answers instead of asking the
Hub again. Other failures are not remembered, so an offline blip or a
gated repo behaves exactly as before. The per-download-state fields of
the response are still computed fresh on every request; only the Hub
listing is shared.

**Testing**
- Real Hub, `unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF` listed 6 times in a row: 6
`model_info` calls on `main`, 1 on this branch, same 26 variants.
- `tests/test_gguf_listing_cache.py` (new): one call per window and per
credential, a fresh call after the window, a 429 waits out
`Retry-After`, other failures are retried. 3 of its 4 tests fail with
the `gguf.py` change reverted (the 4th, other failures retried, passes
on both by design).
- All 67 backend test files that touch GGUF variant listing: the failing
set is identical on `main` and this branch (pre-existing environment
failures here), and this branch adds the 4 new passes.

Studio: keep a Windows iGPU's carve-out usable when a load is memory-mapped (#18448)

Fixes https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/issues/18001

## Problem

On a Windows Vulkan iGPU with a BIOS carve-out, a paged (memory-mapped)
load used only about half of the dedicated GPU memory. The reporter's
Ryzen 7 8700G / Radeon 780M has a 16 GiB carve-out; Vulkan reads 23161
MiB free (16 GiB dedicated plus 7.8 GiB shared). Studio launched
gemma-4-12B-it-qat UD-Q4_K_XL with

```
--fit on --fit-target 512 ... --load-mode mmap --fit-target 15872
```

so llama.cpp's fitter could only use 23157 - 15872 = 7285 MiB, put 42 of
49 layers on the GPU and the rest on the CPU, even though the whole
model (8306 MiB with context) fits in the carve-out. Task Manager after
the load: 7.3 / 16.0 GB dedicated in use.

Two things combine. First, the load should never have been paged: in
Manual mode with Auto layers Studio launches with `--fit on`, and its
host-RAM preflight credits a shared iGPU's memory only when argv forces
every layer onto the GPU. Under `--fit on` it credited nothing, priced
the whole model as system RAM ("About 7 GB of this model does not fit in
GPU memory and would run from system RAM"), and switched the load to
mmap. A discrete card is credited in the same situation.

Second, the 15872 is the paging headroom from #16857: a flat
`_IGPU_PAGED_FIT_HEADROOM_MIB` (15 GiB) added to the margin whenever an
oversized load is switched to mmap on a Windows iGPU. It was measured on
a 127 GiB Strix Halo, where it keeps the fit out of the shared memory
that also backs the mapped pages. On an iGPU whose carve-out is smaller
than that, it takes most of the carve-out away. On this machine almost
every load takes that path: with 16 GiB of system RAM left to Windows, a
6 GB model already prices as oversized.

## Change

1. Pricing: when the fitter owns placement (`--fit on`, no layer cap,
nothing pinned to the CPU), the preflight now credits a shared Vulkan
iGPU with what the fitter can place there: its free reading less the
`--fit-target` margin, still bounded by what host RAM can back (the same
bound as the every-layer case). On the reporter's readings gemma-4-12B
(6.24 GiB) and gpt-oss-20b (11.3 GiB) are no longer priced as oversized:
no false warning, no mmap override, plain `--fit-target 512`. A model
larger than the pool (21 GiB in the test) is still priced as oversized
and paged.

2. Headroom, for loads that are really oversized: For a single Vulkan
iGPU on Windows, the headroom is now capped at what the device reads
above the free part of its carve-out. The carve-out size is the DirectX
`DedicatedVideoMemory` + `DedicatedSystemMemory` value Studio already
reads for the carve-out advice; its use is the `GPU Adapter
Memory\Dedicated Usage` counter of the same adapter (joined on its
LUID):

`headroom = min(15360, max(0, raw_free - (carve_out - dedicated_used)))`

so the fit still stays out of shared memory, which is what the headroom
is for, but can use the whole free carve-out. For the reporter (about
0.3 GB of the carve-out in use before the load): headroom about 7.1 GiB,
and the fitter gets about 15.8 GiB, enough for every layer.

Unchanged: no carve-out or usage reading (Intel, two adapters, registry
or counter failure), a carve-out at its automatic size, a large
carve-out with 15 GiB or more of shared memory on top (the Strix Halo
case from #16857), ROCm/CUDA iGPUs, Linux, more than one device, and
every case #16857 already skipped (fitter off, a user `--fit-target`,
per-device lists). When the carve-out covers everything the device
reads, no headroom pair is added. The per-device margins and the
arch-crash retry withdraw the same amount that was added.

Note: #18352 edits the same helper for Windows ROCm APUs (raising the
margin there); the two touch different backends and should merge cleanly
in either order apart from the `_paged_fit_headroom_flags` signature.

## Testing

- New full `load_model` pricing test on the reporter's readings (Vulkan
row 22137 MiB, 7843 MiB available of 15992 MiB RAM, Manual mode):
gemma-12B and gpt-oss-20b launch unpaged with no warning (both fail on
main), a 21 GiB model is still paged.
- New full `load_model` headroom test on a simulated 780M (Vulkan row
22137 MiB, 16 GiB carve-out with 300 MiB used, Manual mode with Auto
layers, the reporter's path): main emits `--fit-target 15872`, this
branch a margin that leaves exactly the free carve-out to the fitter. A
half-occupied carve-out keeps a correspondingly larger margin. Controls
(automatic 512 MiB carve-out, 96 GiB Strix Halo carve-out, unreadable
carve-out, unreadable usage) emit 15872 on both. The headroom helper,
the LUID join of the usage counter, the flag, margin and withdrawal math
have unit tests; the behaviour tests fail on main.
- Real Windows hardware (AMD DevLab, Radeon 8060S / gfx1151, Windows 11,
Adrenalin 32.0.32015.7029, the reporter's llama.cpp build
b12347-mix-241a0f3, Vulkan), base vs this branch running Studio's own
readers: carve-out 337 MiB (automatic), Vulkan free 99437 MiB, Dedicated
Usage counter read for that adapter (35.8 MB). Both emit `--fit-target
15872` and llama-server loads a Qwen3-0.6B Q4_K_M with `--fit on
--load-mode mmap`. So this host is unchanged, as intended; its carve-out
cannot be set to the reporter's 16 GiB, so the 780M case itself is
covered by the simulated test only.
- `test_llama_cpp_placement.py`, `test_llama_server_args.py`,
`test_amd_apu_unified_memory.py`, `test_igpu_carveout_advice.py`,
`test_llama_cpp_gpu_oom_respawn.py`, `test_llama_cpp_context_fit.py`:
1306 passed on this branch vs 1297 on main, with the same 16
failing/erroring test IDs on both (local environment: no GPU, missing
optional modules).

Studio: list safetensors models under the chat picker's Safetensors filter on GPU hosts (#18636)

**Problem:** In the chat model picker, Discover with the **Safetensors**
filter is empty on every machine that is not a Mac: NVIDIA, AMD (ROCm)
and Intel GPU hosts all show nothing, and so do CPU-only machines. This
is not Hugging Face rate limiting. The listing arrives and GGUF rows
still show; the safetensors rows are dropped by the Discover gate before
the format filter runs.

## Why it happens

Discover keeps a Hub result only if it matches the Recommended rule
(every GGUF, plus FP8 / NVFP4 checkpoints only where the GPU runs them
natively). The one exception is a Mac, which also gets plain safetensors
and MLX. `checkpoint_quant_formats` is `[]` on anything but an sm_89+
NVIDIA card, so on AMD, Intel, older NVIDIA cards and CPU hosts no plain
safetensors repo ever becomes a Discover row, and picking the
Safetensors filter leaves an empty list with no explanation. The header
picker never had this gap: it lists every format on any host that is not
chat-only.

## Fix

- When the Safetensors filter is picked and the host runs checkpoints
(not chat-only), Discover lists plain safetensors repos with the same
browse gates the Mac path uses (support check, provider logo or likes,
no GPTQ / AWQ / EXL2 names, no MLX). The default "All" view is
unchanged, so the Recommended list most users see stays the same.
- A chat-only host (GGUF only) still lists none, and the empty state now
says "This device runs GGUF models only." instead of a bare "No models".
- Fewer Hub requests for sizes: a plain checkpoint's size now comes from
the listing's per-dtype tensor counts, which the search already fetches,
instead of one `/tree/main` listing per row. MLX rows keep their file
listing, since the Hub counts packed MLX weights at full width. A failed
size listing (often a 429) now waits 5 minutes before it is asked again,
instead of being re-sent on every new page.

GRPO vLLM sync on TRL >= 0.28: stream merged LoRA weights without merging into the training model (#18638)

## Summary

With `fast_inference = False` and a PEFT LoRA model, TRL >= 0.28 syncs
its own vLLM engine through `VLLMGeneration.sync_weights`. That calls
`_iter_named_params`, and its PEFT branch runs `model.merge_adapter()`
and then `model.unmerge_adapter()` on the training model. In bf16 or
fp16 this round trip rounds twice (`W + BA - BA != W`), so the frozen
base weights change a little on every sync. The model being trained
slowly moves away from the checkpoint, and vLLM gets `round(round(W) +
BA)` instead of `W + BA` rounded once.

Unsloth already avoids this on TRL < 0.28. There, `_move_model_to_vllm`
goes through `_unsloth_vllm_sync_peft_merged`, which computes the merged
weight out of place. This PR uses the same merged-tensor stream on TRL
>= 0.28:

- `_unsloth_vllm_iter_peft_merged` is factored out of
`_unsloth_vllm_sync_peft_merged`, and the TRL < 0.28 path now uses it
too, with the same behaviour.
- `VLLMGeneration._iter_named_params` is wrapped. For an unsharded,
mergeable PEFT model it yields merged copies (`W + scaling * B @ A` in
fp32, rounded once) under the same vLLM names, so it serves both
colocate and server mode. The training model is never mutated.
- Sharded runs (DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, FSDP), quantized or offloaded bases,
unmergeable adapters and dense models keep TRL's own branch.
`UNSLOTH_VLLM_INPLACE_MERGE=1` restores TRL's behaviour.
- The frozen-weight skip from #18609 still works: non-adapter frozen
weights are still yielded as the live tensors, so they are sent once.
Adapted weights arrive as fresh merged tensors and are sent every sync.
- Engagement counter:
`vllm_generation._unsloth_vllm_out_of_place_syncs`.

## Evidence

GRPO with TRL's own colocated vLLM on Colab L4. Setup:

- Libraries: TRL 1.15.0, vLLM 0.29.0, torch 2.13.0, transformers 5.17.0,
peft 0.22.0.
- Model: Qwen3-0.6B bf16, LoRA r=16 on all linear layers.
- Run: 50 steps, one sync per step.
- Arms: base is the merge base, head is this PR. Three runs each,
interleaved on one VM.

| | base (3 runs) | head (3 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| frozen base elements changed after 50 syncs | 2.02% / 2.02% / 2.13% |
0 / 0 / 0 |
| max abs change of a frozen weight | 7.3e-4 / 7.3e-4 / 9.8e-4 | 0 |
| LoRA'd weights sent to vLLM equal to `W0 + BA` rounded once | 0 of 196
| 196 of 196 |
| `sync_weights` median ms (20 calls each) | 315.0 / 305.0 / 311.8 |
305.9 / 299.3 / 295.9 |
| extra CUDA memory during a sync | 18 MiB | 42 MiB |
| out-of-place syncs counted | 0 | 50 |

- TRL 1.18.0 on the same stack, 2 runs each, gives the same picture:
- base: 2.26% of frozen elements changed, max 9.8e-4, 0 of 196 weights
exact, sync 315.9 / 320.8 ms
  - head: 0 changed, 196 of 196 exact, sync 303.0 / 301.4 ms
- QLoRA is not affected by this change. vLLM 0.29 rejects
`quantization=bitsandbytes`, so a 4-bit base cannot start TRL's own vLLM
engine on either arm. Quantized bases keep TRL's path here.
- Sync time is not slower. The head medians sit at or below the base A/A
spread.
- Reward over 50 steps is the same within run-to-run noise:
  - base mean: -1.49 / -1.53 / -1.53
  - head mean: -1.50 / -1.51 / -1.49
- Over a longer run the drift compounds. On CPU, with the adapter moving
between syncs, a tiny bf16 Qwen3 had 46% of base elements changed after
200 syncs.

## Tests

`tests/test_vllm_generation_peft_sync_no_drift.py` (CPU, under 1 s):

- On the merge base, with TRL 1.15 installed: 6 failed, 1 passed. The
real `VLLMGeneration.sync_weights` test fails with
`q_proj.base_layer.weight drifted after sync 1`.
- On this branch: all pass with TRL 0.24 (the real-TRL test is skipped
there), TRL 1.15 and TRL 1.18.
- The existing vLLM sync suites still pass:
`test_vllm_sync_skips_frozen_weights.py`,
`test_grpo_move_model_to_vllm_sync.py` and
`test_online_dpo_move_model_to_vllm_sync.py`.

DoRA factored norm: fp32 rank terms on GPUs above rank 32, no fp64 on XPU, fp16 accumulation fallback (#18629)

Follow-up fixes for #18515, found while re-checking the PRs merged on
2026-11-19. One commit per fix; every fix has a test that fails on main
and passes here.

| Fix | Follows up | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| DoRA norm: float64 rank terms only on CPU and on CUDA / ROCm up to
rank 32 | #18515 | P1 |
| DoRA norm: float32 fallback for float16 weights under
allow_fp16_accumulation | #18515 | P1 |

## Tests (this branch vs main `54af93780b`, CPU)

- New and changed tests: main 9 failed / 12 passed, this branch 21
passed. Each test loads the code of its own tree.
- Neighbouring suites on this branch: DoRA suites: 40 passed.
- `prepush_gate.py` passes.

## DoRA norm: float64 rank terms only on CPU and on CUDA / ROCm up to
rank 32 (follows up #18515)

#### DoRA factored norm: float64 rank terms only where float64 exists
and is cheap

##### What broke

#18515 computes the rank-sized terms of the factored DoRA norm (`A @
A.T`, `B @ (A @ A.T)`) in float64 on every device except MPS
(`_rank_dtype` in `unsloth/kernels/dora.py`). That causes two problems.

1. **Intel Arc XPUs have no float64.** PyTorch raises `Required aspect
fp64 is not supported on the device` there (intel/torch-xpu-ops#628,
pytorch/pytorch#147731; Unsloth already guards the same case in Studio,
#14848). The patch is installed at import with no fallback, so every
DoRA forward on such a device fails, where PEFT's dense path ran before.
2. **High-rank DoRA is slow on consumer NVIDIA cards.** The rank terms
cost `4 r^2 (d_in + d_out)` float64 FLOPs per call, and float64 runs at
1/64 rate on T4, L4 and RTX cards. At `d_in = d_out = 4096`:

| r | float64 FLOPs | cross-term bf16 GEMM FLOPs | float64 time on an L4
(about 0.49 TFLOPS) |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 16 | 4.2 M | 1.07 G | about 9 us (launch bound) |
   | 64 | 67 M | 4.3 G | about 0.14 ms |
   | 256 | 1.07 G | 17.2 G | about 2.2 ms |

The cross-term GEMM reads W once (about 0.1 ms on an L4). At rank 256
the float64 part is about 20x that. A reported RTX 3090 measurement of a
rank-256 Qwen3-0.6B DoRA step was 261 ms on this code vs 95 ms with
`UNSLOTH_DORA_FACTORED_NORM=0`, with 183 ms of it in the float64 GEMMs.

##### Fix

`_rank_dtype(device, rank)`:
- float64 on CPU.
- float64 on CUDA (including ROCm) up to rank 32.
- float32 everywhere else: MPS, XPU, and CUDA above rank 32.

The rank is a static weight shape, so the choice adds no guard,
recompile or host query. float32 rank terms lose precision only when the
user enables TF32. With realistic updates they stay within 1e-5 of fp64
at rank 64 and 256.

##### Tests

New `tests/test_dora_factored_norm_fp64_devices.py` (CPU, prints the
`dora.py` it loaded):
- The rank dtype per device and rank.
- The float32 rank path produces no float64 tensor (a TorchFunctionMode
raises on any float64 output, as the device would).
- Accuracy against an fp64 oracle: realistic, 97% cancellation, and
ranks 64 / 256.

| Arm | Result (new file + `tests/test_dora_factored_norm.py`) |
|---|---|
| origin/main 635532fede | 7 failed, 28 passed |
| this branch | 35 passed |

##### Not covered

- Not run on a real Intel Arc GPU.
- The step-time change was not timed here. The float64 cost above is a
FLOP estimate plus the reported RTX 3090 measurement.

## DoRA norm: float32 fallback for float16 weights under
allow_fp16_accumulation (follows up #18515)

#### DoRA factored norm: chunked float32 cross term for float16 under
allow_fp16_accumulation

##### What broke

#18515 computes the DoRA cross term with `torch.mm(A_2, W.t(), out_dtype
= torch.float32)` on CUDA. cuBLAS refuses float16 inputs with a float32
output when `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_accumulation` is on.
The check is in `aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDABlas.cpp`,
`gemm_internal<at::Half, float>` and `gemm_and_bias` (torch 2.10 and
2.14):

`TORCH_CHECK(false, "gemm input type at::Half and output type float is
not supported with allowFP16AccumulationCuBLAS")`

So every float16 DoRA forward crashed with that flag set. A Colab L4 and
A100 (torch 2.14.1) run of the factored norm reproduced the RuntimeError
on origin/main.

##### Fix

Only when the weight is float16 and the flag is on, the cross term takes
the existing chunked float32 GEMM: W upcast in 64 MiB row chunks, which
is exact for float16 values. Every other case keeps `mm.dtype`
unchanged. The common path gains one host-side flag read and no kernels.

Reading the flag inside a trace is a graph break
(`torch._C._get_cublas_allow_fp16_accumulation`). The helper therefore
goes through `torch.compiler.assume_constant_result`, so a compiled
graph takes the value at trace time. It is compile-clean under
`fullgraph = True` on torch 2.10 and 2.14.

##### Tests

New `tests/test_dora_factored_norm_fp16_accumulation.py` (CPU; the CUDA
route is selected with a patched `is_cuda` and a spy on `torch.mm`;
prints the `dora.py` it loaded):
- float16 / bfloat16 weight, with the flag off and on. Only float16 with
the flag on skips `mm(..., out_dtype = ...)`. The norm stays within 1e-5
of fp64 in all four cells.
- Reading the flag compiles under `fullgraph = True` with no graph
break.

| Arm | Result (new file + `tests/test_dora_factored_norm.py`) |
|---|---|
| origin/main 635532fede | 2 failed, 22 passed |
| this branch | 24 passed |

##### Not covered

- Not run on a GPU here.
- Two edge cases are left as they are on main:
- a float32 `lora_A` entry above 65504 with a float16 base gives a NaN
norm;
- the low half of the float16 split is subnormal at Kaiming scale. The
Colab L4 / A100 runs showed no loss from that (fp64-oracle error about
1.5e-7 on both arms); T4 and RTX cards were not run.

## Not proven here

Intel Arc XPU was not run (no XPU available); the float64 crash is shown
with a device stub. The fp16 subnormal precision concern did not show on
T4, L4 or A100 and is untested on consumer Ampere cards. A float32
lora_A above 65504 with a float16 base still gives a NaN norm (unchanged
from main).

## QAT round checksum hashes 8-byte dtypes by their bits (follows up
#18434)

#### QAT round: checksum the bits of 8-byte dtypes, not their values

##### What broke

#18434 marks a rounded QAT base weight with `_checksum`
(`unsloth/models/_qat_round.py`) so a later device move or reload of the
same values is recognised as already rounded. `_checksum` views 1, 2 and
4 byte dtypes as integers, but an 8-byte dtype (float64) is converted by
value with `.to(torch.int64)`. Every float64 tensor below 1 in magnitude
therefore hashes to 0 and matches any other float64 tensor of the same
shape: two random 64 x 64 float64 weights give the same checksum.

Reachability today: none found. torchao fake quantization rejects
float64 inputs (`Unsupported input dtype: torch.float64`), so no QAT
model rounds a float64 weight yet. This is a latent fix so the checksum
means what its docstring says.

##### Fix

View every dtype wider than 2 bytes as int32 words (4-byte dtypes
exactly as before; 8-byte dtypes as two words). Checksums of 1, 2 and 4
byte dtypes are unchanged.

##### Tests

New `tests/test_qat_round_checksum_bits.py` (CPU): different values give
different checksums and a clone gives the same one, for float64 /
float32 / bfloat16 / float16; the file asserts it imports its own tree.

| Arm | Result (new file + `tests/test_qat_round_rewrite.py` +
`tests/test_qat_weight_memo_guards.py`) |

passed, 1 skipped |
| this branch | 31 passed, 1 skipped |

## QAT round: re-round after an in-place reload under inference mode
(follows up #18434)

#### QAT round: detect an in place reload of an inference-tensor base
weight by value

##### What broke

#18434 re-rounds a rounded QAT base weight that was rewritten after
preparation. It detects the rewrite from `(data_ptr, _version)`. An
inference tensor (built under `torch.inference_mode`, as base weights
shared with vLLM can be) has no version counter, so its state is
`(data_ptr, None)` before and after an in place reload.

Repro (CPU): prepare a real torchao int8 QAT LoRA model under
`torch.inference_mode()`, then `load_state_dict` a different base weight
into the same storage, still under inference mode.
- The post-load hook and a later `round_frozen_qat_weights` both treat
the weight as unchanged.
- The raw incoming weight stays in service with fake quantization off.
- It is 0.0162 away (max abs) from per call fake quantization of the
same weight.

The parent behaves the same way.

##### Fix

For an unversioned weight whose `(pointer, None)` state did not change,
compare its values with the checksum recorded at rounding time. A
mismatch is handled like a versioned rewrite: the quantizer comes back
and the weight is rounded again, in place under inference mode.
Versioned weights take exactly the old path. The extra checksum runs
only for inference-tensor weights, on load and on
`round_frozen_qat_weights`.

##### Tests

New `tests/test_qat_round_inference_reload.py` (CPU, asserts it imports
its own tree):
- An inference weight reloaded through `load_state_dict` or `copy_` then
`round_frozen_qat_weights` matches `UNSLOTH_QAT_ROUND_INPLACE=0`
bitwise, and the quantizer is off again (rounded in place).
- An unchanged inference weight is not rounded twice. int8 rounding is
not idempotent, so a second rounding would show.

| Arm | Result (new file + `tests/test_qat_round_rewrite.py` +
`tests/test_qat_weight_memo_guards.py`) |
|---|---|
| origin/main 635532fede | 2 failed, 28 passed, 1 skipped |
| this branch | 30 passed, 1 skipped |

## QAT round: cross-recipe state_dict loads keep the target fake
quantizer (follows up #18434)

#### QAT round: name the fake quantization recipe in the rounded-weight
marker

##### What broke

#18434 marks a rounded QAT base weight in `state_dict()` metadata with a
checksum of its values. A load whose incoming weight matches the marker
is kept as already rounded. The marker does not say which grid the
values were rounded to.

Repro (CPU, real torchao QAT layers):
1. Load an int8-prepared model's `state_dict()` into an int4-prepared
model.
2. The checksum matches, so the destination keeps the int8-rounded
values verbatim with its int4 quantizer off.
3. Its output differs from per call int4 fake quantization of the same
weights (up to 0.0059 on the weight).

The reverse direction behaves the same. The parent also left the
destination disabled.

##### Fix

The marker now carries the quantizer type and its config repr (dtype,
granularity, mapping, precision). A marked weight from another recipe
fails the check and is rounded for this module like any new weight.
Same-recipe loads, including through `torch.save` /
`torch.load(weights_only = True)`, are still kept as is. Markers written
by the previous format no longer match, so those loads are rounded again
(the pre-marker behaviour).

##### Tests

New `tests/test_qat_round_recipe_marker.py` (CPU, asserts it imports its
own tree): int8 to int4 and int4 to int8, in memory and through
`torch.save` / `torch.load`. The destination must match
`UNSLOTH_QAT_ROUND_INPLACE=0` bitwise and end with its quantizer off.

## NF4 dequant cache: inference-tensor scales and packed weights
(follows up #18433)

#### NF4 dequant cache: read each scale's version on its own; never
cache an inference packed weight

##### What broke

#18433 keys a cached dense NF4 weight on the address and version of
every scale tensor (`_scales_key`). When any of them was an inference
tensor (no version counter), the whole key fell back to `(absmax
pointer, None)`. That dropped the versions of the ordinary scales too.

Repro (CPU, real bitsandbytes nested NF4 state):
1. Make only `offset` an inference tensor and admit the weight to the
cache.
2. Double `state2.absmax` in place, outside inference mode.
3. The next lookup is a hit and returns the old dense weight, 1.47 away
(max abs) from a fresh decode. Making `absmax` the inference tensor
instead behaves the same.

Separately, an inference packed weight raised `RuntimeError: Inference
tensors do not track version counter` on admission.

No default training path was found that builds these states. They need
weights or scales created under `torch.inference_mode` that outlive it.

##### Fix

- `_version(t)` returns `None` for an inference tensor and `t._version`
otherwise. `_scales_key` reads it per tensor, so one inference tensor no
longer hides writes to the others.
- `_lookup` decodes an inference packed weight afresh instead of
admitting it.

The ordinary path is unchanged apart from one `is_inference()` call per
tensor on the hit path, which is host only.

##### Tests

New `tests/test_nf4_dequant_cache_inference_tensors.py` (CPU, reuses the
scales test fixtures, asserts it imports its own tree):
- An inference `offset` or `absmax` with an in place write to
`state2.absmax` is served fresh.
- An inference packed weight is decoded and not admitted.

| Arm | Result (new file + the three existing
`tests/test_nf4_dequant_cache*.py`) |

| origin/main 635532fede | 3 failed, 42 passed |
| this branch | 45 passed |

Studio: show why the NPU model list failed in the chat model picker (#18528)

**Problem:** When the NPU model list fails, the chat model picker hides
the whole NPU section and shows no message. A user with a working NPU
just sees no NPU models. This happened on a Windows laptop where Smart
App Control blocked `lemond.exe`.

**Change:** The picker keeps the NPU section and shows why the list
failed. The backend no longer answers a bare "Internal Server Error" for
three failures. When `lemond` cannot start or stops answering, it
returns a readable error. An unreadable folder of converted models is
skipped, and the list loads.

**Status:** Tested live on the AMD DevLab Strix Halo runners, Linux and
Windows, against `main`.

![Before and
after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oobabooga/unsloth/pr-media/pr/npu-list-error/before-after-127033317109.png)

## Why it happens

When `GET /api/npu/models` fails, the error is stored in `listError`.
The Hub shows it, but the composer picker only draws the NPU notice
before the runtime is ready. With no rows, the NPU section is dropped.

Three backend failures also reached the route as unhandled exceptions
(HTTP 500):

- **`lemond` cannot be spawned:** `Popen` raises `OSError`, for example
when Smart App Control refuses `lemond.exe`.
- **`lemond` stops answering after it started:**
`LemonadeServer.request` raises `LemonadeUnavailable`.
- **A folder of converted Q4NX models cannot be read** (#17636): the
permission checks raise `PermissionError` and fail the whole list.

## Fix

- `composer-model-picker.tsx`, `npu-rows.ts`: Discover shows the NPU
notice when the runtime is not ready or the list failed
(`npuNoticeShown`). The notice already renders `listError`.
- `npu_backend.py`: both `lemond` failures become `NpuError`, so the
route answers 409 with the message. A Windows code integrity refusal
gets the existing `code_integrity_user_message` that `llama-server`
uses, which names Smart App Control. An exit status of 0xC0000602 alone
is reported as a crash, since an ordinary crash can also exit with it.
- `lemonade_server.py`: keeps the exit status of a `lemond` that died
during startup, read before Studio's own kill. One still running at the
deadline is reported as a health check timeout.
- `npu_local_models.py`: an unreadable folder is skipped with a warning.
Files are checked with `lstat()`, so on Python 3.14 a denied file is not
mistaken for a missing one.

## Not changed

- The On Device tab still shows no NPU notice when the list fails.
- Smart App Control still blocks `lemond.exe`. This PR shows the block
and names the fix.

## Testing

Live on DevLab Strix Halo: `main` and `main` plus this PR side by side,
NPU enabled on both.

| Case | `main` | PR |
|---|---|---|
| Healthy list (Linux, Windows) | 50 models | 50 models |
| Unreadable scan folder (Linux) | HTTP 500 | 50 models |
| `lemond` cannot be spawned (Linux, Windows) | HTTP 500 | HTTP 409,
"Lemonade could not start (...): Permission denied / Access is denied" |
| `lemond` killed, list requested while it exits (Linux) | HTTP 500 |
HTTP 409, "Listing NPU models failed: ... Connection refused" |

The DevLab Windows runner has Smart App Control off, so the real refusal
(`winerror` 4551, exit status 0xC0E90002) is covered by unit tests only.

New unit tests in `test_npu_backend.py`, `test_npu_local_models.py` and
`composer-npu-rows.test.ts` cover each case above, the code integrity
messages and the startup timeout. The backend tests fail on `main`. NPU
backend tests: 554 passed, 1 skipped on Python 3.13; the two changed
test files also pass on Python 3.14. Frontend typecheck and picker tests
pass.

[Bug] AMD NPU: non-streaming chat completions return no usage (#18577)

Non-streaming `/v1/chat/completions` on an AMD NPU model never returns
`usage`, so the OpenAI SDK reads `usage=None`. Streaming with
`stream_options.include_usage` does return it.

**Cause.** `_npu_chat_completions` always streams from FastFlowLM and
collects the stream for a JSON caller. FastFlowLM sends usage in its own
empty-choices chunk, and `_proxy_to_external_provider` drops that chunk
unless the payload opts in (`_is_openai_usage_only_sse`). The
non-streaming payload never opts in, so `_NpuStreamRelay` never sees
usage and the collected body has none.

**Fix.** When the caller didn't ask for a stream, set
`stream_options.include_usage` on the upstream copy of the payload.
Streaming requests are unchanged.

**Test.** `test_non_streaming_reply_keeps_a_separate_usage_chunk` makes
the fake FastFlowLM send usage the way the real one does: a separate
chunk, only on `include_usage`. It fails on main with `KeyError:
'usage'` and passes here. The existing fake put usage inline on the
finish chunk, which the proxy never drops, so the existing test passed
on main. All 657 NPU backend tests pass (2 skipped).

Studio: skip a render's prompt upsampler when it cannot fit on the GPU (#18627)

#17792 made the prompt enhancer on by default for MiniMax-H3-Image,
matching its reference workflow, next to the FLUX.3 Klein upsampler.
Both run Qwen3.5-9B (UD-Q4_K_XL, about 6 GB) on the llama-server
sidecar. The sidecar sizes `-ngl` to the memory the loaded image model
leaves free, so with less free memory than the GGUF needs, most layers
end up on the CPU.

An outside benchmark measured this on simulated 8, 12 and 16 GB cards
(RTX 6000 Ada with ballast) with MiniMax-H3-Image:

- The first enhanced render took 512 s, of which 507 s was before the
sampler. The next three took 574 s, 608 s and 609 s, about 608 s median.
Later captions hit the 600 s request timeout ("failed (timed out);
prompt as typed").
- The same render with the enhancer off took about 7.8 s.
- The split server also held about 2.8 GB of the simulated card.

`release_if_tight` then unloads the server after every call on such a
card, so each render starts it again.

The default stays on. This PR keeps the enhancer wherever it can run on
the GPU, and stops a render from waiting minutes on a mostly-CPU decode.

## Change

`flux3_prompt_upsampler.py`:

- `enhance_for_generation` (the generate path, used by both families)
now requires every layer to fit on the accelerator. It does this through
a context variable, so no signatures change.
- In `_spawn_server`, if the layer plan for a CUDA or ROCm host that
holds the image model is anything other than all layers, the render's
start raises `UpsamplerUnavailableError` before a port is reserved or a
process is spawned. The render then runs the prompt as typed with
`prompt_enhancement: "unavailable"`. The frontend already treats that
status as silent and keeps the toggle on, so the next render tries again
when memory allows. The log names the free memory and the planned
`-ngl`.
- A server that is already running split, for example started by a
preview, is not used for a render either.
- Unchanged:
- Cached captions still apply, because the check sits at the server
start.

GRPO PrefixGrouper: cover transformers-native Qwen3-MoE attention (opt-in) (#18616)

## Summary

GRPO PrefixGrouper (shared-prompt dedup: one forward over `[prompt, c_0
.. c_{G-1}]` instead of G full rows) never engaged on MoE models. Both
GRPO gates excluded every config with `num_experts` /
`moe_intermediate_size`, because Qwen3-MoE loads through FastModel with
transformers' own attention, which drops `prefix_seg_info` and would
leak completions into each other (9.05 nats on a tiny Qwen3-MoE when
forced on main).

This PR adds an opt-in path for Qwen3-MoE:

- `unsloth/utils/prefix_grouper_hf.py` (new): a per-class wrapper on
`Qwen3MoeAttention.forward`. On a call that carries a segment table, it
points the attention-interface lookup at the existing shared-prefix flex
kernel for that one call, so transformers still computes q / k / v
(projections, q/k norm, RoPE). If the kernel was not reached, it raises
and the caller falls back to the packed path. Calls without a table run
the original forward unchanged, bit for bit.
- `prefix_seg_info_applied(model)`: when no hand-written forward is
marked, it asks the wrapper. Every decoder layer must qualify. A
qualifying MoE model is marked `_unsloth_prefix_grouper_moe_ok`.
- No-grad gate (`unsloth/models/rl_replacements.py`): the MoE exclusion
is lifted only for models with that mark.
- unsloth-zoo (companion PR unslothai/unsloth-zoo#2631): the grad-path
gate passes the model to `prefix_grouper_enabled(model)`, falling back
to the old no-argument form on older unsloth. Its MoE exclusion is
lifted the same way.

- `unsloth/models/_block_compile.py`: a compiled decoder block now keeps
the stock forward for any layer carrying a PrefixGrouper table, not only
Unsloth's own layers. The int segment table otherwise recompiled the
block at every new prompt length, which cost about 4.7 s per step on L4
and made the first A/B 2x slower.

The MoE block routes each token on its own, so sending the shared prompt
through once leaves every token's routing unchanged. Each expert also
receives the same set of distinct tokens as before, so no expert's grad
changes from zero to None.

Opt-in with `UNSLOTH_GRPO_PREFIX_GROUPER_MOE=1`. It stays off with
`UNSLOTH_GRPO_ROUTING_REPLAY=1`, because replay matches rows by
`position_ids` resets and the shared stream has none per completion. It
also stays off when `output_router_logits` puts the router aux loss into
the loss.

## Correctness

- CPU, fp32, tiny Qwen3-MoE (3 layers, 8 experts top-2, GQA),
`tests/test_prefix_grouper_qwen3_moe.py`, torch 2.15 / transformers 5.23
and torch 2.12 / transformers 4.57.6: 9 passed on both stacks.
- Per-completion logps vs unshared rows: max 4.8e-6 nats (sdpa) and
7.6e-6 (eager).
  - Changing one completion moves no other completion by a single ulp.
- Param grads, router and experts included: rel-L2 1.9e-6. On CPU, flex
has no backward, so this test swaps the kernel for a dense-mask SDPA
reference built only from the group specs.
- Flip, same tiny model with PrefixGrouper forced: main gives 9.05 nats,
this PR 1.0e-5. New block-compile test fails on main and passes here.
- Existing PrefixGrouper / DPO prefix-share suites: 94 passed, 2 skipped
on both base and head. zoo PrefixGrouper / zero-advantage suites: 492
passed on both.

- Colab L4, torch 2.14.1 / transformers 5.18 / TRL 1.15, real kernel:
  - Same pytest: 9 passed. fp32 logps 9.1e-6 nats, grads rel-L2 3.9e-6.
- Unsloth FastModel + LoRA on a tiny Qwen3-MoE (head_dim 128, 16 experts
top-4, gradient checkpointing), PrefixGrouper vs per-row: fp32 logps
1.9e-6, total LoRA grad rel-L2 7.1e-5 (48 grads, 16 on experts), kernel
reached on every layer. bf16: 0.11 / 3.0e-2. The fp32 match shows the
math is exact, so the bf16 gap is rounding.

## Speed (Colab L4, GRPO)

Setup: random-weight Qwen3-MoE with Qwen3-30B-A3B layer dims (128

2.801 | 0.6% | 186 per run | 9.26 GB |

Unsloth Studio: raise the mlx-vlm floor to 0.6.4 and hold the MLX gate to the installed unsloth-zoo's floors (#18487)

## Summary

Companion to https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth-zoo/pull/2618, which
raises unsloth-zoo's mlx-vlm floor to 0.6.4. This PR:

1. Raises Unsloth Studio's mlx-vlm install floor to match.
2. Fixes a gap in the MLX chat-only gate that the higher floor exposes.
3. Drops two guards for MLX APIs older than any stack the gate admits.

## What changed

**Install floor (`chore(studio): raise mlx-vlm install floor to
0.6.4`)**

`install_python_stack.py` (`_MLX_VLM_SPEC`) and the self-heal specs in
`utils/mlx_repair.py` (`_MLX_INSTALL_SPECS`) move from
`mlx-vlm>=0.4.4,<=0.8.0` to `>=0.6.4,<=0.8.0`. 0.6.4 is the last mlx-vlm
release that admits transformers 5.5; 0.6.5 and later need
`transformers>=5.14`.

**Chat-only gate (`fix(studio): hold the MLX chat-only gate to the
installed unsloth-zoo's MLX floors`)**

The gate that decides whether MLX training is usable compared the
installed stack against `_MLX_MIN_VERSIONS`. Those are the oldest floors
any published unsloth-zoo declares (mlx 0.22.0, mlx-lm 0.31.2, mlx-vlm
0.4.4). The `--local` overlay installs unsloth-zoo with `--no-deps`, so
nothing lifts an older stack to a newer zoo's floors. As a result, a
stack with mlx-vlm 0.6.3 or mlx 0.32.2 cleared the gate beside a zoo
that requires 0.6.4 or `==0.32.4`. That zoo then failed at runtime, or,
for mlx 0.32.2, read row 0's KV for every batch row in GQA decode.

The new `_mlx_minimum(name)` returns the higher of the gate's floor and
the lower bound the installed zoo declares (`>=`, `==` and `~=` all
count). The gate and the self-heal warning both use it. An older
published zoo still declares the old floors, so a working older stack
beside it is not forced into chat-only.

**Old MLX API guards (`chore(studio): drop guards for MLX APIs older
than the supported stacks`)**

- `mx.synchronize` already exists in mlx 0.22.0, the gate's lowest
floor, so the guard in `_drain_generation_streams` is removed.
- MLX diffusion only activates on `mlx>=0.32.0,<0.33.0`, where
`mx.device_info` exists (it ships from 0.30.4), so the
`mx.metal.device_info` fallback in the diffusion backend is removed.
- Comments citing mlx 0.30 and 0.32.3 are corrected.

The `mx.metal.device_info` fallback in `utils/hardware/hardware.py`
stays. The gate still admits mlx below 0.30.4 beside an older zoo.

## Known limitation (pre-existing, unchanged)

The gate does not check the installed zoo's upper bounds. An older zoo
that declares a lower ceiling can clear the gate with a newer mlx-vlm.
The installer and the self-heal both honour the ceiling when they run.

## Validation

- New gate test: mlx-vlm 0.6.3 against a zoo declaring `>=0.6.4`, mlx
0.32.2 against `==0.32.4`, and mlx-lm 0.31.2 against `>=0.31.3` are each
blocked. The same stacks clear the gate against the old floors. The test
is mutation-checked: hard-coding `_MLX_MIN_VERSIONS` in place of
`_mlx_minimum` fails it.
- Install tests are updated to the new range: 0.6.3 and 0.8.1 are
rejected, 0.6.4 is accepted.

```bash
cd studio/backend && python -m pytest tests/test_mlx_inference_backend.py tests/test_utils.py tests/test_mlx_repair.py tests/test_mlx_stack_blockers.py -q
python -m pytest tests/studio/install/test_mlx_install.py tests/studio/install/test_dependency_pass_skips.py -q
```

Add opt-in memory and batch efficiency reports (#18603)

## Summary

Two opt-in diagnostics. Both are off by default; when the variable is
unset nothing is installed and no step does any extra work.

### `UNSLOTH_MEMORY_REPORT=1`

Per device, prints the memory held outside torch's caching allocator
(`total - free - reserved`: CUDA context, NCCL buffers, vLLM, cuBLAS
workspaces, other processes) at four points:

- model load (every `from_pretrained` return goes through
`_mark_requested_float32`)
- vLLM init (`fast_inference = True`, after `load_vllm` in `llama.py`
and `vision.py`)
- the first forward (a one-shot forward hook on the trainer's model)
- the first optimizer step (a `TrainerCallback`)

`torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved` never sees this memory, so it is the
part of an OOM the allocator numbers cannot explain. Each stage prints
once per model / trainer. Only devices this process already uses are
queried, so the report never opens a CUDA context on another card.

```
Unsloth: memory at first forward on cuda:0: 22.03 GB total, 21.12 GB free, torch reserved 0.68 GB (allocated 0.61 GB), outside torch's allocator 0.24 GB (CUDA context, NCCL, vLLM, other processes).
```

### `UNSLOTH_BATCH_REPORT=N` (`1` / `true` = 16)

Wraps the SFT trainer's `training_step` for the first N micro-batches
and prints one line: the share of token slots holding real tokens and
the share carrying a loss (the shifted causal targets, so a row's first
label is not counted, matching what the loss sees). Real tokens come
from `attention_mask`, else `packed_seq_lengths`, else every slot. It
sits outside `UNSLOTH_TOKEN_BUDGET`, so it sees each micro-batch before
any split. It costs one host sync per sampled micro-batch and nothing
after. A run shorter than N micro-batches prints its line at
`on_train_end`.

```
Unsloth: first 4 micro-batches (padded rows): 1,962 of 2,996 token slots hold real tokens (65.5%), 1,946 carry a loss (65.0%); 16 rows, widest 208 tokens.
Unsloth: first 4 micro-batches (padding-free): 1,962 of 1,962 token slots hold real tokens (100.0%), 1,946 carry a loss (99.2%); 4 rows, widest 550 tokens.
```

This makes it easy to compare padded rows against packing / padding-free
on your own data before choosing one.

## Tests

`tests/test_run_report.py` (CPU, 11 tests):

- token counts for padded rows, packed rows (`packed_seq_lengths`), and
padding-free rows without a mask but with `completion_mask`
- off by default: `training_step` is not wrapped, and the memory report
never touches `torch.cuda`
- the line prints exactly once after N micro-batches, every real
`training_step` still runs, and a short run is flushed at train end
- the memory report computes the outside-allocator figure, dedupes per
stage, and does not query a device the process has not used
- end to end on a tiny Llama with `transformers.Trainer`: the batch line
has the exact expected counts, the forward hook fires once, and the step
callback runs
- wiring: the SFT init installs the batch report after
`install_token_budget`, every TRL trainer gets the memory report, and
both load points and both vLLM init points call `report_memory`

The new tests fail on the base commit (the module does not exist) and
pass with the change. `tests/test_mfu_logging.py` and

| Arm | Report lines |
| --- | --- |
| reports off (padded rows) | none |
| padded rows | load, first forward, first optimizer step; batch line
65.5% real |

Skip the LoRA MLP down projection in gradient checkpoint replays (#18607)

## Summary

Under gradient checkpointing, the replay of a Llama-style decoder layer
re-runs the whole fused LoRA MLP, including the down projection.
`LoRA_MLP.backward` only reads `X`, `e` and `g`. The down output `i`
feeds `residual + i`, which is the layer output and so the checkpoint
output, and the checkpoint's nested backward never reads that value.
This PR skips `h = act(e) * g` and the down GEMM (plus its 4-bit
dequantize) during that replay. Gradients come out the same.

Needs the companion unsloth-zoo change (unslothai/unsloth-zoo#2630),
which adds `gradient_checkpoint_replay_module()`. With an older
unsloth_zoo nothing is skipped.

## When it engages

All of these have to hold:

- An Unsloth reentrant checkpoint (`unsloth_gradient_checkpoint`, the
offloaded one, or `UnslothCheckpointFunction`) is replaying, and its
checkpointed function is exactly this layer's call. The forms accepted
are the module itself, its bound `__call__` / `forward`, a
`functools.partial` over those (transformers'
`GradientCheckpointingLayer` and the block-compile `partial(forward,
self)`), or the tagged `custom_forward` in `LlamaModel_fast_forward`. If
one checkpoint wraps several layers, nothing is skipped.
- The layer is `LlamaDecoderLayer_fast_forward`, which covers Llama,
Qwen2, Qwen3 and Mistral. Gemma 2 / 3 (post-FFN norm), Cohere, Granite,
MoE and hybrid layers keep their own forwards and never arm the skip.
- Neither the layer nor the MLP has a forward hook, and there are no
global forward hooks.
- The MLP has no LoRA dropout and no LoRA bias.
- Nothing is being traced. Blocks compiled by block compile (torch >=
2.11 by default) still run the down projection: the arm call folds away
under tracing, and `fullgraph=True` still traces the layer.

`UNSLOTH_GC_SKIP_MLP_DOWN=0` turns it off.
`fast_lora.MLP_DOWN_SKIP_STATS["skipped"]` counts the skips.

## Tests

- `tests/test_gc_skip_replay_mlp_down.py` builds tiny Llama and Qwen3
models with PEFT LoRA and the real `LlamaDecoderLayer_fast_forward` and
`apply_lora_mlp_swiglu`. It runs three checkpointers against three call
forms. The skipped output is filled with NaN. Every LoRA gradient and
the input gradient must be bitwise equal to the same run with the skip
off, and the skip count must be exactly one per layer per backward. The
file also covers: a two-layer checkpoint (0 skips), a forward hook (that
layer is not skipped and its replay output stays real), LoRA dropout (0
skips), calls outside a replay (0 skips), a `fullgraph=True` compile of
the layer, and a check that only the Llama layer arms the skip. The
`UnslothCheckpointFunction` cases need CUDA; they passed on an L4.
- The zoo side adds `tests/test_gc_replay_module.py` (which call forms
resolve, set only during a replay, nested restore).
- On base, the new unsloth test fails 17 of 17 cases.

## Numbers

r=16 on all projections, `use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth"`, batch

Base and head arms were interleaved, 3 runs each. Base is the merge
base.

| 2048 | 1.459 s (1.405 to 1.461) | 1.365 s (1.363 to 1.385) | 1.474 s |
-6.5% |
| 4096 | 3.042 s (3.035 to 3.061) | 2.852 s (2.848 to 2.879) | 3.061 s |

Studio: fit the MCP match search to the room left for a reply (#18624)

Follow-up to #18529.

## Problem

1. Near a full context window, a later MCP lookup message can now come
back as an empty reply. #18529 adds the message's matching tools after
it as an `mcp_tool_search` exchange. That exchange sits next to the
message, so truncation cannot remove it, and on a near-full window it
takes the room the reply needed. Before #18529 the same turn either
answered or showed a clear "Message too long" error.
2. Each request checks the MCP tools remembered from earlier searches
one at a time at the start of the tool loop, and each check rebuilds the
whole tool catalog. Since #18529 every search card adds up to 5 names,
so this grows over a chat: 200 remembered names against a 346-tool
catalog took about 400 ms before the first model call.

## Change

- The match search gets at most the room left after the tool listing,
the message, a reply reserve (the larger of 1024 tokens and a quarter of
the window, as the knowledge-base whole-document budget uses) and a
512-token margin, capped at its existing 15% share. When nothing fits,
no search is added. The tools stay reachable through `mcp_tool_search`.
- Remembered tools are checked with the bulk `_mcp_tool_specs` lookup,
one catalog build for all of them.

## Results

Studio from current main vs main + this PR. `unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF`
Q4_K_M on CPU, 4096 window, a 96-tool MCP server. Second message =
filler text + a document lookup:

| second message | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| short lookup | `mcp_tool_search` card added | `mcp_tool_search` card
added |
| ~4,000 tokens (filler x186) | empty reply | answers, calls `list_user`
|
| ~4,140 tokens (filler x190) | empty reply after 7.9 s | "Message too
long: 4142 tokens exceeds the 4096-token context window" |

Controller setup with 200 remembered names and a 346-tool catalog: 398
ms on main, 6 ms with this PR.

## Tests

- `test_a_message_that_fills_the_window_gets_no_search_after_it`: fails
on main (the exchange is added), passes here.
- `test_controller_checks_remembered_tools_with_one_catalog_build`:
fails on main (6 catalog builds), passes here.
- MCP, llama.cpp and safetensors tool-loop, controller, external tool
result and admission suites pass.

AsyncGRPO: run prefix-trie rows through the FlexAttention tree mask on fast backbones (#18614)

## AsyncGRPO: run prefix-trie rows with a FlexAttention tree mask on
fast backbones

TRL >= 1.17 packs each AsyncGRPOTrainer row as a prefix trie
(`TreeRow`): tokens shared by several samples (the prompt, a common
system prompt, a shared multi-turn prefix) are forwarded once, and TRL's
`tree_attention` shows each segment the K/V of its root-to-segment path.
Unsloth's fast backbones ignore that attention implementation, so
`_forward_tree_unrolled` expanded every row back into one full copy per
sample. That is exact, but it forwards every shared prefix once per
sample, and because TRL budgets rows by unique tokens, the real forward
length is the packing ratio larger than the budget (3x to 4x for a
typical GRPO group).

### What changes

- `unsloth/utils/prefix_grouper_kernel.py`: a `TreeSegInfo` alongside
`PrefixSegInfo`. `TreeRow.pack` lays the trie out in DFS pre-order, so
every segment's subtree is one contiguous token range. One per-token
tensor `reach_end` then defines the mask: kv token `j` is visible to
query `q` iff `j <= q < reach_end[j]`. `build_tree_seg_info` checks the
pre-order layout and raises on anything else. `get_block_mask` picks the
tree `mask_mod` for a `TreeSegInfo`, and the existing flex path (compile
check, padding, block-mask cache) is reused unchanged.
- `unsloth/models/rl.py`: when the backbone's decoder layers apply
`prefix_seg_info` (Llama, Mistral, Qwen3, Cohere, Granite, ...) the row
is forwarded once over its unique tokens with
`prefix_seg_info=TreeSegInfo`. It is also checked against TRL's own
`tree_cu_seqlens_k` path lengths. Rows go through the unroll as before
when any of these holds:
  - the row has no fork (plain packing, where varlen is faster),
  - a path is longer than the sliding window,
- the model has softcapping, SSM / MoE layers or length-dependent RoPE,
- context parallelism is active, the device is not CUDA, or the kernel
fails its compile check (`PrefixGrouperCompileError` drops back to the
unroll),
  - `UNSLOTH_ASYNC_GRPO_TREE_ATTENTION=0` is set.
- The unroll now prints once when it expands a row by 2x or more, with
the unique and unrolled token counts, so an out-of-memory error under
TRL's unique-token budget can be explained. `_ASYNC_GRPO_TREE_COUNTS`
counts both paths.

### Tests

- `tests/test_prefix_grouper_tree_mask.py` (CPU):
- FlexAttention forward with the tree block mask equals TRL's
`tree_attention` definition on random DFS pre-order tries. That

Studio: build the MCP catalog once per loaded-tool lookup and price the listing off the event loop (#18486)

In MCP search mode, a tool loop looks up the full spec of every MCP tool
it has loaded. This covers `UNSLOTH_STUDIO_MCP_SEARCH_ONLY=1` and any
catalog too big to list in full (over 10% of the context window). The
lookup is `ToolLoopController.active_tools(include_deferred=True)`,
called on every GGUF tool round (`llama_cpp.py`), on every external
transport turn and on every executed call (`studio_tool_loop.py`). Each
name went through `_mcp_tool_spec` -> `tools.mcp_tool_spec`, and each of
those rebuilt the whole catalog through `_cached_mcp_catalog()`. That
opens `studio.db`, lists every server, re-resolves the managed rows (the
Blender launch path, the Unreal token file), and builds every server's
specs again (`public_tool`, `_mcp_tool_names`, `note_mcp_tool`). It then
keeps one spec and throws the rest away. With 10 loaded tools, every
round rebuilt the catalog 10 times. `mcp_tool_search` results went
through the same per-name path.

There is also a separate problem in `get_enabled_mcp_tools`, which a
send awaits. Its tail builds the specs and runs `_mcp_listing`, and that
tail ran on the event loop. When the catalog does not fit,
`_mcp_listing` prices the listing, the search declaration and each
preloaded tool with `count_chat_tokens`. That is a synchronous HTTP call
to llama-server on every cache miss.

## Change

- `core/inference/tools.py`: a new `mcp_tool_specs(names)` returns
`{name: spec}` from a single `_cached_mcp_catalog()` build. If two specs
share a name, the first one wins, which matches the old linear scan.
Names without the `mcp__` prefix never trigger a build.
`mcp_tool_spec(name)` now calls it. Nothing is cached between calls, so
an edit is still seen by the next lookup.
- `core/inference/tool_loop_controller.py`: `_mcp_tool_specs(names)`
makes one batch lookup and then neutralizes each spec on its own, as
before. `active_tools(include_deferred=True)` and
`_mcp_tool_search_specs` both use it, and they keep their order and
duplicates. `prepare_call` still looks up its single name.
- `get_enabled_mcp_tools`: the listing tail now runs in
`asyncio.to_thread`, as `cached_mcp_tools` already does for the count
route. Discovery, the on-loop re-read and the cache writes stay where
they were.

## Results

Real `studio.db` with N cached tools spread over HTTP servers (10, 12
and 30 tools per server). Median of 7 repeats, max minus min in
brackets. `main` was run twice as an A/A.

`active_tools(include_deferred=True)` with k loaded tools:

| N tools | k | main | main (A/A) | this PR | speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 30 | 10 | 7.02 ms (3.22) | 4.99 ms (0.33) | 1.02 ms (0.16) | 4.9x to
6.9x |
| 30 | 20 | 10.02 ms (2.46) | 9.85 ms (0.46) | 1.48 ms (0.19) | 6.8x |
| 96 | 5 | 4.16 ms (0.23) | 4.13 ms (0.14) | 1.26 ms (0.45) | 3.3x |
| 96 | 10 | 8.45 ms (1.25) | 8.50 ms (0.82) | 1.51 ms (0.56) | 5.6x |
| 96 | 20 | 16.74 ms (0.29) | 16.99 ms (0.72) | 1.91 ms (0.17) | 8.8x |
| 300 | 5 | 9.67 ms (4.34) | 8.51 ms (0.38) | 2.37 ms (0.18) | 3.6x to
4.1x |
| 300 | 10 | 17.19 ms (0.97) | 17.55 ms (11.43) | 2.77 ms (0.25) | 6.2x
|
| 300 | 20 | 36.50 ms (2.89) | 35.89 ms (3.25) | 2.99 ms (0.14) | 12x |

One catalog build (`_cached_mcp_catalog()`) costs 0.8 ms at 30 or 96
tools and 2.5 ms at 300. A round now pays roughly one build instead of

Event-loop blocking in `get_enabled_mcp_tools`: a 1 ms heartbeat task

Studio: import and export Appearance theme files (#16564)

## What

Appearance settings can now be exported as a theme file and imported
back, so people can share a look or try one someone else made. It lives
in Settings > Appearance under "Theme file", below Code.

- **Export** writes `<name>.unsloth-theme.json`: color theme, light and
dark colors, contrast, element outline, fonts and sizes, code display,
chat width, composer outline and glass (including where it shows).
Sidebar layout, and imported fonts plus the background image, are opt-in
switches.
- **Import** opens a preview before anything changes: the name, light
and dark swatches, what will change, and any warnings (unknown keys,
invalid or out-of-range values, an unknown color theme, a file from a
newer Studio). Apply shows a toast with **Undo**, which puts back the
previous look.
- Personal settings never leave the device and are never overwritten,
Undo included: light/dark/system mode, interface scale, reduce motion
and pointer cursors.

## File format

```jsonc
{
  "kind": "unsloth-studio.appearance",
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "name": "Midnight Matcha",
  "palette": "matcha",
  "look": { "colors": {...}, "contrast": 62, "uiFont": "Lato", "chatWidth": "wide", ... },
  "glass": { "material": "frosted", "strength": { "light": 40, "dark": 15 }, "lens": "off", "menus": true, "scope": "all" },
  "layout": {...},     // opt-in
  "fonts": [...],      // opt-in
  "background": {...}  // opt-in
}
```

`look` and `layout` use the customization field names directly. One
table, `FIELD_GROUP` in `appearance-theme/theme-file.ts`, says where
every `AppearanceCustomization` field goes (look, layout, fonts or
personal), and the typecheck fails if a new field has no entry. Applying
a theme first resets every look setting to its default, so the same file
always gives the same look; an older file just gets defaults for
settings added later, and a newer one is applied best-effort with a
warning.

## Untrusted input

- `JSON.parse` only, a 256 KB cap (8 MB when the file carries fonts or a
background) checked before the file is read, and at most 50 warnings
("And N more").
- Fields are read through own-property checks, so `__proto__` keys are
never followed, and every value goes through the existing
`sanitizeCustomization`, glass and background sanitizers.
- Embedded fonts must load through `FontFace.load()`, as in the font
picker, or they are dropped with a warning. Font names match
case-insensitively, as in CSS, and a theme never pushes a selected font
out of the 3-font limit.
- The background must be a PNG, JPEG or WebP base64 data URL and is
decoded and re-encoded through the normal upload path
(`uploadBackgroundImage`). No raw CSS, no URLs fetched.

## Also fixed

The sidebar menu's Appearance item defaults to visible in the frontend
since #16287, but the backend default (`SIDEBAR_MENU_ITEM_DEFAULTS`)
still said hidden, so a GET filled it in as hidden for records missing
it. It now says visible, and `sidebar-nav-backend-parity.test.ts` keeps
the two in sync.

## Verification

- `tests/appearance-theme-file.test.ts`: round trip, personal fields,
hostile input, case-variant and capped fonts, local fonts, layout
opt-in, unloadable fonts, Undo keeping personal settings.
- Frontend node suite, `npm run typecheck`, eslint on touched files,
`npm run i18n:check:strict`, and backend
`test_personalization_settings.py` pass.

## Before / after on two real installs

Two `install.sh --local` Studios, main and this branch, driven in
Chromium. The import file had a newer `schemaVersion`, an unknown key
and an out-of-range UI font size.

![Theme file
section](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielhanchen/unsloth-staging-2/pr-media/pr/16564/pr16564_pair_00-5333ba1fe1e2.png)

![Import

After Apply: Matcha, contrast 64, element outline 40, UI font size
