Merge pull request #2992 from d2lang/perf/10x-e2e

performance: speed up isometric SVG export, repeated renders and the e2e suite

tests: pin the golden comparison and two details of the isometric code

Nothing failed if the e2e golden comparison stopped comparing, because
the suite only hands it output that matches. Test both outcomes and
the acceptance path directly.

The order tree's tie-break test passed with the tie-break removed,
because its input was already sorted, and nothing checked that
nativePremultiply goes on consulting the context after its first row.

svgAppendCanonicalLoop now clears its buffer itself instead of
requiring an empty one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

changelog: note the isometric and repeated-render speedups

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

textmeasure: read the rune set once when sharing an atlas

Take one copy of Runes for the key and for the measurement, and say on
Runes that a different set must be a new slice. Note in the two tests
that modify a bundled font's bytes in place that nothing may measure
or subset the font meanwhile, since those results are now shared.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

isometric: reclaim removed fragments while a face is solved

A removed fragment kept its slot and its cell entries until the next
face, so a face whose fragments are replaced again and again needed
memory for every fragment it ever had: tens of megabytes where the
previous solver, with maps of live fragments, needed a few. Renumber
the survivors once removed fragments far outnumber them. The budget
charges for live fragments only, so the accounting does not change.

Return a worker that has outgrown the retention limit to the pool
empty instead of dropping it. A pool that keeps its entries in a
slice, as TinyGo's does, could go on referring to a dropped worker.

The equivalence test's scene for the bounding-box tree ran out of work
in both solvers, so only two error strings were compared. Use a scene
that fits, and fail when a scene that is meant to complete does not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

e2etests: render four isometric fixtures at a time

The isometric renders of the suite are bounded separately from go
test's parallelism because of their memory use. A render now allocates
far less, so allow four at once instead of two.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

isometric: premultiply surface textures without draw.Draw

Rasterized label and icon surfaces are converted to premultiplied
textures. draw.Draw multiplies and divides every channel of every
pixel, but 97.6% of the pixels in the e2e suite are fully transparent or
fully opaque. Skip the former, copy the latter, and do the arithmetic
for antialiased edges only. A test compares the result with draw.Draw
for every channel value at every alpha.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

isometric: reuse buffers when ordering faces and writing paths

Paint ordering clips pairs of polygons the way the visibility solver
does. Use the solver's in-place helpers and two reused buffers instead
of three slices and a closure per edge.

svgFillPath numbers each vertex, so an edge is one word in its tables
instead of two points, and keeps adjacency in flat arrays. Loops are
walked in the same order, so the path text is unchanged. Canonical
loops are rotated in place in a buffer shared across polygons.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

isometric: solve SVG visibility without allocating per fragment

The solver subtracts every nearer face from every fragment of a face.
It allocated three slices per clipped edge, clipped each overlapping
pair twice, kept its fragment index in maps, sorted each face's
occluders with a comparator, and asked the context whether it was
canceled on every unit of work: 1.9 billion times in one run of the
e2e suite.

Keep the algorithm, its output and its work accounting, and change how
it is carried out:

- Clip a fragment against a cut once. The second pass repeated the
  first to collect the outside pieces; collect them in the first and
  charge the budget for the pass that is no longer run.
- Take polygon storage from a per-solve pool with free lists, and copy
  what survives into slabs. The scratch is reused between renders
  unless it has grown past 8 MB.
- Rank occluders once per scene; a face sorts the ranks of its
  candidates.
- Index fragments with slices and stamps instead of maps.
- Charge the budget with one inlined comparison, and consult the
  context every 4,096 units of work.

On a generated scene of 3,000 faces this takes 44 ms instead of 110 ms
and allocates 1 MB instead of 41 MB.

svg_visibility_reference_test.go freezes the previous solver as an
oracle. The new tests require bit-identical fragments, and identical
errors wherever a limit stops the solve, on generated scenes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

d2svg: scan for Markdown text only in documents that contain it

embedFonts ran a regular expression over the whole SVG to collect the
text of natively rendered Markdown. A match needs the literal md-text
class, which most diagrams never contain, so look for that first.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

d2fonts: remember encoded subsets of the bundled fonts

Cutting a font down to the characters of a diagram, compressing it to
WOFF and encoding it is most of the cost of embedding fonts in an SVG,
and it was repeated for every render. The result depends only on the
font file and the characters, so remember it for the bundled fonts.

The cache is guarded by FontFamiliesMu and emptied when its keys and
values pass 8 MB. Fonts registered at run time are not cached.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

textmeasure: share glyph metrics of the bundled fonts between rulers

A Ruler measured all 352 runes of every font and size it met, and each
compile, legend, tooltip and Markdown block creates its own Ruler. One
run of the e2e suite built 2,429 such atlases for 78 distinct ones.

Keep the glyph map and line metrics of a bundled font in a process-wide
table keyed by font file, size and rune set. The map is never written
after it is built, and every Ruler keeps its own face. The table stops
growing at 256 atlases, about 10 MB.

Only the font files compiled into D2 are shared. internal/bundledfont
recognises them by backing array, so a font registered at run time is
measured as before and is never kept alive by the table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

d2layouts: list a nested graph's objects only when the log is written

LayoutNested logs every nested graph before and after its layout. The
attribute was g.PrintString(), which builds the absolute ID of every
object, and Go evaluated it whether or not debug logging was on.

Pass a value that prints the graph when a handler formats it. It has
both String, for log.PrettyHandler, and LogValue, for slog's handlers,
so the logged text is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

e2etests: compare goldens in memory and start the groups together

diff.Testdata writes a .got file and runs git diff for every golden,
which is 2,801 processes in one run of the suite. Nearly every golden
matches, so compare the bytes first and call diff.Testdata only when
they differ. A mismatch is reported, and accepted with TESTDATA_ACCEPT,
exactly as before.

The cases of a group already ran in parallel, but the twelve groups ran
one after another, each waiting for its slowest case. Start the groups
together so the run is bounded by its total work. With -failfast, the
groups after a failing one are no longer skipped, because their cases
already exist when the first failure is reported.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.2 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
test(skills): pin that a skill_view dedup stub keeps the entry it points at

The release is keyed on the call that recorded the entry, so the stub a
repeat view returns (which never records) can't drop it. Nothing pinned
that: a third view after a stubbed second view must still get the stub.
Release by (name, file) or re-stamping the entry with the stub's call id
both fail this test.

Suggested by @danfye on #151194.

fix(skills): keep a skill_view dedup entry when a guardrail notice follows the whole result

The release compared the delivered row's digest with the recorded one, so
any suffix counted as a replacement. The guardrail appends its "[Tool loop
warning ...]" after the result, and after a mid-turn compaction (which
clears the dedup bucket but not the guardrail's per-turn counts) the next
full view of an already-seen skill arrives whole plus that warning. Its
entry was dropped, and every later view re-ran the skill instead of
getting the dedup stub.

Each entry now keeps the recorded result's length, and the release keeps
it when the delivered row starts with that whole result. A preview or a
reference stub still never does.

Reported by @danfye on #151194.

fix(skills): release a skill_view dedup entry the model only saw as a preview

skill_view records the digest of its full result inside the handler, but
the executor replaces the result afterwards: maybe_persist_tool_result
spills a result over the per-result budget, enforce_turn_budget spills the
largest results of a batch over the turn budget, and the guardrail swaps a
second byte-identical result for a reference stub. The entry survived all
three, so the next view of the unchanged skill got "unchanged, refer to the
earlier skill_view result; it is still current and complete" while the
model held only a 1,500-char preview.

Each entry now keeps the tool call that recorded it (the id model_tools
binds around the handler). After persistence the executor releases that
call's entry unless the model received exactly the recorded result, and
the turn budget releases the entries of the rows it spilled. Call ids are
unique within a session (turn_tool_validation uniquifies them), and
compaction resets the bucket.

Refs #151192

docs(ci): workflow_run is not a GITHUB_TOKEN exception

The workflows README named workflow_dispatch and workflow_run as the
events GITHUB_TOKEN still starts. GitHub's docs name workflow_dispatch and
repository_dispatch, and this repo shows the rest: the human-dispatched
rc.1-v0.23.3 Stable Release run started its two workflow_run listeners
within 4 s of finishing, while the github-actions[bot]-dispatched canary
run 44784160658 started none of its three. That is why the red tracker
moved into Stable Release.

fix(ci): never count the tracker's own job as a red release

track-canary-red runs inside the Stable Release run it reports on, with
continue-on-error. When it fails (a GitHub API error, say), the jobs API
still lists "Update the install-e2e-red tracker" as failure, as it does
for the continue-on-error diagnostic Linux builds in run 44784160658. The
manual replay someone runs to recover then counted that job as a red
release job and opened or kept the tracker for a green canary.

Treat the tracker job like the diagnostic builds: drop it from the red
list, and let a failed run whose only red jobs are non-gating close the
tracker. test_canary_e2e pins the workflow job name the tracker matches.

fix(release): find the MSIX executable under its percent-encoded part name

MakeAppx stores ZIP part names percent-encoded, so the stable bundled
package's Executable="app\Hermes Agent.exe" is the entry
app/Hermes%20Agent.exe (the published rc.3-v0.22.0 x64 MSIX reads that
way). The packaged-executable lookup compared raw entry names, found
nothing, and record() raised on every stable Windows candidate. Canary
never showed it because its executable is hermes-canary.exe.

Decode each entry name before comparing it with the manifest's path.
fix(ci): treat diagnostic-only run failures as green on red-tracker replays
fix(ci): share install-e2e-red-tracker-auto lock on track-canary-red
fix(ci): update install-e2e-red from Stable Release canary runs
fix(release): probe Windows executableVersion from the packaged MSIX

Merge pull request #158056 from victor-kyriazakos/feat/mcp-parallel-http-calls

fix(mcp): allow opted-in Streamable HTTP tool calls to overlap

fix(desktop): log a handled launch link as handled, not brought forward

A launch link that arrives while the window is still booting is consumed
without activating it, so "app brought forward" was wrong for that case.

fix(desktop): hermes://launch restores any window that has been revealed

The launch link waited on the renderer's deep-link listener before it would
restore the window. That listener never comes up when the first load lands
on the repair page, so a minimized repair page could not be brought back
with the link (and second-instance skips its own focus when a URL is given).

The gate is now "this main window has been revealed once", recorded from
wireWindowReveal's onRevealed. A window still booting keeps its own reveal;
anything already on screen, the repair page included, is restored and
focused.

fix(desktop): check hermes://launch first and leave a booting window to its reveal

Two review findings on the launch link:
- handleDeepLink decoded the URL path before reaching the launch check, so
  hermes://launch/% threw in decodeURIComponent and never focused the app.
  The check now runs on the raw URL before any parsing of the path.
- On a Win/Linux cold start the link arrives right after createWindow, and
  activating then showed the window before its first paint. A window whose
  renderer is not ready yet is now left to its normal reveal; the launch
  itself already opened it.

handleLaunchDeepLink in deep-link-protocol.ts owns both rules and is
tested through its behaviour (malformed tails, booting window, non-launch
links untouched).

feat(desktop): hermes://launch opens the app and does nothing else

A page or shortcut that only wants to bring Hermes Desktop up had no link
for it: every hermes:// link carries a route or an action, and the bare
scheme still travels to the renderer's deep-link handler.

hermes://launch is handled in Electron main: it restores, shows and
focuses the window (activateWindow) and returns. It is never queued for
the renderer and nothing after `launch` (path, query) is read, so it
cannot pre-fill, navigate or open a dialog. Every existing link is
unchanged.

The argv URL finder moves into deep-link-protocol.ts beside the new
predicate so main.ts does not grow past its line ratchet.

Merge pull request #155300 from victor-kyriazakos/fix/cron-suppressed-tick-session-leak

fix(cron): end the gateway-admitted session row when a gate suppresses or refuses a fire

Merge pull request #155346 from victor-kyriazakos/fix/startup-recovery-off-loop

fix(gateway): read startup session-recovery backlogs off the event loop (native + local)

fix(agent): drop guardrail-removed calls from native replay sidecars

Symptom: on Bedrock Converse a turn fails with "ValidationException:
Expected toolResult blocks at messages.N.content for the following Ids"
right after "Removed duplicate tool call: <tool>". Retries and every
fallback model fail the same way because they replay the same history.
The delegate_task concurrency cap hits the same path with any model.

Root cause: run_tool_round passes the batch through
_cap_delegate_task_calls and _deduplicate_tool_calls, which remove
entries from tool_calls only. The ordered native sidecars
(bedrock_content_blocks, anthropic_content_blocks) still hold the
dropped call's toolUse/tool_use block, and both converters replay the
sidecar instead of rebuilding blocks from tool_calls. The dropped call
never gets a result, so the next request carries an unanswered toolUse.

Fix: prune_native_tool_blocks (next to replace_native_tool_blocks)
removes only the blocks whose id belongs to a call the guardrails
dropped. Thinking/text blocks, signatures and block order are untouched,
as are blocks it cannot attribute. run_tool_round calls it only when the
guardrails returned fewer calls, before id normalization so the sidecar
ids still match. Mixed invalid-name calls stay in tool_calls (they get an
error result) and keep their blocks.

Tests: tests/agent/test_guardrail_sidecar_prune.py drives the real
transports and run_tool_round up to staging, then builds the Converse
request with bedrock_adapter and asserts every toolUse has a matching
toolResult: duplicate call in a parallel Bedrock batch, capped
delegate_task, mixed invalid batch plus a duplicate, Anthropic sidecar,
and the no-drop path leaving the sidecar object identical. 4 fail on
main, 5 pass with the fix.

fix(skills): a malformed index_desc_limit falls back to 60 instead of raising

str.isdigit() accepts "²" and int() refuses it (and >4300-digit strings), so the
prompt build raised ValueError. Parse with int() and fall back on failure. The
cache test now changes the width with the in-process LRU still warm, so dropping
the limit from the LRU key goes red too.

fix(skills): index_desc_limit reaches every surface and rebuilds the cached index

Follow-up to the configurable skills.index_desc_limit:

- Drop the HERMES_SKILLS_INDEX_DESC_LIMIT env var (non-secret config
  belongs in config.yaml) and clamp the value to 60..1024, the
  frontmatter's own cap, so a typo cannot shrink the index below the
  bundled-skill standard.
- Key the on-disk skills snapshot and the in-process LRU on the limit:
  without it, a changed limit kept serving rows clipped at the old width
  until some SKILL.md changed.
- skill_manage's schema states the configured budget through
  dynamic_schema_overrides; the default keeps the static schema bytes,
  so an unconfigured install's tools[] is unchanged.
- /learn and the curator prompts quote the configured width instead of
  a hardcoded 60.
- Register the key in DEFAULT_CONFIG and document it.
- Replace the added tests with two behaviour contracts (config -> index
  incl. snapshot rebuild; config -> skill_manage budget + schema).
feat(skills): make skill index description limit configurable via skills.index_desc_limit (#150523)

docs(gateway): say when deliver_wake display_text becomes a card

The deliver_wake docstring said display_text "is shown"; a blank value, a
non-local source or a fallback admission carry no card. Also drop the test
helper docstring, which named one notification where it returns a list.

test(gateway): drive the split Kanban batch through the local authority to the CLI

The split-batch regression checked the notifier's deliver_wake kwargs on a
Telegram adapter, so it would still pass if the local card dropped or swapped
receipts. Both tests now share one helper that runs a real local-chat
subscription through a notifier tick, the authority's published
message.start frames and the classic CLI's queue_admitted_turn, and the
mixed batch is built with a real crashed event instead of patching
complete_task.

Also drop _local_receipt's docstring, which overstated what it returns, and
say in deliver_wake when display_text is used.

fix(gateway): each Kanban wake of a split batch names its own receipt

With warning notifications off for the subscription's platform, the notifier
splits a batch into a diagnostic wake and a result wake. build_wake_text ran
once per group and overwrote self.receipt, but the saved per-wake tuple did
not carry it, so both wakes went out with the last group's receipt: a crashed
task's wake showed "[kanban] Task <id> completed." in the classic CLI.

wake() now derives the receipt from the wake's own text, so no separate
state can drift from it. The notifier test now runs a real local-chat
subscription through the authority's message.start and the classic CLI's
queue_admitted_turn (the old one used a Telegram subscription, which never
carries a card), plus a crashed+completed split batch. Comments that
overstated the CLI's rule or what the test asserts are removed.

fix(gateway): a Kanban wake shows in an idle classic CLI chat

A Kanban wake into a local chat ran and saved its reply, but a classic CLI
sitting idle on that chat never showed it. The idle CLI only opens a
gateway-admitted turn whose message.start names a card, and the wake named
none. Process completions, async delegations and heartbeats already do.

The notifier now hands the wake its own first line as a one-line receipt,
and deliver_wake names it on a local route as an internal_notification
card, the same shape a heartbeat tick uses. The stored row stays the
machinery kind, so the TUI and Desktop are unchanged, and messaging routes
carry no card.

fix(desktop): check WSL again after a registry read times out

A reg.exe query that timed out or failed to start was cached as "no WSL" for
the whole run, so one slow read at launch turned path bridging off for a user
who has WSL until Desktop restarted. Keep a definite answer (a distribution
found, or reg.exe exiting with a missing-key or access error) for the run, and
check again 30 s after an uncertain one. A host whose registry keeps timing
out pays one bounded check per 30 s, not one per path read.

Raised by Gille on #158184.

test(desktop): pin a registered WSL distribution in the bridge tests

The bridge and profile suites expect an active bridge, which now depends on
the registry check. On a Windows machine without WSL they failed although the
app behaves correctly. Mock reg.exe and wsl.exe in both files so they no longer
depend on the host; the no-WSL cases stay in the availability suite.

Reported by Greptile on #158184.
chore(contributors): map hsiaopan@outlook.com to Hsiaopan (#151354 salvage)

fix(desktop): keep the picker's drive-alias mapping when WSL is missing

With no registered WSL distribution, `resolvePickerDefaultPath` returned before the `/mnt/<drive>` conversion, so a local or unknown profile's `/mnt/c/projects` default reached the native dialog unchanged instead of opening at `C:\projects`. That conversion never touches WSL. The picker now returns early only for remote profiles, maps `/mnt/<drive>` paths as before, and sends other POSIX paths to the WSL share only when a distribution is registered.

`isWslBridgeActive` no longer stores the registry answer in the per-profile map, which holds backend intent only; availability is cached on its own. Before, a read on an unknown profile recorded it as inactive, and the picker could then treat that profile as remote.

Reported by kvnloo on #156661.

fix(desktop): keep a colon after /mnt/ or /cygdrive/ on the POSIX side

The colon branch sat in the same optional chain as the prefix group, so it
also applied after `mnt/` and `cygdrive/`: `/mnt/c:/notes.md` resolved to
`C:/notes.md` whenever that file existed. Those are POSIX paths whose
directory is literally named `c:`, not the `C:` drive, so Desktop could
silently read an unrelated Windows file — including for a remote profile.

Give the colon spelling its own prefix-less alternative and read the letter
as `drive[1] ?? drive[2]`. `/mnt/c:/notes.md`, `/cygdrive/c:/notes.md` and
`/mnt/c:` now stay on the WSL bridge, while `/E:/x`, `/e:/x`, `/E:`, `/E:/`,
`/E://x` and the `/E:Users` rejection are unchanged.
test(desktop): cover colon-relative paths and repeated separators
fix(desktop): reject colon-relative shell paths, collapse repeated separators

fix(desktop): accept the /E:/ drive spelling in WSL path bridging

Some shells spell a Windows path as /E:/Users/... . SHELL_DRIVE_RE only
matched /e/..., /cygdrive/e/... and /mnt/e/..., so such a path missed the
native conversion and fell through to the WSL branch, where it became
\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\E:/Users/... — a stat that can never succeed.
That is the "File preview failed: UNKNOWN" seen in desktop-stderr.log.

The regex also consumes the optional slash after the colon now, so the
rebuilt path does not end up with a double separator (E://Users/...).

fix(desktop): skip WSL bridging when no distribution is registered

Probe HKCU then HKLM Lxss for a registered DistributionName before the
bridge resolves a distro or touches a \\wsl$ share; on WSL-less Windows
either one pops the WSL install console (#128770).

Co-authored-by: Austin Pickett <austinpickett@users.noreply.github.com>

fix(desktop): check the day being frozen for unadopted legacy frames

The daily-retry path checked pending days once before the first send. A frame
receipt that arrived after UTC midnight made the previous day eligible on the
next freeze while its legacy frames and visible time were still unadopted, so
that day settled incomplete. The check now runs per candidate day under the
freeze lock.

docs(desktop): describe the current streaming markdown cost in profile-typing-lag

The "elephant" section described a build that re-parsed the whole message
on every flush. It also credited a <DeferStreamingText> wrapper that no
longer exists, and a Streamdown useTransition that 2.7 does not have.

The section now records what holds on main:
- settled Blocks are frozen by the Block memo plus the cached splitter;
- preprocess is deferred at MarkdownTextSurface;
- stream end no longer re-parses;
- the splitter cache is bounded.

It also lists what is still O(N) per flush: preprocess and the remend
scan, the cheap splitter bookkeeping, and a single giant tail block. The
parser swap and the Web Worker are noted as not pursued.

perf(desktop): stop the block splitter retaining every streamed prefix

parseMarkdownIntoBlocksCached put every flush's full text into a
256-entry exact LRU, so one stream kept up to 256 full-length prefixes
plus their block arrays alive: ~256 x N bytes per lineage.

When a text supersedes its lineage's previous tip in the append ring,
that tip now also leaves the exact cache. The live tip keeps its exact
entry, and with it its array identity, which is what Streamdown's
per-block memos need. A rewind to an older prefix is an edit and
re-lexes, which is the same result it got before.

Retained heap after streaming one reply in 40-char flushes (vitest node,
--expose-gc, heapUsed delta after gc; throwaway script):
  5 KB  (126 flushes):  0.7 MB  -> 0.5 MB
  50 KB (1251 flushes): 11.9 MB -> 0.2 MB
  200 KB (5001 flushes): 40.6 MB -> 0.5 MB

Test: markdown-blocks.test.ts "keeps one streamed prefix per lineage"
(fails on main: the superseded prefix is still served from the exact
cache). The existing full-lex equivalence and fuzz properties pass
unchanged.

perf(desktop): end a markdown stream without re-parsing the whole message

`isStreaming` sat in the `components` useMemo deps, so when a reply
finished the table changed identity: Streamdown's Block memo compares
components key-by-key, every Block failed it and re-ran remark/rehype on
unchanged markdown, and the adapter minted a new `code` component type so
every code subtree remounted.

Streaming state now travels through MarkdownStreamingContext, read by the
two consumers that need it (MarkdownParagraph's directive leaf and the new
MarkdownCodeBlock, which carries the artifact / RichCodeBlock /
SyntaxHighlighter routing that the inline SyntaxHighlighter closure used
to hold). `components` stays stable across the transition; only those
consumers re-render, so the fence that streamed as PlainCode still
switches to Shiki once the stream ends, in place.

Stream-end commit (jsdom, throwaway script, isRunning true -> false on the
final text, until the commit plus two macrotasks; two runs each):
  5 KB:  110-154 ms -> 6.5-6.7 ms
  50 KB: 755-819 ms -> 10.5 ms

Test (markdown-text.stream.test.tsx): across the stream -> settled
transition of a reply ending in an open-then-closed code fence, 0 Block
parses (counted per remark transform; 13 on main), the same code-card DOM
nodes before and after, and all three fences, including the last one,
end up Shiki-highlighted.

perf(desktop): keep markdown preprocess off the urgent render of a stream flush

StreamdownTextPrimitive runs `preprocess(messagePart.text)` before its own
`useDeferredValue`, so `preprocessWithTailRepair` (preprocessMarkdown's
full-text regex passes + the tailBoundedRemend boundary scan, both O(N))
ran at urgent priority on every token flush; only splitting and parsing
were deferred.

MarkdownTextSurface now defers the context part itself and republishes it
through TextMessagePartProvider, so the urgent render hands the primitive
an unchanged part (its useMemo bails) and all text work runs in the
interruptible deferred render. The primitive's own `defer` prop is dropped:
the text it sees is already deferred. No library fork; output unchanged.

Per-flush urgent render (jsdom, flushSync of one +40-char flush into a
growing assistant message, median over 50 flushes; throwaway script, host
under load so ranges over two runs each):
  5 KB:  base 0.74-1.67 ms -> 0.70-0.83 ms
  50 KB: base 5.1-9.8 ms   -> 0.45-0.72 ms (now flat in N)

Tests: markdown-text.stream.test.tsx
- a render-phase spy on preprocessMarkdown proves the urgent (flushSync)
  render of a new flush does not preprocess it, and the deferred render
  does (fails on main: the urgent render preprocesses the new text);
- streamed DOM at cuts mid-fence/table/math/reasoning-tag and after the
  stream ends is byte-identical to a fresh render of the same text

re-rendered its whole log list and re-armed its scroll effect per message.
Subscribe through a frame-coalesced reader: the first append schedules one
animation frame; later appends in the same burst are dropped because the
callback reads the latest list. Store append semantics are unchanged.

before it (the inverted branch rendered five times).

The AudioWorklet meter reports at the audio rate (60 Hz) and setLevel lived in
useMicRecorder's React state, so every report re-rendered ChatBar and its
controls while listening or dictating. Each recorder owns a level atom (lazily
initialized); only ConversationIndicator and the dictation meter subscribe.
Regression test: a visible level update does not re-render the recorder

plain store stub so vi.mock factories stay self-contained.

perf(desktop): keep trigger state when the detected token is unchanged

Re-detecting the same token (input flush followed by keyup, or a caret move)
installed a fresh object and re-ran the composer render and item search.
Extract sameTriggerState and keep the previous state when kind/query/inline/
scope/tokenLength/value are identical. Time-based throttling was not kept: it
could drop the last caret-only refresh, and the identity bail already removes
the redundant work.

perf(desktop): typed URL/path conversion stops snapshotting every key serializeTextBefore cloned the selected DOM into a scratch div and rewrote every chip and BR node after each keystroke. Read the prefix in place with a Range boundary instead: a chip contributes one U+FFFC, a
one newline, and text its UTF-16 prefix. At 15 KB, 200 calls: 20 ms -> 6 ms, zero cloneContents calls. Output is identical for every caret Chromium places; a (chip|br element, offset 0) boundary, which no caret path produces, now yields the prefix before that element. The undo snapshot for typed URL/path conversion is taken only when the key is Space and covers both attempts in one transaction; other keys no longer pay two whole-draft serializations for edits that immediately return false.

perf(desktop): do not republish steady activity values per event

setPetActivity re-asserts reasoning/tool flags on every delta of those streams
and always allocated a new object, notifying pet subscribers dozens of times
per second for an unchanged flag. setToolProgress likewise rebuilt the record
for repeated MCP progress readings. Both publish only on a real change; tests
pin that a repeated reading notifies once and a change notifies again (the old
behavior notified on every write).

perf(desktop): one armed deadline for both streaming watchdogs

Both watchdogs swapped a timeout on every event: the silence timer on every
gateway token and the busy-session watchdog on every streamed publish (~20/s).
Each keeps one timer and a last-activity timestamp, re-arming only when the
deadline moved; a fired timer re-arms for the remainder. Semantics are
unchanged (silence measured from the last event, in-flight verdicts invalidated,
stalled hint after a full silent window).

New tests pin one timer allocation for bursts of events/publishes (5 -> 1 on
the previous implementation) and the stalled transition.

perf(desktop): publish live deltas without re-reconciling the transcript

A live flush took the same authoritative-refresh path as resume/hydrate: the
error-preserving splice and a whole-transcript deep compare ran every ~40 ms
even though the cache's message array is already authoritative.

Mark the publish cause at the producer instead of inferring it from streamId:
mutateStream passes liveDelta=true, so a running-turn resume (which also
carries a streamId) keeps preserve+compare and its no-repaint guarantee. A
view-only assistant error still falls back to the full path.

The live path still folds view-only timing (hydration carries no live
completion stamps) through reconcileLocalAssistantTimeline. A memo keyed
weakly by (stored row, view row) returns the previous merge for an unchanged
pair, so unchanged rows keep identity without pinning earlier streamed
snapshots and a row-wise reference compare replaces the deep compare. A no-op
stream event (e.g. a reasoning replace after answer text) returns the previous
state instead of publishing a new transcript.

Regression tests: equal-content resume leaves $messages identity untouched;
view-only completion timing survives a hydration refresh followed by live
deltas and the merged row is reused; a part-only completion stamp is lifted
onto the message when the view holds the same row; a no-op reasoning replace
keeps the session state; earlier streamed snapshots of a reply are collectable.

perf(desktop): mirror view metadata only when it changes

syncRuntimeMetadataToView runs twice per published state and on every streamed
delta, and each persisting setter did a localStorage read+write; the effort
setter also cleared and re-stamped the wire atom. Compare each value against
the live atom first and write only genuine changes.

perf(desktop): patch only the streamed tail row per delta

mutateStream scanned the transcript with .some then rebuilt it with .map on
every flush, and completion allocated a reversed copy just to find the last
visible row. Probe the tail first (the live row is almost always last), copy
the array once and patch the one slot; use findLast for the completion scan.

perf(desktop): memoize the warm-transcript pending scan during prune

prune() runs after every published state, including each streamed delta, and
hasDraftOrInFlightMessage scanned each settled transcript's messages every
time. Cache the boolean by the transcript array identity (settled arrays are
stable), so repeated prunes cost one WeakMap lookup per cached session. Probe:
two prunes scan once instead of twice.

perf(desktop): dedupe tool-call ids only on a repository cache miss

withUniqueToolCallIdsWithinMessage rebuilt a parts array for every settled
message on every flush, then discarded it when the normalized ThreadMessage was
already cached. Move the defensive dedupe inside the cache-miss branch. A
before/after probe shows one dedupe for the new tail instead of one per row.

perf(desktop): keep settled transcript identity through reconciliation

The live path republishes the transcript through preserveLocalAssistantErrors
on every flush. reconcileLocalAssistantTimeline returned a fresh message and
parts array for every matched assistant even when the timing merge changed
nothing, defeating the runtime repository's identity cache and forcing a full
re-normalization of prior turns.

Return the incoming object/array when nothing changed; cache whitespace-
normalized part text; skip the error merge and error-id scan entirely when the
local view holds no assistant error. The new test pins settled object and part
identity (fails on the previous implementation).

perf(desktop): keep the agent-terminal backlog as a chunked deque

The capped backlog was one string: (backlog + chunk).slice(-256_000) copied the
whole tail twice for every output event once a terminal passed the cap. Chunks
are appended by reference and trimmed by dropping whole head entries (releasing
the evicted string immediately), with the joined string materialized only for
mount replay and snapshot diffing. The retained cap is exact: the loop drops
whole chunks and a bounded slice trims the head overhang, including a single
oversized snapshot chunk.

Microbenchmark (30k x 64-byte chunks): 291-305 ms before, 9-13 ms after
(~23-30x). New tests cover a 300 KB single chunk and multi-chunk overhang.

fix(desktop): fail a profile switch whose route lookup fails instead of dialing a second socket

On main every local non-primary profile rides the primary's one multiplexing
gateway: Electron answers `hermes:connection` for it with the primary
descriptor tagged `sharedPrimary: true` (resolveProfileBackendRoute case 6,
joinPrimaryBoot). That lookup is slow exactly when the primary is still
booting (`gateway ensure` up to 60 s hard / 75 s kill).

`sharedPrimaryRoute` turned every failure, including its own 20 s timeout,
into `false` ("not shared"). `ensureGatewayForProfile` then created a
secondary and `openSecondary` repeated the same getConnection under another
20 s budget. The user saw a ~40 s overlay and then "Timed out connecting to
profile", or, once the boot landed, a second WebSocket to the shared process
(the #120005 duplicate-event class). The agent door (`ridesPrimaryBackend`)
had the same fallthrough for a local primary.

Now a failed or timed-out lookup rejects:
- sharedPrimaryRoute propagates the error. ensureGatewayForProfile rejects,
  so selectProfile's existing "Failed to switch to profile" toast fires after
  one RECONNECT_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS (20 s) instead of two, and no secondary is
  created.
- gatewayForProfile records the failed lookup in the dial-failure ledger, so
  background pollers keep the #121865 cooldown (one dial per attempt now
  instead of two; the #121865 tests' counts are halved).
- ridesPrimaryBackend rethrows on a local primary. It still never collapses a
  pooled local profile onto the primary (#101416), and a remote primary keeps
  its prefer-the-primary fallback (#96493).

Every await on the switch path is bounded by an existing budget, so nothing
new needed a bound. The secondary's `gateway.connect` keeps the shared
client's DEFAULT_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS of 15 s (HermesGateway does not override
it), and public-dial readiness has its own 15 s.

This adds no desktop backend pool or TTL. On main a local profile has no
process of its own to keep warm, and main never reaps one.

Also removed:
- openSecondaryCount, the dead "pool cap" counter. It had no callers since
  prewarm stopped consulting it.
- the stale openSecondary comment about pooled children spawning (~9 s).

Tests (fail on 3d4dd108c, pass here):
- gateway.test.ts: a wedged lookup fails at 20 s with one getConnection call
  and no secondary socket; a rejected lookup surfaces with no second dial.
  These replace the test that pinned the fallthrough.
- gateway-profile-request.test.ts: an owner-route activation on a local
  primary whose lookup fails rejects with no second dial.

fix(desktop): the perf harness attaches on a Linux Wayland session

On Wayland, electron/entry.ts relaunches the app with
--ozone-platform=wayland unless argv already names a platform. The parent the
harness spawned holds the --remote-debugging-port, so the relaunched child's
DevTools bind fails ("Address already in use") and the harness polls a browser
with zero pages until its 120 s driver wait times out. Every --spawn run on a
Wayland desktop failed this way.

Pass --ozone-platform=wayland ourselves on a Linux Wayland session so the app
never relaunches. Verified on Hyprland: before, `/json/list` on the harness
port was `[]` and startIsolatedInstance timed out; after, it lists the
http://127.0.0.1:<devPort>/ page and connects (RESULT CONNECTED).

fix(desktop): the perf harness's isolated home never starts the user's
messaging platforms

`--spawn` seeded its throwaway HERMES_HOME with a verbatim copy of
~/.hermes/config.yaml, so the isolated gateway started every platform the user
enabled. With Photon (iMessage) its sidecar binds the fixed 127.0.0.1:8789:
the isolated adapter "reaped" the live gateway's sidecar, the user's real
gateway logged SIDECAR_CRASHED and reconnected, and inbound messages could
land in the throwaway process. Observed on a real machine during a harness run
(two reaps, ~13 minutes of flapping) and confirmed in the live gateway.log.

A platform starts on any activation evidence: a config block (top-level
`<name>:`, `platforms.<name>`, `gateway.platforms.<name>`), credentials in
.env, or an auth.json credential-pool record. The seeder now pins every
platform the gateway knows (core Platform members + bundled
plugins/platforms/*) to `enabled: false` under top-level `platforms:`. An
explicit disable outranks .env and auth.json evidence (gateway/config_env.py
_enable_from_env, _enable_plugin_platform), so .env and auth.json still copy
over for model/provider auth. Disabling only the blocks a config names is not
enough: a top-level `discord:` block plus DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN in .env still
enabled Discord. Moved into scripts/perf/lib/seed-home.mjs with a test; the
copy no longer swallows errors (a failing seed is a broken harness, not
"onboarding may appear").

Test: scripts/perf-seed-home.test.mjs fails against the verbatim copy (photon
stays enabled) and passes on this change. Against the real loader
(load_gateway_config) on a home seeded from a live ~/.hermes: verbatim copy
enables [discord, photon, telegram]; this change enables []. A re-run of the
harness after the fix left the live sidecar's pid unchanged and added no reap

Found in review. With `security.allow_private_urls: null` in the managed
scope, the profile's own `security.allow_private_urls: true` and

fix(release): keep an unreadable desktop attempt image from aborting the sequencer

631b9d18c9's stable-desktop recovery check read the attempt's -desktop image through
_version_digest, which raises on any registry error. A failed read there, with the pointer
and the slim alias current, aborted the whole production pass before it could plan anything
newer. Either image failing to read is now inconclusive (not behind), like the alias itself;
promote_stable still reads both strictly when it actually moves them.

fix(release): never move stable aliases whose owner cannot be read

9bf56ac5a9 counted an unreadable `stable` alias as current. When the head read and the
recovery read both fail, a stale desktop pointer then got the full advance, whose Docker
promotion can move a newer Docker-only release's aliases back. An unreadable alias now leaves
the owner unknown, and like a newer owner it gets only the desktop-only `finish`.

Production always has the `stable` alias, so "unreadable" is a registry error there. A
registry where the alias was never created gets no Docker promotion from recovery either,
as on main, where channel_head counted the desktop head as done in that case.

fix(release): pick a stale stable pointer's repair by alias ownership too

631b9d18c9 checked alias ownership only when the pointer was current. With a stale or
missing pointer the pass returned the desktop head straight away, and plan() chose a full
advance because the head read matched it, which it can only do after a registry error
dropped a newer Docker-only release out of the head. That advance repeats the Docker
promotion and moves the aliases back to the older release.

_unfinished_desktop_head now returns the step itself. While a newer release owns the
aliases (it holds the channel head, or the alias carries its digest) a stale pointer gets
the desktop-only `finish`; otherwise a stale pointer or provably behind aliases get the
full `advance`.

fix(release): judge stable alias recovery on ownership and the desktop variant

4e8b5fd31b's alias check probed the registry a second time and compared the slim `stable`
alias with the desktop head's digest. Two gaps:

- A registry error on the head probe drops the combined head back to the desktop release;
  if the second probe then succeeds with a newer Docker-only release's digest, that digest
  read as a stopped promotion and the pass moved the aliases back to the older release.
- promote_stable moves the slim aliases before the desktop ones, so a slim alias that
  carries the release says nothing about stable-desktop/latest-desktop.

The aliases now count as behind only when the alias read succeeds, its digest belongs to no
newer published release, and either the slim alias misses the head's digest or the
stable-desktop alias misses the attempt's desktop image (docker.stable_desktop_alias_behind).
An unreadable alias proves nothing and is left alone.

fix(release): finish an unfinished stable head's Docker step and repair it under a newer head

91fbd83fc8 re-advanced the desktop head only when its candidate pointer was wrong. Two cases
still read as done: the pointer PUT landed but its read-back failed, or the Docker promotion
itself failed, so the next pass saw a matching pointer and the Docker vX.Y.Z tag and
stable/latest aliases never moved. And with a newer release at the combined head the pass
refused outright, leaving the stale pointer for an operator.

While the desktop head is also the channel head, a Docker-carrying release whose stable alias
does not carry its digest now counts as unfinished too, and advances again through the normal
production advance. Under a newer head only the desktop advance repeats (a new `finish` step,
advance_stable alone), so that release's aliases stay where the newer release put them.

fix(release): refuse to prune when a new canary head has no retention pointer

The pruner compared the canary pointer with the protected canary head only when the pointer
existed, and found the head by the record name `canary`. The first canary after today's legacy
v<stable>+canary.<stamp> head has no pointer until its write lands, so if that write failed the
live canary's archive was protected by nothing but its age; and a canary channel bootstrapped
under another name read as no head at all, so every prune refused with no way to fix it.

The pruner now picks the protected channel the way publication does
(channel_releases.select_channel): the one listed record whose policy is canary-release,
refusing when two claim it. It reads that head whenever the record exists, refuses when a
canary.<stamp>-vX.Y.Z head has no pointer, and fails closed on an unreadable record or head
manifest. A legacy head with no pointer prunes as before.

fix(release): advance an unfinished stable head again, Docker aliases included

The pointer repair from 196d082b74 ran after the pass, against the combined publication head,
and called only advance_stable. Two gaps: production_advance moves the Docker vX.Y.Z tag and
stable/latest aliases after advance_stable, so a pointer write that failed after the head
moved also skipped them and the repair never ran them; and a newer Docker-only release could
become the combined head and hide the desktop head's stale pointer.

The pass now asks, before planning, whether the protected desktop head's candidate pointer
names it. If not, plan() advances that release again ahead of anything newer, through the
normal production advance (idempotent desktop advance, then the Docker promotion), so a
newer release can never run before it finishes. If a newer release already holds the head,
the pass refuses instead of moving that release's aliases back.

refactor(release): tag release images with claim-tag again; drop the identity docker_tag

docker_tag() turned a retired vX.Y.Z+canary.<stamp> tag's `+` into `-`. Since canaries are
canary.<stamp>-vX.Y.Z claims it returns its input, yet admit still emitted it as a separate
docker-tag output that three stable-release.yml consumers read, with comments describing the

fix(webapp): read a portless callback as port 80 only for a specific bind

Reading a registered callback with no port as port 80 everywhere changed
what hermes webapp opens for a wildcard or loopback bind on webapp.port 80
with a hand-edited portless callback: main stays on loopback, the previous
commit opened the registered LAN address. The port is now read as 80 only
where a specific bind compares the callback with its own address and
builds the note, so every other bind behaves as on main.

fix(webapp): choose a port free on loopback too for a specific webapp.host

LAN Start for a standalone profile with no webapp.port picks the first
free port above the default. Since Start keeps a specific webapp.host, it
probed only that address, but the gateway also binds the port on loopback
for that address's loopback socket. A port something held on loopback was
chosen and saved, and the loopback socket then could not bind on every
later start. A candidate port must now be free on both the address and
loopback.

docs(gateway): say where a specific address is checked against the interfaces

_bind_primary checks the address against this machine's interfaces before
binding, so the classifier's docstring no longer calls that the bind's
verdict.

test(gateway): run the wildcard busy-port case only where the bind is refused

macOS lets a 0.0.0.0 bind under SO_REUSEADDR succeed beside the fixture's
127.0.0.1 rival (main behaves the same), so the case failed there. Mark it
for Linux and Windows, where it still checks the refusal against a
loopback holder of the port.

fix(gateway): name the loopback socket's own bind error

On a specific-address bind every EADDRNOTAVAIL was reported as the address
not being assigned to any interface, including the loopback socket's
(::1 on a host with IPv6 loopback off), whose reason then blamed the wrong
cause. The rewrite now applies only to the specific address itself; the
loopback socket's error keeps the OS's words beside its address.

fix(webapp): read a registered callback with no port as port 80

A registration record whose callback names no port
(http://192.168.0.11/auth/callback) read as port None, so a Webapp on
webapp.port 80 at that address got a note saying the addresses differ,
with nothing named to change. The port is now normalised once where the
callback is read.

fix(gateway): clear the loopback-socket flag when the gateway mount closes

The gateway's dashboard mount sets loopback_companion on the process-wide
web_server.app for a specific-address Webapp, so the Host check also
accepts a loopback Host there. Closing the mount left it set, so a
standalone dashboard bound to that address later in the same process
accepted Host: localhost, which main refuses. The mount now clears it, and
start_server sets it to None explicitly.

fix(webapp): keep a specific webapp.host when Web Access starts LAN access

The Web Access pane counts a webapp.host that names one address of this
machine as LAN access, but LAN Start always wrote webapp.host: 0.0.0.0. A
user who chose one interface ended up listening on every interface after
one Stop and Start in the pane, and the pane showed the machine's primary
LAN address instead of the bound one.

LAN Start now keeps a specific webapp.host (on or off) and registers the
sign-in callback for that address, and the pane's address is that address
(bracketed for IPv6). Every other host still gets 0.0.0.0 and the primary
LAN address, as before.

fix(webapp): warn when a specific-IP Webapp's Nous client is still registered for an HTTPS URL

Web Access in public mode registers its own Nous client for `https://<public_url>/auth/callback`.
After a move from that URL to a specific `webapp.host`, the gateway still signs browsers in with
that client, but `sign_in_address` only recognised an http LAN callback, so `hermes webapp` opened
the bound IP with no note and Nous sign-in could not return there. It now keeps opening the bound
IP and adds a note naming the saved HTTPS registration and the way forward (a password provider,
or restoring webapp.public_url). `webapp.public_url` still wins, and wildcard/loopback binds keep
the registered LAN lookup unchanged.

Test: test_specific_bind_reports_an_own_client_still_registered_for_https.

Reported in review of #157376.

fix(gateway): refuse a specific webapp.host no interface holds before binding

Linux lets a TCP socket bind a directed subnet broadcast (the .255 of a local /24), so a bind
succeeding did not prove the address was this machine's: `webapp-status` reported such a Webapp as
serving. A specific-address bind now checks the machine's interface addresses (psutil) once before
it binds, and refuses with EADDRNOTAVAIL, which the runtime reports as "the address is not assigned
to any network interface on this machine"; native clients keep the private listener. Loopback,
wildcard and name binds skip the check, as before.

Test: test_an_interface_broadcast_is_not_served_as_a_machine_address (Linux).

Reported in review of #157376.

feat(gateway): let webapp.host be one IP address of this machine

`webapp.host` now also accepts one literal IP address of this machine (a LAN or Tailscale address,
IPv4 or IPv6), as `hermes dashboard --host` takes it. On main an enabled Webapp with such a host was
refused: the listener stayed off and `hermes webapp --status` named the error.

The gateway's Webapp then listens on that address and, on the same port, on loopback (127.0.0.1, or
::1 for an IPv6 address), because Desktop and the CLI accept only a loopback origin. Both sockets
serve one app under one boundary state, so sign-in is required exactly as on a 0.0.0.0 bind: the
browser credential is never a way around it, cookie writes come only from the Webapp's own page, a
missing sign-in provider refuses the bind with the gate's message, and webapp.public_url works the
same. Unlike a wildcard bind, the Host check accepts only the address, loopback names and the
Webapp's public host. When the address is on no interface, or the loopback port is taken, neither
socket stays open and the gateway keeps its private listener with the reason.

Only unicast addresses an interface can hold qualify: names, other loopback addresses, broadcast,
multicast, reserved, 0.0.0.0/8, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped addresses stay refused;
the refusal message lists the new choice. Loopback, wildcard and disabled configs behave as on main
(tests/gateway/test_webapp_host_parity.py passes on main and here). The gateway reports the address it is
bound to (an `address` field in webapp-status, only for such a bind). `hermes webapp` opens it, ahead
of a Web Access LAN registration, which never sends the browser to another address: when that
registration names one, the command says Nous sign-in cannot finish here. `--status` prints the
bound address and the loopback one this machine's clients use, and names a different webapp.host in
config.yaml that waits for a restart. Web Access counts the address as LAN. Docs: configuration, desktop, cli-commands, gateway-local-sessions.

feat(ci): warn, never fail, naming each lost core name and the plugins' catalog records

  interface) or already on plugin_api.json (judged against the base's copy), and
  which plugins import it;
- for each affected plugin: its title, version, tier, category and maintainer;
  its repository, subdir and pin; links to its plugin-catalog/<name>.yaml and its
  marketplace page; and a link to each import line at the pin.

The breaks-catalog-plugin label is gone: with nothing to block, there is nothing
to override. The step runs after setup-pm because the catalog loader needs
ruamel.yaml.

Review fixes in the same pass: a try nested in a branch that still runs can lose
its own feature and is reported (greptile, BearHuddleston); a lost branch only
names imports that resolved on the base; a bare annotation binds nothing; the
daily refresh parses with Python 3.14, the shipped runtime (BearHuddleston).

Co-authored-by: unsupportedpastels <274530371+unsupportedpastels@users.noreply.github.com>

fix(ci): keep a nested try's fallback inside the branch that holds it

Greptile (P1): each import was filed under its innermost catching try only, so a fallback nested
in an outer handler became its own choice and the outer try lost it. Joust's get_data_dir has that
shape: `try: from plugins.plugin_storage import plugin_data_dir` / `except: try: from
hermes_constants import get_hermes_home`. Removing plugin_data_dir was reported as a break even
though the plugin falls back to get_hermes_home.

An ImportBranch now carries its own nested ImportChoices. A branch runs when its imports resolve
and every try inside it has a branch that runs; a try still reaches Hermes when some branch runs
and imports from Hermes (directly or through a nested try). The index stores a nested try inline as
{"try": [branch, ...]} and is rebuilt in that shape (1.0 MiB, largest shard 201 KiB). The new test
removes the primary import with the nested fallback alive (no break) and then the fallback (its
site is named); it fails on the previous head.

fix(ci): judge a try's imports branch by branch, and re-read failed or moved index rows

Review fixes for the catalog core-imports check (Greptile, five findings):

- A try is now one ImportChoice: the body and each handler are branches, and the plugin keeps the
  import while every Hermes import of one branch resolves. Before, any one surviving name from the
  other branch hid the loss, so dropping one name from both spellings of a multi-name import passed
  (vector-platform's internal/setup.py has that shape). A try that can run without Hermes imports
  (an empty branch) still reports its loss, labelled as a lost feature.
- Only writes through globals() make a module's names dynamic (passed to a call, .update /
  .setdefault, a subscript store). A read like globals().get(name) no longer turns off the name
  check for the whole file (hermes_cli/auth.py reads it).
- Index rows decode into frozen dataclasses (Row, CoreImports, ImportChoice, ImportSite, the last
  three owned by the parser in plugin_validate_private_imports) at read_index; the compact JSON
  stays inside read/write.
- `build` re-reads a row whose last read failed, and a row whose subdir changed at the same sha (two
  entries can pick different plugins from one commit). The two network failures from the first
  build are now indexed; only the three deleted repos stay unreadable.

The index is rebuilt in the new format (31 shards, 1.0 MiB, largest 201 KiB).

feat(ci): name the pinned catalog plugins a core PR breaks, before it merges

Catalog plugins live in their own repos, pinned by sha, and many import Hermes modules that are not
on the published plugin API. When a core PR removes or renames such a module or name, nothing in
this repository's CI sees it: the plugin's code is not here. This week the storage rewrite broke
three that way (OpenViking via agent.message_content, Honcho via hermes_state_common, holographic
via hermes_state_wal: #157818), each found only after users upgraded.

- scripts/ci/catalog_core_imports/ (31 shards, ~780 KiB) records every Hermes import each of the
  2,514 catalog entries makes at its pinned sha, parsed by
  plugin_validate_private_imports.hermes_import_sites (the same parser `hermes plugins validate`
  uses). An import inside a try that catches ImportError carries its alternatives, so a plugin
  that already falls back is not reported.
- `catalog_core_imports.py check` (Repository guards, PR python lane) resolves each import against
  the base and the merge commit from git objects alone: no network, no plugin code, nothing
  imported. It only resolves imports whose module files the PR touches (every import when
  compat/moves.py changes): 0.3 s on a typical PR, 2-3 s on the storage-rewrite commits.
- On failure it names plugin, file:line and import, and offers: open a PR for an official seam
  (ctx method, hook, plugin_api.json entry), keep the old name via compat/moves.py, or the
  breaks-catalog-plugin label.
- catalog-core-imports.yml re-indexes added or repinned entries daily and opens a bot PR.

The check asks only whether a name still exists; a name that stays but changes behaviour or
signature passes.

fix(profiles): a normal rename return commits even when the directory ID changes

On FAT/exFAT and CIFS mounted with `noserverino` a directory's ID does not
survive a rename, so the identity check alone read every successful rename
as "not moved": it re-served and re-registered the old name, then
registered the new one as well. A normal return from `rename()` is now the
commit; the identity check runs only for an interrupt that lands after the
move, which `test_interrupt_after_the_move_never_revives_the_old_name`
still covers. The rename block's comments are condensed so profiles.py
stays under main's line count.

Suggested by unsupportedpastels (review m1 on e010934541). New guard
`test_rename_that_changes_the_directory_id_still_commits` fails without
the change.

fix(profiles): restore service on early interrupted rename

Extend the guarded rollback to backend/service shutdown, where Ctrl-C
previously left an unmoved profile with its s6 slot unregistered.
One focused regression covers the pre-unroute stop interruption.

Builds on kshitijk4poor's interrupted-rename commit e010934541b71be7a8c2a3a428ea935d475a7680.

(cherry picked from commit 77aeaae51df7e739238a14ecb7916d582825c534)

fix(profiles): an interrupted rename never leaves the profile hidden or doubled

Under a live multiplexer, `rename_profile` tombstones and unroutes the old
name, then waits up to 60 s for the gateway to release the home before it
moves the directory. Its undo ran only on `Exception`, and the tombstone
write and the rescan request sat outside the guarded block. Ctrl-C during
the owner wait or the rescan request (which waits up to 8 s on the gateway)
therefore left the untouched profile behind its tombstone: missing from
`hermes profile list`, `-p <name>` and `profile show` reported that it did
not exist, and the multiplexer stopped serving it. Recovery took a manual
`rm` of `profiles/.deleted/<name>`.

The tombstone-before-move protocol arrived in cd49c3badc (xielevi) and
a7254e2d4c (teknium1), both 2026-09-13, to fix #109267. Only the interrupt
path is new here.

The fix moves the unroute into the guarded block and settles it in a
`finally` keyed on the commit point: whether the directory now sits at the
new path, matched by inode, not on how the block exited.

- Not moved (an interrupt before the move, EXDEV, a racing writer
  that took the new name): clear the tombstone, re-serve the old name and
  re-register its service. This is the old failure handling, now run for
  interrupts too.
- Moved, even if an interrupt lands right after `rename()`: clear both
  tombstones and never re-serve or re-register the old name, so cleanup
  cannot bring a second identity back. Changing only the `except` to
  `BaseException` would undo a rename that already landed.

Normal failures and successful renames behave as before. The line count of
`profiles.py` is unchanged.

Regression guard `tests/hermes_cli/test_profile_rename_interrupt.py` covers
an interrupt during the unroute rescan, an interrupt during the owner wait,
a racing creator at the new name, and an interrupt right after the move.

  with a listed country's territories. Cloudflare's /cdn-cgi/trace loc=
  is looked up through the same proxy choice the Claude accounts use,
  once per distinct choice: at the start, when the network or a proxy
  changes, every 15 minutes, and on Check again. Never per request, and
  nothing without a Claude account. XX, T1, a failed or odd answer is

  line over the Providers list (egress.js, lazy) naming the region in
  the reader's language, with Check again (POST /api/egress/check), and

  says anything of bans or safety; no text goes to the vendor.

  claudeRegionHold): off by default. Cloudflare's loc can differ from
  what Anthropic sees: a rule-based proxy (Clash and the like) may send

  Unsupported must not stop anyone's requests. On, a Claude request whose
  way out last read Unsupported is held before any Claude Code starts

  looked up again first, a held try is failProxy so nobody rests. The

gateway: GET /v1/magpie/accounts lists every account and key, and X-Magpie-Account pins one by its id

@tmr11235 on X: a plugin that tests whether an account works could find
only the accounts /v1/magpie/quotas has a card for. API keys and ChatGPT
API accounts were missing.

GET /v1/magpie/accounts (accounts_list.go) lists each provider's
AccountIDs(): an account or a key, whether or not its vendor reports a
quota. Each entry has provider, id (a login id, or a key's KeyID
fingerprint), kind, label, user, plan, on and pin ("<provider>/<id>", the
form a gateway key's account list takes). No key, token or refresh token
is ever written. It is guarded like the quota routes: local or
LAN-with-key, read-only keys allowed (readOnlyRoutes), and a held key goes
through scopeQuotas and sees only the providers and accounts it may use.

The pin reuses X-Magpie-Account and pinTo, with no routing and no
failover, so the vendor's own error is the reply. pinTo now also takes the
listed pin or a bare id. pinTargets resolves it among the planned
providers; it reads logins.json, so it runs only when the header is sent.
pinnedBy matches an account by user and a key by its candidate's own
fingerprint, so a provider's only key that is on, which is planned under
the provider's id, can be pinned too. The 404's "its accounts are" list
now names keys as well.

Docs: docs/reference.md, docs/subsystems/provider-plugins.md, and the
en/zh/ja plugins pages (#pin).

accounts, ?provider=, no secret in the body, refused from the LAN without
a key), TestAccountPinnedByListedID (a refused key's 401 comes back and the
working key is not asked; the only key on, pinned by its fingerprint; a key
that is off is 404), TestAccountPinnedByLoginID. TestHeldKeyToldItsOwnQuotas
now checks the list per held key. TestLANGuard and TestHeldKeyToldNoAccounts
now cover the route.

plugin: a plugin is told which agent asked, here or through Remote magpie

@febsincos on X: a plugin on the magpie that serves a request couldn't
tell which agent it came from. The gateway knew (callerFrom, in the
request's context), but nothing reached the plugin, and on a magpie a
Remote magpie provider passes requests to, the agent ended at usage.

Now forwardOnce tells every plugin fetch the caller (tellCaller), as the
gateway records it, for a local agent and one passed on alike:

- fetch headers x-magpie-caller-agent (id), x-magpie-caller-name (the
  name people know it by, usage.AgentName) and x-magpie-caller-via (the
  computers it came through, comma-separated, the agent's first; none
  for an agent on this computer), each percent-encoded UTF-8;
- chat.headers gets them as input.caller = {agent, name, via}.
  input.agent stays OpenCode's "build", and OpenCode never sets caller,
  so a plugin that ignores it sees nothing different.

The headers are on host.js's MAGPIE_ONLY list, so unsaid() takes them
off whatever a plugin sends on: no vendor is told, and the vendor's
request is byte-for-byte the same whoever asked. A client's own
X-Magpie-Caller-* headers are dropped first.

For the whole chain, passOnCaller now sends X-Magpie-Via-Chain beside
X-Magpie-Via (the computers before, then this one). The receiving
magpie takes it only from a magpie's request, only when it begins with
X-Magpie-Via and each part is a label (at most catalog.MaxVia), else the
chain is X-Magpie-Via alone, as an older magpie sends (chainOf);
withCaller takes it off every request as it arrives.

gateway: run_code's script runs in a process of its own, ended at its time or memory

run_code ran the agent's script in goja inside magpie. Its 50s limit
was vm.Interrupt, and its 512 MB limit a watcher that interrupted too,
but goja checks an interrupt only between its own instructions: a
builtin is Go and runs to its end. A model (or a prompt injected
through a tool's result, or anyone with a gateway key) could:

- return "x".repeat(3e9).length: 3 GB allocated at once in magpie's
  heap before the watcher could look (on the old code it returns
  3000000000 after ~11s on Linux; larger counts OOM-kill magpie);
- /^(a+)+$(?!x)/.test("a".repeat(40)+"b"): backtracks for ever,
  pins a core, and the request never returns, since RunProgram is
  synchronous and never sees the interrupt;
- the same with [].indexOf over length 4e9.

Now the script runs in `magpie run-code-helper` (internal/coderun,
dispatched first thing in cli.Main, before any setup; it reads and
writes no file). The gateway sends the script, tool names and limits
as JSON lines on stdin and serves each tool call the helper asks for
(still hubCallNamed + hubCall + logMCPCall, call limit enforced on
both sides). The helper interrupts itself at Wait as before, so a
normal timeout keeps its logs; it exits itself (3) when its heap is
512 MB over its start; the gateway kills it 2s past Wait whatever it
is doing, and cancels any call still running. The goja engine moved
unchanged from hub_code.go to coderun/script.go. proc.CommandContext
starts it (hidden window on Windows, process tree ended).

Test: TestHubCodeBuiltinsEndWithTheirProcess runs the three scripts
above with Wait 2s, each must come back an error within 10s and grow
the test process's heap by under 256 MB. Red on the old code
(WSL, repeat took 11.1s and returned the length); green with the fix.

mcp router: code mode, one run_code tool that calls several tools and gives back only its result

The router lists one more tool, run_code, beside its servers' tools and
says so in its instructions. Its code is the body of an async function
run in goja: each tool is an async function on `tools` by its
<server>__<tool> name, a tool's error is thrown, and only what the code
returns and console.logs reaches the model. So a loop over five cities,
or Promise.all over search results, is one tool call, and the long
replies never enter the context.

- hub_code.go: the event loop, 8 calls at a time, at most 100 calls and
  50s a script, a 512MB heap guard and a 2000-deep call stack. No
  require, import, fetch, files or timers. A call resolves as call_tool
  does (a known server passes an unknown tool through, else a unique
  case-insensitive name), keeps to the agent's own tools, and is a
  request-log row of its own beside run_code's.
- The Library's MCP router card has a Code mode row under Tools on
  demand, on by default (settings.RouterNoCode turns it off; KeepOwn,
  the settings save and servers/hub-code keep it), in five languages.

usage: a pairing's set of message ids holds only the ids whose hash slot is shared

visibleLocal put every Claude message id of the period in one map to find
the ones written again, ~24 MB for ~1M ids on the owner's history: the
largest single thing a page's open held, and kept as scratch for 30 s
after. A first pass now marks each id's hash slot in a bit set (8 bits an
id), and the slots marked twice in a second. An id whose slot was marked
once is the only id with that slot, so it repeats nothing and never goes
in the map; only the rest do, and the map holds a few percent of them.
What is left out is exactly what the full set left out. A settled chunk's
ids are read once into one list for both passes, not decoded twice.

library: Pi gets the Library's environment variables, from an extension magpie writes

@norcleeh on X: "magpie咋还不能给pi agent管理自定义环境变量？" Pi now sits
in Library > Environment variables beside Claude Code and Codex, with no
setup.

Pi has no settings field for environment variables (its
docs/environment-variables.md lists only what Pi reads itself), so magpie
uses the closest route Pi offers: an extension. Pi loads every .ts in
<agent dir>/extensions/ by itself, and magpie writes
extensions/magpie-env.ts there. As Pi loads, it sets each variable in
process.env unless the variable is already set, and Pi's bash tool spawns
commands with process.env (getShellEnv in dist/utils/shell.js), so they
get the values.

- The file's first line marks it as magpie's. A magpie-env.ts without
  that line is the user's: it is reported as one problem and left alone.
- syncEnv's rules hold as for Claude and Codex. A value the file already
  has, or one the user edited after magpie wrote it, is theirs and is
  never written over or removed. Unticking Pi takes out only magpie's
  values. The file is removed with its last variable, and the user's
  other extensions are untouched.
- Values are JSON-encoded on one line (quotes, backticks, ${}, newlines,
  U+2028 and </script> round-trip; no raw U+2028 is written).
- Pi in WSL stays greyed, as Codex and Claude are there.

cli: magpie library project plugin turns a plugin on or off for one project

jinpwng on X (v0.1.4599) sets up three machines from the CLI. The GUI's
Library can turn a plugin on or off for one project, and the project CLI
could not. This adds:

  magpie library project plugin [list] <dir> [--json]
  magpie library project plugin on|add <dir> <plugin…> [agents=a,b…]
  magpie library project plugin off|rm <dir> <plugin…>

It makes the same two calls as the project card's Plugins chips:
- library.ProjectPlugin ("projects/plugin") for a library plugin, which
  goes to its agents;
- library.ProjectClaudePlugin ("projects/claude-plugin") for a plugin
  Claude Code installed itself. That one is named name@marketplace, or by
  its name alone when only one installed plugin has it, and is turned on
  in <dir>/.claude/settings.local.json.

A library plugin's name wins over a bare Claude Code name. With no
agents=, a library plugin goes to the agents the project's plugins are
already for, or else to every agent here that reads a plugin's part in a
project.

Every name, agent and flag is checked before anything is written. Each
of these is refused with nothing written:
- an unknown plugin;
- a name more than one Claude Code plugin has;
- any -flag, or a k=v other than agents=;
- an agent that reads none of a project's parts;
- agents= other than claude for a Claude Code plugin;
- off for a plugin the project doesn't have on.
--help prints usage. A plugin the view reports as not written prints its
reason and exits 1.

library: OpenClaw takes MCP servers and the MCP router (@JeffreyCalm on X)

OpenClaw had no Library target, so Library -> MCP had no switch for it,
and the router couldn't be turned on there. OpenClaw 2026.11.6 reads MCP
servers from openclaw.json's mcp.servers. Its schema is strict: an
unknown key such as timeout, type or toolFilter.allow fails the whole
config. So the new fmtOpenClaw writes only keys OpenClaw accepts:
- remote servers: url, transport (streamable-http or sse) and headers;
- local servers: command, args and env;
- requestTimeoutMs for magpie's own long servers (its default is 60s).
The transport is written for every remote server, because OpenClaw
treats a url with no transport as SSE. Keys the user set themselves are
left alone: toolFilter, requestTimeoutMs, auth, enabled and the rest.
OpenClaw fails the whole file on an unset ${VAR}, so it gets no env
refs.

Image generation and built-in search (2nd half of the report): magpie
wires OpenClaw as openai-completions. OpenClaw's native OpenAI web
search applies only to direct OpenAI traffic, and image_generate needs
an image provider configured in OpenClaw. The gateway drops nothing.
With this target, Magpie Image and Magpie Web Search can now be given to
OpenClaw as MCP servers. Native wiring is #7334. Refs #5897.

@gptchan404 on X: magpie wrapped a vendor's error in its own words, e.g.

  magpie: claude-opus-5-5 refused this request (safety filter:
  content_policy_rejected) via Factory — <the plugin's advice>

(provider.VendorWords), then (HTTP status, code, request id), each
left out when the words already hold it. magpie's own notes go on a
second line that starts "magpie: ". A plugin's advice after " — " goes
on magpie's line (pluginWords). The vendor's JSON error fields
(type/code/param/request_id) still pass through as before
(writeVendorErrorFrom).

whole and streamed, for any vendor error (writeVendorErrorFrom ->
upstreamTold) and for a safety-filter refusal no one else answered
(failTo -> refusalTold).

keep magpie's reading, because the rest scope, the rate hold, the

gateway: a reading that finds a vendor-timed quota rest's window renewed has the vendor asked once

RookieRicardoR on X: a GLM Coding Plan key ran out, they used a reset
card (重置卡) on Zhipu's side, and magpie kept answering "limit reached"
without asking Zhipu. Zhipu's 1308/1310 names the reset time, so the key
rests by "resets" till it and timedHeld answers every request locally.
Since #2718 a reading that finds the window less than full (renewed)
doesn't lift a rest the vendor timed, only a window truly started again
(restarted) does, because a vendor's usage can read low while its
refusal stands. A reset bought on the vendor's side moves neither, so it
was never noticed before the named time.

Now liftRests, on renewal, lets such a hold go once for its named time
(askOnRenewalLocked: askAt = now, the rest itself kept, recorded in
restingUntil.renewAsked). The next request asks the vendor: an answer
clears the rest as any answer does; refused again with the same time,
it is held till then whatever later readings say, so #2718's repeated
refusals don't come back. This applies to every provider whose windows
magpie reads (Zhipu/Z.ai plan quota, sub2api balance URLs, subscriptions)
and to quota and credit rests, not rate rests. Where no windows are
read, the rest line's "Try now" (Unrest) already asks at once.

The same tweet said the same prompt from Pi got Claude Code's earlier
DeepSeek reply word for word. magpie keeps no reply to give a later
request (classify caches routing verdicts, vision_cache image
descriptions, prev_response rebuilds input; held answers are errors
only), and magpie sets no temperature or seed for DeepSeek.
TestSameRequestIsAskedEveryTime now holds that: the same bytes from
Claude Code's and an OpenAI client's protocol, twice each, reach the
vendor four times and get its four answers.

  an existing copy; one that can't be made stops the write), then writes
  magpie's shape.
